cards.front:
NOHKALIKAI FALLS, often cited as India's tallest plunge waterfall, is located in:

(A) Meghalaya (Cherrapunji region)
(B) Arunachal Pradesh easternmost area
(C) Sikkim's eastern Himalayan region
(D) Manipur in northeast hill state
cards.back:
(A) Meghalaya (Cherrapunji region)

Rivers & Water Bodies — NOHKALIKAI FALLS — INDIA's TALLEST PLUNGE (single-drop) WATERFALL at ~340 m (1,115 ft). Located in MEGHALAYA, near CHERRAPUNJI (Sohra), East Khasi Hills district. Cherrapunji is famous for being one of the WETTEST PLACES on EARTH (~11,777 mm annual rainfall). LEGEND: 'Nohkalikai' = 'jump of Likai' in Khasi — local legend tells of a woman 'Likai' who, after horror of finding out her infant was unintentionally killed, leaped from the cliff. SOURCE: small mountain stream; almost dries in winter (December-March), but FULL during monsoon (June-September). NEARBY: (1) MAWSMAI CAVES — limestone caves. (2) DAINTHLEN FALLS — another fall in the area. (3) NOHSNGITHIANG (Seven Sisters Falls) — 315 m, also in same area. (4) MAWSYNRAM (16 km from Cherrapunji) — wettest place in India by some measures (11,873 mm/yr, beating Cherrapunji's 11,777). MEGHALAYA = 'abode of clouds' in Sanskrit. STATE TRIVIA: capital SHILLONG ('Scotland of the East'). UMIAM LAKE near Shillong. LIVING ROOTS BRIDGES of Cherrapunji — UNESCO heritage natural engineering marvels. PYQ FREQUENCY: Meghalaya-rainfall-waterfall MCQs in SSC, UPSC.

(2) DAINTHLEN FALLS — another fall in the area. (3) NOHSNGITHIANG (Seven Sisters Falls) — 315 m, also in same area. (4) MAWSYNRAM (16 km from Cherrapunji) — wettest place in India by some measures (11,873 mm/yr, beating Cherrapunji's 11,777). MEGHALAYA = 'abode of clouds' in Sanskrit. STATE TRIVIA: capital SHILLONG ('Scotland of the East'). UMIAM LAKE near Shillong. LIVING ROOTS BRIDGES of Cherrapunji — UNESCO heritage natural engineering marvels. PYQ FREQUENCY: Meghalaya-rainfall-waterfall MCQs in SSC, UPSC.

cards.front:
Which state hosts the SHIVANASAMUDRA Falls, used for India's earliest hydropower project?

(A) Karnataka (Kaveri river falls)
(B) Tamil Nadu also on Kaveri now
(C) Andhra Pradesh on Krishna here
(D) Kerala on Periyar river bend
cards.back:
(A) Karnataka (Kaveri river falls)

Rivers & Water Bodies — SHIVANASAMUDRA FALLS — on the KAVERI RIVER in MANDYA district, KARNATAKA. SEGMENTED INTO TWO: (1) GAGANACHUKKI (left/west) and (2) BHARACHUKKI (right/east) — Kaveri SPLITS around Shivanasamudra ISLAND, then both branches re-merge downstream. HEIGHT: ~98 m. HYDROPOWER HISTORY: HOUSE OF MYSORE (Wodeyars) commissioned the SHIVANASAMUDRA HYDROELECTRIC PROJECT in 1902 — INDIA's FIRST major hydroelectric power plant; transmitted power to KOLAR GOLD FIELDS (147 km away) — at the time, the LONGEST high-voltage transmission in the world. POWER OUTPUT today: ~42 MW. ENGINEER: Sir M. VISVESVARAYA (1860-1962) — the legendary Indian engineer; later DIWAN of MYSORE. He's the namesake of ENGINEER'S DAY (15 September, his birthday). KAVERI WATERFALLS RANKING: (1) Shivanasamudra ~98 m (Karnataka). (2) Hogenakkal ~20 m (KA-TN border). (3) various rapids upstream. KOLAR GOLD FIELDS: closed permanently in 2001 after deep mining became unprofitable. SHIVANASAMUDRA TODAY: ~3-hour drive from Bengaluru; popular weekend destination + photographer's haven. PYQ ANGLE: Shivanasamudra-first-hydropower link in UPSC, KAS, SSC — 1× per cycle.

The LONGEST river in India is:

(B) Ganga
(C) Godavari

cards.back:

The source of the GANGA is:

Which of the following rivers FLOWS WESTWARD and drains into the Arabian Sea?

The SUNDARBANS delta is formed by the joining of which rivers?

Which Himalayan river is NOT a tributary of the Ganga?

cards.front:
The GANGA originates at which glacier, and what is its traditional name at the origin point?

(A) Siachen Glacier; Shyok
(B) Gangotri Glacier (Gomukh)
(C) Yamunotri Glacier; Yamuna
(D) Milam Glacier; Gori
cards.back:
(B) Gangotri Glacier (Gomukh)

Rivers & Water Bodies — BHAGIRATHI — emerges from GAUMUKH ('Cow's Mouth') — the snout of GANGOTRI GLACIER (30 km long, Uttarkashi district, Uttarakhand, ~3892 m altitude). Called BHAGIRATHI until it meets the ALAKNANDA (from Satopanth Glacier) at DEVPRAYAG — after that, it's called GANGA. Alaknanda's tributaries: Dhauliganga, Nandakini, Pindar, Mandakini, Bhagirathi itself — together the 'Panch Prayag' (5 confluences): Vishnuprayag, Nandaprayag, Karnaprayag, Rudraprayag, Devprayag. The Ganga traverses 2,525 km through 5 states (Uttarakhand, UP, Bihar, Jharkhand, WB) + Bangladesh (as Padma-Jamuna) → Bay of Bengal. World's most sacred river in Hinduism + world's 3rd-largest river by discharge to ocean. NATIONAL RIVER since 2008.

The YAMUNA — longest tributary of the Ganga — originates from which glacier?

(A) Gangotri Glacier
(B) Yamunotri Glacier
(C) Milam Glacier
(D) Pindari Glacier
cards.back:
(B) Yamunotri Glacier

Rivers & Water Bodies — YAMUNA (~1,376 km — India's LONGEST Ganga tributary) originates from YAMUNOTRI GLACIER near BANDERPOOCH Peak (~6,316m, Uttarakhand Himalayas), ~6,400m elevation. Yamunotri Temple (one of 4 Char Dham sites of Uttarakhand — others: Gangotri, Kedarnath, Badrinath). Main tributaries: TONS (largest, from Har-ki-Dun), GIRI, HINDON, CHAMBAL, SIND, BETWA, KEN. Flows through Haryana (Delhi at Yamuna's bank), UP. Meets GANGA at PRAYAGRAJ (formerly Allahabad) — TRIVENI SANGAM (Yamuna + Ganga + mythical Saraswati). Major cities on Yamuna: Yamunanagar (Haryana), Delhi, Mathura, Agra (Taj Mahal on its bank), Etawah, Kanpur area. Heavily polluted by Delhi and Agra. Chambal is surprisingly the CLEANEST of its tributaries (flows through ravines, less human settlement). near Champasar, Uttarakhand.

cards.front:
The BRAHMAPUTRA's origin in Tibet has a local name. What is it?

(A) Tsangpo / Yarlung Tsangpo
(B) Sutlej / Langchen Zangbo
(C) Indus / Sengge Zangbo
(D) Kosi / Tamakoshi
cards.back:
(A) Tsangpo / Yarlung Tsangpo

Rivers & Water Bodies — BRAHMAPUTRA rises near Mt Kailash/Lake Manasarovar on the Tibetan Plateau (south Tibet) as the YARLUNG TSANGPO. Flows ~1,700 km east through Tibet, then takes a sharp U-turn ('THE GREAT BEND' around Namcha Barwa peak — deepest canyon in world), enters Arunachal Pradesh as SIANG/DIHANG. At Kobo village, joined by LOHIT + DIBANG → becomes BRAHMAPUTRA. Flows westward through Assam (1,000+ km), then south into Bangladesh as JAMUNA, meets Padma (Ganga), then MEGHNA (combined flow), → Bay of Bengal. Total length 2,900 km. World's 9th-longest river, 4th by discharge. Majuli (world's largest RIVER ISLAND) is in the Brahmaputra near Jorhat, Assam. Indus-Yarlung Tsangpo all rise in the same Kailash-Manasarovar region.

cards.front:
The INDUS RIVER SYSTEM, under the 1960 Indus Waters Treaty, allocates EASTERN rivers (Sutlej, Beas, Ravi) to India and WESTERN rivers (Indus, Jhelum, Chenab) to Pakistan. Which river passes through Ladakh and Kashmir before entering Pakistan?

(A) Sutlej
(B) Indus
(C) Ravi
(D) Beas
cards.back:
(B) Indus

Rivers & Water Bodies — INDUS SYSTEM (5 Punjab rivers + Indus main = PUNJ-AB = 'land of 5 rivers'). INDUS (Sengge Zangbo in Tibetan) rises near Mt Kailash, flows through LADAKH (Leh on its bank) and across the GILGIT-BALTISTAN region (Pak-occupied), through Pakistan to Arabian Sea. INDUS WATERS TREATY 1960 (signed by Nehru + Ayub Khan, mediated by World Bank): Eastern Rivers (SUTLEJ, BEAS, RAVI) to INDIA for unrestricted use; Western Rivers (INDUS, JHELUM, CHENAB) to PAKISTAN. India can use western rivers for limited purposes (domestic, non-consumptive, some hydroelectric). Has survived THREE Indo-Pak wars. Sutlej rises in Rakshastal (Tibet); Beas rises in Rohtang Pass (HP); Ravi rises in HP near Bara Banghal; Chenab formed from Chandra + Bhaga (Lahaul HP); Jhelum rises from Verinag (Kashmir). All meet eventually to form Indus. main stream.

cards.front:
The 'SORROW OF BIHAR' — notorious for causing annual floods — is which river?

(A) Gandak
(B) Kosi (Koshi)
(C) Mahananda
(D) Son
cards.back:
(B) Kosi (Koshi)

Rivers & Water Bodies — KOSI RIVER — left-bank tributary of the Ganga. Called 'SORROW OF BIHAR' because of its frequent floods — historical records show the Kosi has shifted its course westward by over 120 km in the last 250 years. Origin: Nepal (tributaries: Sun Kosi, Arun, Tamur — all from high Himalayas — convergence called Sapta Kosi, 7 Kosis). Famous 2008 Kosi embankment breach — 3 million displaced. Other rivers with similar 'sorrow' nicknames: DAMODAR — 'Sorrow of BENGAL' (before Damodar Valley Corporation dams tamed it 1948); BRAHMAPUTRA — 'Sorrow of Assam' (though unofficial) due to major annual floods. HWANG HO (YELLOW RIVER, China) = 'Sorrow of China'. Kosi Barrage controls some flow; Kosi High Dam proposed in Nepal but delayed. Kosi brings huge sediment load from Himalayas.

cards.front:
Which of the following is a LEFT-BANK tributary of the Ganga (i.e., joins from the north side)?

(A) Yamuna
(B) Ghaghra (Karnali)
(C) Son
(D) Chambal
cards.back:
(B) Ghaghra (Karnali)

Rivers & Water Bodies — GANGA tributaries by bank: LEFT-BANK (Himalayan, north side): Ramganga, GHAGHRA (Karnali in Nepal — main left tributary, longest tributary by discharge), Gandak (Gandaki), Kosi, Mahananda. RIGHT-BANK (Peninsular, south side): Yamuna (largest by total contribution including its own tribs), Chambal, Betwa, Son, Damodar. Left-bank tributaries originate in the HIMALAYAS (via Nepal); right-bank from the Peninsular Plateau. This is the classic 'comb' pattern of Ganga basin drainage. Ghaghra is the LARGEST LEFT-BANK tributary of Ganga by volume. Son is the LARGEST RIGHT-BANK tributary by length from Peninsular India (southern plateau).

cards.front:
The SUTLEJ river — 1,500 km long, easternmost of the 'five Punjab rivers' — originates from:

(A) Gangotri Glacier
(B) Lake Rakshastal
(C) Pir Panjal range
(D) Manimahesh Lake, HP
cards.back:
(B) Lake Rakshastal

Rivers & Water Bodies — SUTLEJ (LANGQEN ZANGBO in Tibetan = 'Elephant River') — originates from RAKSHASTAL ('Demon Lake'), near the sacred MANASAROVAR lake in Tibet. Flows westward through Himachal Pradesh (entering via Shipki La pass), then Punjab. Joins BEAS near Harike Wetlands — then joined by CHENAB near Uch (Pakistan) to form PANJNAD ('5 rivers together' in Persian) which joins the INDUS. The BHAKRA DAM — one of India's tallest dams (226 m, gravity dam — 2nd highest in Asia) — is on the Sutlej, HP. Creates GOBIND SAGAR reservoir. India's Sutlej-Yamuna Link (SYL) canal is a contentious irrigation project between Punjab and Haryana. Indus Waters Treaty 1960 gave full Sutlej rights to India. near Lake Manasarovar, Tibet.

cards.front:
The FARAKKA BARRAGE (1975) on the Ganga river, at the West Bengal-Bangladesh border, was built to:

(A) Generate hydroelectric power
(B) Divert Ganga waters into the Bhagirathi-Hooghly system to flush Kolkata port silt
(C) Support canal irrigation in Bihar
(D) Create a flood buffer for Assam
cards.back:
(B) Divert Ganga waters into the Bhagirathi-Hooghly system to flush Kolkata port silt

Rivers & Water Bodies — FARAKKA BARRAGE (Murshidabad district, West Bengal, ~17 km from Bangladesh border) — operational 1975. PRIMARY PURPOSE: divert ~40,000 cusecs of Ganga waters into the 38-km Farakka feeder canal → BHAGIRATHI-HOOGHLY river, to flush sediment from KOLKATA (CALCUTTA) PORT (the Hooghly was silting, threatening port viability). Bangladesh objected that reduced Ganga flow would damage its deltaic ecology (Sundarbans etc.) — INDO-BANGLADESH GANGES WATER TREATY signed 1996 for 30 years (equitable sharing of dry-season water). Other major barrages: TEESTA (WB), SARDA on Sharda River, GANDAK (Valmiki Nagar, Bihar-Nepal border). Hirakud is a DAM not barrage. BARRAGE = low-height gated structure to regulate flow; DAM = taller, stores water.

cards.front:
The TEHRI DAM — India's TALLEST dam — is on which Himalayan river?

(A) Alaknanda
(B) Bhagirathi
(C) Kosi
(D) Gandak
cards.back:
(B) Bhagirathi

Rivers & Water Bodies — TEHRI DAM (Uttarakhand, at Tehri town where the Bhagirathi + Bhilangna rivers meet) — India's TALLEST dam at 260.5 m. Type: earth-and-rockfill embankment. Built 1978-2006 (long delay due to protests — Sunderlal Bahuguna led anti-Tehri movement on environmental + cultural grounds; Old Tehri town was submerged). Capacity: ~3.55 km³. Power: 1000 MW (being expanded with Tehri Pumped Storage Plant — 1000 MW more). BHAKRA (SUTLEJ, HP — 226m, concrete gravity) and IDUKKI (PERIYAR, KERALA — 168m, double-curvature arch) are also notable for height. KARAPUZHA DAM (Kerala) = smallest. LONGEST DAM: HIRAKUD (Mahanadi, Odisha, 25.8 km main+dykes — world's longest earthen dam). cards.front:
Major Himalayan rivers by length (in India or partially in India). Arrange from LONGEST to SHORTEST: (1) Indus, (2) Brahmaputra, (3) Ganga, (4) Sutlej

(A) Brahmaputra > Ganga > Indus > Sutlej
(B) Brahmaputra > Indus > Ganga > Sutlej
(C) Ganga > Brahmaputra > Sutlej > Indus
(D) Indus > Brahmaputra > Ganga > Sutlej
cards.back:
(B) Brahmaputra > Indus > Ganga > Sutlej

Rivers & Water Bodies — Major Himalayan rivers TOTAL length (including portions outside India): BRAHMAPUTRA ~2,900 km (in India ~1,800 km; originates Tibet, India, Bangladesh). INDUS ~3,180 km (most in Pakistan after Partition — only ~700 km in India through Ladakh). GANGA ~2,525 km (entirely in India + Bangladesh as Padma — largest catchment in India). SUTLEJ ~1,500 km (in India ~1,050 km). So by total length: Indus (3180) > Brahmaputra (2900) > Ganga (2525) > Sutlej (1500). But by Indian length: Ganga (2525) > Brahmaputra (1800) > Sutlej (1050) > Indus (700). LONGEST RIVER within India: GANGA. Longest river ORIGINATING in India: MAHANADI (fully in India). Longest peninsular river: GODAVARI (1,465 km, 'Dakshin Ganga'). Longest WESTWARD river: NARMADA (1,312 km).

cards.front:
Which is the LONGEST Peninsular river of India, flowing through six states and emptying into the Bay of Bengal?

(A) Krishna
(B) Godavari
(C) Cauvery
(D) Mahanadi
cards.back:
(B) Godavari

Rivers & Water Bodies — GODAVARI (1465 km) is the LONGEST Peninsular river and 2nd longest in India overall (after the Ganga). Called 'Dakshin Ganga' (Southern Ganges). Source: Triyambakeshwar (Nashik district, Maharashtra, Western Ghats). Flows E/SE through Maharashtra, Telangana, AP (and touches MP, CG, Odisha in catchment) → Bay of Bengal at Antarvedi (Andhra delta). Tributaries: Manjira, Wainganga, Pranhita, Indravati, Sabari. Rank of peninsular rivers by length: Godavari (1465) > Krishna (1400) > Mahanadi (851) > Cauvery (800) > Narmada (1312 westward) > Tapi (724 westward). Narmada is longer than Cauvery/Mahanadi but flows WESTWARD into the Arabian Sea.

cards.front:
Which of the following peninsular rivers flows WESTWARD into the Arabian Sea (not eastward into Bay of Bengal)?

(A) Krishna
(B) Cauvery
(C) Narmada
(D) Mahanadi
cards.back:
(C) Narmada

Rivers & Water Bodies — Most peninsular rivers flow EASTWARD (due to the gentle eastern slope of the Deccan Plateau) — Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, Cauvery. Only a few flow WESTWARD into the Arabian Sea: NARMADA (longest westward-flowing, 1312 km; source Amarkantak MP; flows through a RIFT VALLEY between Vindhya & Satpura ranges; NO delta — forms an estuary at Gulf of Khambhat near Bharuch Gujarat); TAPI / TAPTI (724 km, second-longest westward; source Multai MP; parallel to Narmada; also rift valley through Satpura; estuary at Surat Guj); SABARMATI (Rajasthan→Gujarat, Gandhi's ashram on its banks at Ahmedabad); MAHI (MP→Guj); LUNI (Thar, ends in Rann of Kutch). Western Ghats coastal streams (Bharatpuzha, Periyar, Netravati) also flow west.

cards.front:
The Cauvery river originates in which hill range, and which three states does it primarily flow through?

(A) Nilgiri Hills; Kerala, Karnataka, TN
(B) Brahmagiri Hills (Western Ghats); Karnataka, TN, Puducherry
(C) Satpura Hills; Maharashtra, MP, AP
(D) Eastern Ghats; AP, TN, Kerala
cards.back:
(B) Brahmagiri Hills (Western Ghats); Karnataka, TN, Puducherry

Rivers & Water Bodies — CAUVERY (~800 km) originates at TALAKAVERI in the BRAHMAGIRI HILLS (Western Ghats) in Kodagu (Coorg) district, KARNATAKA. Flows primarily through Karnataka, Tamil Nadu — enters Bay of Bengal near POOMPUHAR (TN) + Karaikal (Puducherry). Small catchment in Kerala (Wayanad) too. Major tributaries: Harangi, Hemavati, Shimsha, Arkavati, Kabini (from Kerala), Bhavani (Nilgiris), Noyyal, Amaravati. Famous dams: Krishna Raja Sagar (KA, near Mysuru), Mettur / Stanley Reservoir (TN). Water dispute (CAUVERY DISPUTE) between KA-TN-Kerala-Puducherry is one of India's oldest — CWDT 2007 award, SC settlement 2018. Cauvery is sacred; its delta in TN is called the 'Rice Bowl of South India'.

cards.front:
The Krishna river originates in Maharashtra (Western Ghats). Its main tributary, the largest by discharge, is:

(A) Bhima
(B) Tungabhadra
(C) Koyna
(D) Ghataprabha
cards.back:
(B) Tungabhadra

Rivers & Water Bodies — KRISHNA (~1400 km, 2nd-longest peninsular) originates at MAHABALESHWAR (Maharashtra, Western Ghats) and flows through Maharashtra, Karnataka, Telangana, AP → Bay of Bengal near Vijayawada/Machilipatnam. Major tributaries: TUNGABHADRA (formed by union of Tunga and Bhadra in Karnataka; largest by water volume — joins Krishna at Alampur), BHIMA (longest tributary — rises in Bhimashankar Maha), KOYNA (major dam), GHATAPRABHA, MALAPRABHA, MUSI (flows through Hyderabad), MUSI. Famous dams: Nagarjuna Sagar (Telangana-AP — world's largest masonry dam; multi-purpose), Srisailam, Almatti (KA), Tungabhadra (KA-AP). Nagarjunasagar-Srisailam is also India's largest tiger reserve.

cards.front:
The Mahanadi river, with the Hirakud Dam — the world's LONGEST EARTHEN DAM — flows primarily through which state?

(A) Chhattisgarh
(B) Odisha
(C) Jharkhand
(D) Andhra Pradesh
cards.back:
(B) Odisha

Rivers & Water Bodies — MAHANADI (~851 km) rises at Sihawa, Dhamtari district, CHHATTISGARH, but flows primarily through Odisha (empties into Bay of Bengal via its delta at Paradip). HIRAKUD DAM (Sambalpur district, Odisha, 1956) — built across Mahanadi. Length ~25.8 km (main + dykes) — world's longest EARTHEN / earth-and-concrete composite dam. Also India's first major post-independence multi-purpose river valley project. Main Mahanadi tributaries: Seonath, Ong, Jonk, Hasdeo, Ib, Mand, Tel. Mahanadi delta hosts the CHILIKA LAKE (via distributaries) and the BHITARKANIKA mangroves. Historically called 'Mahan' (great) + 'Nadi' (river).

cards.front:
The Narmada and Tapi rivers flow through rift valleys between which two mountain ranges?

(A) Himalayas and Vindhya
(B) Vindhya and Satpura
(C) Satpura and Western Ghats
(D) Aravalli and Vindhya
cards.back:
(B) Vindhya and Satpura

Rivers & Water Bodies — Both NARMADA and TAPI flow westward through RIFT VALLEYS — a block faulted down (graben) between two parallel ranges. NARMADA is between the VINDHYA range (north) and SATPURA range (south). TAPI is south of the Satpura range — technically between the Satpura (north) and the Gawilgarh Hills / Ajanta Hills (south). Both rivers flow ~parallel to each other. This rift-valley origin is WHY they DON'T form deltas (rift-valley topography gives straight confined flow) — they form ESTUARIES at the Gulf of Khambhat (Narmada at Bharuch, Tapi at Surat). Vindhya also marks the TRADITIONAL DIVIDE between North and South India.

cards.front:
The LUNI river, India's only river of the arid Thar desert, originates in the Aravalli Hills and ends in which water body?

(A) Gulf of Khambhat
(B) Rann of Kutch
(C) Arabian Sea near Porbandar
(D) Sambhar Lake
cards.back:
(B) Rann of Kutch

Rivers & Water Bodies — LUNI ('Lavanavati' = 'salty river' due to its saline waters from the region) originates from Pushkar Valley in Ajmer district (Aravalli Hills) at ~550m elevation, flows ~495 km south-west through southern Rajasthan (Pali, Jodhpur, Barmer districts), and DISAPPEARS into the RANN OF KUTCH marshlands (Gujarat) — never reaches the sea. Seasonal/ephemeral flow — heavy during monsoon, dry most of the year. Other Thar desert rivers: GHAGGAR (proposed ancient Saraswati river), Krishnavati, Jojari, Bandi. Sambhar Lake (Raj) is India's largest inland saline lake — tributaries Mendha, Kharian, Rupangarh drain into it but Luni doesn't touch Sambhar. disappears into the marshlands.

The largest freshwater lake in India by area is:

(A) Chilika (Odisha)
(B) Wular Lake (Jammu & Kashmir)
(C) Loktak (Manipur)

Chilika (Odisha) is the largest LAGOON / brackish-water lake (1,165 km²). Vembanad (Kerala) is the longest lake (96 km), used for the famous Nehru Trophy snake-boat race. cards.front:
The world's deepest freshwater lake — containing about 22% of Earth's surface freshwater — is:

(A) Lake Superior
(B) Lake Baikal (Russia)
(C) Lake Tanganyika
(D) Caspian Sea
cards.back:
(B) Lake Baikal (Russia)

Rivers & Water Bodies — Lake Baikal — Siberia, Russia. Maximum depth 1,642 m (~1.6 km — deepest freshwater lake). Holds ~23,615 km³ water = ~22% of world's surface freshwater. UNESCO WHS 1996. ~25 million years old (oldest existing lake). Endemic species — Baikal seal (Pusa sibirica), the only freshwater seal. Caspian Sea is the largest lake (by area, 371,000 km²) but is brackish. Tanganyika — 2nd deepest (1,470 m) and 2nd by volume. Superior is the largest by surface area among freshwater lakes (82,000 km²).

cards.front:
An 'oxbow lake' is formed by:

(A) Glacial erosion
(B) A meandering river that gets cut off when the meander loop is severed
(C) Volcanic crater filling with rainwater
(D) Tectonic subsidence
cards.back:
(B) A meandering river that gets cut off when the meander loop is severed

Rivers & Water Bodies — Oxbow lake — crescent-shaped (named for the U-bend of an ox's yoke). Formation: a river meander loops tighter and tighter; eventually the river cuts a new direct channel across the neck of the loop; the abandoned bend becomes a still-water U-shaped lake. Common on flat floodplains — Ganga, Brahmaputra, Ravi all have many oxbow lakes. Glacial lakes (cirque, tarn) form by glacier carving; crater lakes by volcanic activity (e.g. Lonar Lake, Maharashtra, ~50,000 yrs old, formed by meteorite impact in basalt).

cards.front:
Lonar Lake — a circular saline-soda lake of meteoritic origin, ~50,000 years old, is in:

(A) Tamil Nadu
(B) Maharashtra (Buldhana district)
(C) Madhya Pradesh
(D) Karnataka
cards.back:
(B) Maharashtra (Buldhana district)

Rivers & Water Bodies — Lonar Lake — Buldhana district, Maharashtra. Formed by a meteorite impact in basalt rock ~52,000 years ago — making it the only known hypervelocity impact crater in basalt on Earth. Diameter ~1.2 km; maximum depth 137 m. Both saline AND alkaline (a rare combination). Declared a Ramsar site in 2020. Near Aurangabad — about 175 km. Geologically and astrobiologically significant; ISRO and NASA have studied the site.

cards.front:
The largest lake in the world by area (though technically a lake, sometimes called a sea) is:

(A) Lake Superior
(B) Caspian Sea
(C) Lake Victoria
(D) Lake Baikal
cards.back:
(B) Caspian Sea

Rivers & Water Bodies — Caspian Sea — endorheic (no outlet), 371,000 km² — bordered by 5 countries (Russia, Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan, Iran, Azerbaijan). Brackish. Often called a 'sea' because of its size and salt content (~1.2%, about a third of seawater). Lake Superior is the largest FRESHWATER lake by area (82,100 km²). Lake Victoria — Africa, 2nd largest freshwater by area (68,800 km²); Tanganyika — 2nd longest. The 'lake vs sea' status of the Caspian was settled by the 2018 Convention as a 'special status' body, neither fully sea nor fully lake.

The Tso Lhamo / Tso Lhamu Lake — claimed to be one of the highest lakes in the world (~5,330 m) — is in:

(A) Ladakh
(B) Sikkim (North district, near Tibetan border)
(C) Himachal Pradesh

cards.back:

cards.front:
The NARMADA + TAPI rivers are unique because they:

(A) Originate in Western Ghats and flow east
(B) Flow WEST into Arabian Sea (rift valleys)
(C) Are the only rain-fed rivers in India
(D) Rise from Himalayan glaciers and flow south
cards.back:
(B) Flow WEST into Arabian Sea (rift valleys)

Rivers & Water Bodies — Most peninsular rivers flow EAST into Bay of Bengal (because Western Ghats are higher → eastern slope is gentler). Exceptions: NARMADA + TAPI flow WEST into Arabian Sea via the GULF OF KHAMBHAT. Both flow through RIFT VALLEYS — not classical river valleys but tectonic depressions. NARMADA between Vindhya (north) + Satpura (south); TAPI between Satpura (north) + Ajanta hills (south). Hence these don't form deltas — they form ESTUARIES at their mouths. Narmada source: AMARKANTAK (Maikal hills, MP). Tapi source: MULTAI (Betul, MP).

cards.front:
Peninsular rivers are mostly RAIN-FED, leading to:

(A) Year-round perennial flow always
(B) Seasonal flow with low summer levels
(C) Wide variability in salinity yearly
(D) Fast erosion of new mountain ranges
cards.back:
(B) Seasonal flow with low summer levels

Rivers & Water Bodies — Peninsular rivers — rain-fed (no glacier source like Himalayan rivers). Flow varies seasonally with monsoon — high in monsoon, low (sometimes nearly dry) in summer. Many smaller streams dry up entirely. This restricts navigation, hydropower reliability, irrigation. Hence many DAMS (Hirakud, Nagarjuna Sagar, Tungabhadra, Mettur) for water storage. Compare with Himalayan rivers (perennial, glacier-fed). Western Ghats rivers also have higher slopes → more erosion + waterfalls (Jog Falls, Sivasamudram, Hogenakkal).
cards.option3: Fast erosion of new mountain ranges

The layer of the atmosphere closest to the Earth's surface, in which WEATHER phenomena (clouds, rain) occur, is:

(B) Troposphere
(C) Mesosphere

cards.front:
Consider the following about EL NIÑO. 1. It is a warming of surface waters in the EASTERN equatorial Pacific (off Peru). 2. It typically WEAKENS the Indian summer monsoon, causing below-normal rainfall in India. 3. It occurs roughly every 2-7 years. 4. Its opposite phase — cooling of eastern Pacific surface waters — is called La Niña. Which are correct?

(A) 1, 2 and 3 only
(B) 1, 2, 3 and 4
(C) 2 and 4 only
(D) 1 and 3 only
cards.back:
(B) 1, 2, 3 and 4

Climate & Monsoon — All four correct. El Niño + Southern Oscillation (ENSO) = coupled ocean-atmosphere phenomenon. El Niño reduces the pressure gradient that drives the Indian SW monsoon → weaker monsoon (not all El Niño years mean drought — neutral factors like IOD matter too). La Niña usually aids the Indian monsoon.

The WESTERLIES that bring winter rainfall to north-western India (especially Punjab, Haryana, western UP) are called:

(A) Loo
(B) Western Disturbances

cards.front:
India's CLIMATE is characterised mainly as:

(A) Tropical monsoon (with seasonal reversal)
(B) Temperate (like Europe, year-round even)
(C) Polar (very cold all year long)
(D) Desert (uniformly arid everywhere)
cards.back:
(A) Tropical monsoon (with seasonal reversal)

Climate & Monsoon — INDIA'S CLIMATE: 'TROPICAL MONSOON' — defined by SEASONAL REVERSAL of winds + rains. KEY FEATURE: SW MONSOON (June-Sept) brings ~75% of annual rainfall; NE MONSOON (Oct-Dec, mainly TN, AP). FOUR SEASONS: WINTER (Dec-Feb, cool dry), SUMMER (March-May, hot dry), SW MONSOON (June-Sept, wet), POST-MONSOON / autumn (Oct-Nov, humid hot). CLIMATE VARIATIONS: tropical (Kerala, TN, coast), subtropical (UP, Punjab), semi-arid (Rajasthan), desert (Thar), Himalayan alpine. WORLD'S WETTEST PLACE: Mawsynram (Meghalaya, ~11,872 mm/year); Cherrapunji nearby. THAR: ~150 mm/year. MASSIVE diversity reflects continental size + Himalayas + monsoon dynamics. INSIGHT — India's monsoon is the world's most prominent monsoon system, affects ~1.4 billion people.

cards.front:
SW MONSOON enters India through which route first?

(A) Kerala coast (~1 June onwards)
(B) Mumbai coast (~10-15 June)
(C) Andaman Islands (mid-May)
(D) Delhi (late June onwards)
cards.back:
(A) Kerala coast (~1 June onwards)

Climate & Monsoon — SW MONSOON OFFICIAL ARRIVAL: KERALA coast around 1 JUNE (sometimes earlier). Spreads progressively NORTH-EAST. ANDAMAN-NICOBAR sees rains EARLIER (~mid-May) but monsoon's mainland arrival is dated by KERALA. PROGRESSION: Kerala (June 1) → Mumbai (~June 10) → Bay of Bengal arm reaches Bengal/NE India by June 5; covers Delhi by ~June 29; covers ALL of India by ~July 8. RETREAT begins September from NW. TWO BRANCHES of SW MONSOON: ARABIAN SEA branch (hits Western Ghats; 80%+ rainfall on western slope; rain shadow on Deccan east); BAY OF BENGAL branch (hits Bangladesh + NE; deflected by Himalayas → west along plain → reaches Delhi, Punjab). MAWSYNRAM (Meghalaya) gets HEAVIEST rains due to BoB branch + funnelling effect. IMD (India Meteorological Department) forecasts monsoon onset.

cards.front:
EL NIÑO typically affects India by:

(A) Weakening monsoon → drought tendency
(B) Strengthening monsoon → flooding
(C) No effect on Indian climate at all
(D) Causing extreme cold winters in north
cards.back:
(A) Weakening monsoon → drought tendency

Climate & Monsoon — EL NIÑO = warming of EASTERN PACIFIC equatorial waters (off Peru). DISRUPTS WALKER CIRCULATION → weakens SW monsoon over India → DROUGHT TENDENCY. BUT not absolute — some El Niño years had normal/above monsoon (depends on combined factors). NOTABLE Indian DROUGHTS in El Niño years: 1899, 1972, 1987, 2002, 2009, 2015. LA NIÑA = OPPOSITE (cooling) → STRONGER monsoon, often abundant rains. Recent strong La Niña: 2020-22 (good monsoons). INDIAN OCEAN DIPOLE (IOD) = parallel cycle in Indian Ocean (West vs East Indian Ocean SST difference); +ve IOD → favorable monsoon, −ve → adverse. ENSO + IOD together determine Indian monsoon strength. IMD provides PROBABILISTIC FORECASTS based on these. CLIMATE CHANGE making monsoon more ERRATIC — same total rain but in concentrated bursts → more floods + droughts.
cards.option2: No effect on Indian climate at all
cards.option3: Causing extreme cold winters in north

(C) Tutunendo (Colombia, S America)

(B) South India (Kerala, TN coastal)
(C) NE India (Assam, Meghalaya etc.)
(D) Eastern coast (Odisha, AP, Bay)
cards.back:
(A) North India (esp. Punjab, Haryana, J&K)

Climate & Monsoon — WESTERN DISTURBANCES (WDs) — extra-tropical CYCLONES originating in MEDITERRANEAN sea, travelling east via Iran, Afghanistan, Pakistan into NORTH INDIA. Bring WINTER RAINS (Dec-Feb) + SNOWFALL in Himalayas. KEY for: rabi crops (esp. WHEAT in Punjab/Haryana — winter rain very useful); skiing in Himachal/Kashmir. WITHOUT WDs, North India would be much drier. NUMBER: ~8 in winter; some bring intense rain/snow. EXAMPLES: SNOW in Shimla, Manali, Sonmarg in Jan-Feb directly from WDs. NE MONSOON brings Oct-Dec rains to TN + AP coast (very different system). MAVTHA = local term for surprise WD-rain in Punjab/Haryana. WD ALSO causes COLD WAVES in N India when intense (clear skies + radiation cooling at night). Recent: WDs slightly weakened in some years due to climate change effects.

cards.front:
TROPIC OF CANCER passes through approximately how many Indian STATES?

(A) 8 states (Gujarat to Mizoram E-W)
(B) 5 states (only central India)
(C) 12 states (entire India coverage)
(D) 3 states (only some south)
cards.back:
(A) 8 states (Gujarat to Mizoram E-W)

Climate & Monsoon — TROPIC OF CANCER (23.5°N latitude) — passes through 8 Indian states (W to E): GUJARAT, RAJASTHAN, MADHYA PRADESH, CHHATTISGARH, JHARKHAND, WEST BENGAL, TRIPURA, MIZORAM. Divides India into TROPICAL SOUTH (warmer year-round) + SUBTROPICAL NORTH (more seasonal extremes). EQUATOR (0°) — passes through Indonesia, Brazil, Congo, Kenya, Ecuador, Colombia, Gabon, Maldives — NOT India (closest Indian point: Indira Point, Great Nicobar at 6.74°N). TROPIC OF CAPRICORN (23.5°S) — through Australia, Chile, Brazil, Madagascar, S Africa. INTERESTING: India straddles tropical + subtropical zones → extremely diverse climate. ANTARCTIC + ARCTIC CIRCLES (66.5° each) — well outside India. KEY GEOGRAPHIC FACT: India lies between 8°4'N + 37°6'N latitudes; 68°7'E + 97°25'E longitudes. STANDARD TIME: IST = UTC+5:30 (based on 82.5°E, passing through Mirzapur, UP).

cards.front:
RAINFALL on the EASTERN SIDE of Western Ghats is LOW because of:

(A) Rain-shadow effect (windward side gets rain)
(B) Lack of monsoon entry from west (option here)
(C) Cold ocean currents nearby coast
(D) Insufficient mountain height for rain
cards.back:
(A) Rain-shadow effect (windward side gets rain)

Climate & Monsoon — RAIN SHADOW: WESTERN GHATS face Arabian Sea (W) → SW monsoon hits, rises, cools, RAINS on WINDWARD (western) side (Konkan, Malabar coast — heavy rainfall, ~3000+ mm). Air now DRY descends on LEEWARD (eastern) side → rainshadow → DECCAN PLATEAU is dry (~600-1000 mm). Same effect: Mahabaleshwar (Western Ghat top) ~6000 mm, Pune (~30 km east) ~700 mm. Other RAIN SHADOW examples: TIBET (north of Himalayas — only ~100 mm; Himalayas rain on south side); LEH (north of Pir Panjal); KIBO of Kilimanjaro. ATACAMA DESERT (Chile) = world's driest, in rain shadow of Andes. WHY DECCAN ROCKY → over millennia, less rain + erosion produced PENINSULAR PLATEAU character. KEY GEOGRAPHIC INSIGHT — same monsoon, different rain due to TOPOGRAPHY.

cards.front:
India's climate is best described under the Köppen classification as predominantly:

(A) Tropical and subtropical with strong monsoonal rainfall
(B) Temperate maritime, like that of western European coast
(C) Cold polar, comparable to Siberia and northern Canada
(D) Hot arid desert, like that of the central Sahara region
cards.back:
(A) Tropical and subtropical with strong monsoonal rainfall

Climate & Monsoon — India's climate — TROPICAL MONSOON (most of the country) + sub-tropical highland in the Himalayas + arid in the Thar + small temperate zones in the high Deccan. Köppen subtypes for India: Aw (tropical savanna — most of India); Am (tropical monsoon — Western Ghats, NE); As (tropical with dry summer — small parts); Cwa (humid subtropical with dry winter — northern plains); BSh (semi-arid — Rajasthan/Saurashtra); BWh (arid — Thar). Pure temperate, polar, or pure desert are NOT dominant.

cards.option2: Cold polar, comparable to Siberia and northern Canada

cards.front:
The SOUTHWEST monsoon brings most of India's annual rainfall and arrives because of:

(A) Reversal of pressure as the landmass heats up faster than ocean
(B) A continuous westerly flow from the Atlantic Ocean year-round
(C) The retreat of polar high pressure southward in summer
(D) Diurnal heating of small Himalayan valleys causing local winds
cards.back:
(A) Reversal of pressure as the landmass heats up faster than ocean

Climate & Monsoon — SW Monsoon mechanism — in summer, the Indian subcontinent heats faster than the surrounding Indian Ocean → low pressure forms over land (Thar / NW India is the focal heat-low). Air over the comparatively cooler Indian Ocean (high pressure) flows toward this low. Coriolis force deflects the southerly flow into a southwesterly. The winds pick up moisture as they cross the warm Arabian Sea + Bay of Bengal → torrential rainfall when they hit the Western Ghats and the Himalayas. Onset around Kerala (1 June nominal). The 'monsoon trough' migrates north as summer progresses. Distractor 2 — Atlantic doesn't drive Indian monsoon. Distractor 3 — polar fronts are too far away. Distractor 4 — local winds, not the monsoon.

cards.option2: The retreat of polar high pressure southward in summer

cards.front:
WESTERN DISTURBANCES are extra-tropical storms originating over which region, that bring winter rain to NW India?

(A) The Mediterranean Sea region around southern Europe
(B) The Indian Ocean equatorial belt south of Sri Lanka
(C) The Arctic region near the Northern Pole ice cap
(D) The Bay of Bengal, off the eastern coast of India
cards.back:
(A) The Mediterranean Sea region around southern Europe

Climate & Monsoon — Western disturbances — extra-tropical low-pressure systems originating in the Mediterranean / Caspian Sea region, riding eastward on the subtropical jet stream. Bring December-March rainfall + snow to Punjab, Haryana, J&K, HP, Uttarakhand. Critical for the rabi (winter) crop — wheat, mustard, gram. About 4-6 western disturbances per winter, with year-to-year variation. Climate change is altering their frequency + intensity. Distractor 2 — Indian ocean storms are different (cyclones). Distractor 3 — Arctic systems too far north. Distractor 4 — Bay of Bengal cyclones move WESTWARD, into east coast.

cards.front:
EL NIÑO is associated in India with which typical monsoon outcome?

(A) Strongly above-average rainfall and timely seasonal onset
(B) Below-normal rainfall and frequent drought conditions
(C) Strong cyclonic activity in the Bay of Bengal alone
(D) Earlier onset of southwest monsoon over Kerala state
cards.back:
(B) Below-normal rainfall and frequent drought conditions

Climate & Monsoon — EL NIÑO — periodic warming of the eastern equatorial Pacific (off Peru/Ecuador). Disrupts the normal Walker Circulation, weakens trade winds, and tends to suppress Indian monsoon → drought in India. Major Indian drought years coincided with strong El Niño: 1965, 1972, 1987, 2002, 2009, 2015. LA NIÑA — opposite: cooler eastern Pacific → typically better Indian monsoon. INDIAN OCEAN DIPOLE (IOD) — independent factor; positive IOD favours Indian monsoon (warm western IO, cool eastern), can offset El Niño effect (e.g., 2019 saw +ve IOD compensating for moderate El Niño). MJO (Madden-Julian Oscillation) — intra-seasonal driver.

cards.option2: Strong cyclonic activity in the Bay of Bengal alone
cards.option3: Earlier onset of southwest monsoon over Kerala state

cards.front:
Which Indian region receives the LARGEST share of its annual rainfall from the NORTH-EAST (RETREATING) monsoon, between October and December?

(A) Punjab and Haryana plains in the northwest
(B) Tamil Nadu and southern Andhra coast
(C) Kerala and Karnataka along the western coast
(D) Assam and other NE Indian hill states
cards.back:
(B) Tamil Nadu and southern Andhra coast

Climate & Monsoon — TAMIL NADU and adjoining Pondicherry / coastal AP receive ~50% of their annual rain from the NE monsoon (October-December) — the 'retreating monsoon'. Mechanism — by October, the SW monsoon retreats; high pressure builds over land; cool dry winds blow from NE; pick up moisture over the warm Bay of Bengal; deposit rain on the WINDWARD east coast (TN). Coromandel coast = Coro-mandel = TN + adjacent. Distractor 1 — Punjab/Haryana get most rain from SW monsoon. Distractor 3 — Kerala/Karnataka are heavily dependent on SW monsoon. Distractor 4 — Assam/NE: SW monsoon dominates. Cyclones often develop in the Bay of Bengal during NE monsoon period.

cards.front:
MAWSYNRAM in Meghalaya holds the record for one of the highest average annual rainfalls in the world. The reason is mainly:

(A) Tropical convection only, with no orographic effect at all
(B) Moisture-laden winds forced upward by the Khasi Hills (orographic)
(C) A persistent low-pressure cell that lingers over the area year-round
(D) Glacial meltwater rising as humid air to feed daily rainfall there
cards.back:
(B) Moisture-laden winds forced upward by the Khasi Hills (orographic)

Climate & Monsoon — Mawsynram — Meghalaya, ~11,872 mm annual average (often the world's wettest, occasionally edged out by Cherrapunji nearby). Reason: SW monsoon winds carry moisture from the Bay of Bengal, funnel into the narrow trough between the Garo and Khasi hills, are forced upward (orographic lift), cool, condense, rain. Cherrapunji (Sohra) and Mawsynram are the two long-standing record holders. Most rain falls during SW monsoon (June-September). Distractor 1 — orographic IS the dominant effect. Distractor 3 — persistent low isn't the mechanism. Distractor 4 — no glaciers there.

cards.front:
The MONSOON BREAK refers to:

(A) Holiday period when Indian schools shut for monsoon rest
(B) A short interruption in the rainfall during the SW monsoon season
(C) Final retreat of southwest monsoon in late September
(D) A complete failure of the entire monsoon over India
cards.back:
(B) A short interruption in the rainfall during the SW monsoon season

Climate & Monsoon — MONSOON BREAK — relatively dry spell of several days (sometimes 2-3 weeks) during the active SW monsoon period when rainfall stalls over the Indian heartland but moves either north (towards the Himalayan foothills) or south (towards the equatorial Indian Ocean). Caused by the monsoon trough shifting its position. Long monsoon breaks during sowing season can damage kharif crops; if late, they can be welcome for harvest. Active vs break phases of the monsoon are the subject of intensive forecasting. Distractor 1 = vacation, not climate. Distractor 3 = monsoon retreat (different phenomenon). Distractor 4 = monsoon failure (full-season deficit, more serious).

cards.option3: A complete failure of the entire monsoon over India

cards.front:
The South-West Monsoon normally reaches the southern tip of Kerala around:

(A) 15 April
(B) 1 June
(C) 1 July
(D) 15 August
cards.back:
(B) 1 June

Climate & Monsoon — The IMD's normal onset date for the SW monsoon at Kerala is 1 June. From there it advances north-east and reaches Delhi by around 29 June and the whole country by 8 July. Withdrawal begins from Rajasthan around 17 September and completes by mid-October. June-September delivers ~75 % of India's total annual rainfall.

Most of Tamil Nadu receives the bulk of its annual rainfall from the:

(A) South-West monsoon
(B) North-East monsoon
(C) Western disturbances

cards.front:
The SW monsoon splits into two main branches over the Indian landmass — the Arabian Sea branch and the:

(A) Indian Ocean branch
(B) Bay of Bengal branch
(C) Himalayan branch
(D) Western Ghats branch
cards.back:
(B) Bay of Bengal branch

Climate & Monsoon — The SW monsoon has two arms. The Arabian Sea branch hits the Western Ghats and gives heavy rain to the west coast (Mumbai ~2,400 mm). The Bay of Bengal branch curves north towards the Himalayan foothills and the NE, drenching Meghalaya's Mawsynram and Cherrapunji (the wettest places on Earth). The two arms merge over northern India around early July.

cards.front:
An El Niño event typically has what effect on the Indian SW monsoon?

(A) Increases rainfall above normal
(B) Tends to weaken and reduce rainfall
(C) Has no measurable effect
(D) Delays onset but increases total rainfall
cards.back:
(B) Tends to weaken and reduce rainfall

Climate & Monsoon — El Niño — warming of the central and eastern equatorial Pacific — disturbs the Walker circulation and typically weakens the Indian SW monsoon, often causing deficit rainfall. La Niña (the cooler phase) generally favours above-normal Indian monsoon rainfall. The correlation is strong but not perfect — 1997's record-breaking El Niño saw a near-normal monsoon.

The narrow mountain range that blocks the SW monsoon on the west coast and creates a rain-shadow over the Deccan plateau is the:

(B) Western Ghats

cards.front:
The SOUTH-WEST MONSOON normally arrives over the Kerala coast on:

(A) 1 MAY
(B) 1 JUNE
(C) 1 JULY
(D) 15 MAY
cards.back:
(B) 1 JUNE

Climate & Monsoon — SW MONSOON ONSET over Kerala — NORMAL DATE = 1 JUNE (declared by India Meteorological Department, IMD). IMD officially declares onset based on FIVE OBJECTIVE CRITERIA (since 2006): (1) 60%+ of 14 designated stations in Kerala-Lakshadweep region receive rainfall ≥ 2.5 mm for 2 consecutive days after 10 May; (2) Westerly wind depth ≥ 6 km with speeds 15-20 knots at 925 hPa; (3) Outgoing Long-wave Radiation (OLR) below 200 W/m²; (4) Cloud cover increase; (5) Wind direction WSW-SW. MONSOON PROGRESSES NORTHWARD thereafter: Mumbai ~10 June; Kolkata ~8 June; Delhi ~29 June; reaches entire country by ~15 JULY. WITHDRAWAL (retreat) begins from NW India around 1 SEPTEMBER, complete withdrawal from entire country by ~15 October. DURATION: SW monsoon gives ~75% of India's annual rainfall in 4 months (June-Sep). ANOMALIES: Onset delay of more than 7 days → impacts kharif sowing, drought risk. El Niño years typically weaken monsoon; La Niña strengthens it. 2023 = 'below normal' monsoon (El Niño); 2022 = 'normal'. LGP (Long-Period Average) rainfall = ~880 mm; 'normal' = 96-104% of LPA. normal onset date declared by IMD.

LGP (Long-Period Average) rainfall = ~880 mm; 'normal' = 96-104% of LPA. normal onset date declared by IMD.

cards.front:
The Indian SW Monsoon splits into two branches after striking the southern tip of peninsular India — the ARABIAN SEA BRANCH and the:

(A) Indian Ocean Branch
(B) BAY OF BENGAL BRANCH
(C) Pacific Branch
(D) Himalayan Branch
cards.back:
(B) BAY OF BENGAL BRANCH

Climate & Monsoon — SW MONSOON — TWO BRANCHES: (1) ARABIAN SEA BRANCH — hits the Western Ghats, causes HEAVY rainfall on windward side (Mahabaleshwar, Mangaluru, Kochi); crosses the Ghats creating RAIN SHADOW on leeward Deccan Plateau (Pune gets ~700mm vs Mumbai ~2200mm). Sub-branches continue to Gujarat + Rajasthan + Punjab (light rain). (2) BAY OF BENGAL BRANCH — strikes Myanmar coast + Arakan Yoma + deflects towards Ganga plains; Assam + NE India receive VERY HEAVY rainfall (Mawsynram + Cherrapunji = wettest places on Earth, ~11,800+ mm/yr). Branch moves WESTWARD along Himalayan foothills causing rainfall in UP, Bihar, Punjab (reaches Punjab around end of June). The TWO BRANCHES MEET over NW India (Punjab + Haryana). MECHANISM: Differential heating of land + sea; ITCZ shifts northward to ~25°N in summer; low pressure over Indian subcontinent draws moisture-laden SE trade winds from southern hemisphere that cross equator + deflect RIGHT (NW direction) as per Coriolis — becoming SW winds hitting India. Also driven by Tibetan Plateau heating + Tropical Easterly Jet.

cards.front:
MAWSYNRAM in Meghalaya holds the record for the HIGHEST ANNUAL RAINFALL in the world. The reason it out-rains Cherrapunji is:

(A) It is closer to the sea
(B) It is at a higher elevation and its conical hills FUNNEL the Bay of Bengal monsoon branch into a narrow valley, forcing greater orographic uplift
(C) It has an active volcano
(D) It lies in a rain-shadow
cards.back:
(B) It is at a higher elevation and its conical hills FUNNEL the Bay of Bengal monsoon branch into a narrow valley, forcing greater orographic uplift

Climate & Monsoon — MAWSYNRAM (East Khasi Hills, Meghalaya) — HIGHEST ANNUAL RAINFALL in the world, ~11,871 mm average (some years 15,000+ mm). Just ~15 km from Cherrapunji (Sohra) which records ~11,777 mm — they swap the 'wettest place' title year to year. WHY SO WET: (a) Bay of Bengal branch of SW Monsoon sweeps up moisture-laden air over Bangladesh plains; (b) hits the KHASI HILLS abruptly (south-facing scarp); (c) OROGRAPHIC UPLIFT — moist air forced to rise rapidly, cools, condenses as torrential rain; (d) Mawsynram's CONICAL HILLS form a natural funnel, concentrating clouds into a narrow valley (Cherrapunji, slightly lower elevation, lacks this funnel). RESULT: clouds are literally squeezed dry over these hills. SEASONAL DISTRIBUTION: ~90% of annual rainfall falls June-September. CHERRAPUNJI RECORDS: 9,300 mm in July 1861 (highest monthly); 26,470 mm in 1860-61 (highest annual worldwide). IRONY: despite highest rainfall, both villages face DRINKING WATER SCARCITY in dry months — steep slopes + deforested terrain cause rapid runoff; local people rely on bamboo-pipe rainwater harvesting. Also home to LIVING ROOT BRIDGES of the Khasi + Jaintia tribes (figus elastica roots trained across streams — can last 500+ years).

cards.front:
The RAIN-SHADOW effect of the Western Ghats means the LEEWARD side (eastern slopes + Deccan) receives much less rainfall. Which city represents this rain-shadow?

(A) Mumbai
(B) PUNE
(C) Mangaluru
(D) Thiruvananthapuram
cards.back:
(B) PUNE

Climate & Monsoon — RAIN-SHADOW EFFECT — when moist air is forced to rise over a mountain barrier, it cools + drops rainfall on the WINDWARD side; by the time it descends on the LEEWARD side it is dry + warm (adiabatic warming). WESTERN GHATS + SW MONSOON example: (a) WINDWARD (western coast) — very wet: MUMBAI ~2200 mm, MANGALURU ~3500 mm, KOCHI ~3000 mm, AGUMBE/KUDREMUKH (Karnataka) ~7500 mm — 'Cherrapunji of the South'. (b) LEEWARD (eastern, Deccan) — dry: PUNE ~700 mm, AHMEDNAGAR ~550 mm, SOLAPUR ~720 mm, BELLARY ~550 mm. This rain-shadow is why MARATHWADA + parts of KARNATAKA'S EASTERN DRY ZONE are chronically drought-prone. The belt through which the monsoon passes BEFORE releasing its moisture is the 'Desert belt of the Deccan'. ANANTAPUR (Andhra Pradesh) — only ~550 mm — is India's SECOND-DRIEST DISTRICT (Jaisalmer being driest). Note: NE monsoon (Oct-Dec) partly compensates the Tamil Nadu + Rayalaseema coastal rain-shadow, giving them another shot at rain. AURANGABAD gets 725mm. 'LEEWARD' = downwind side; 'WINDWARD' = upwind side. ~700mm annual vs Mumbai's ~2200mm — just 150km away, on the leeward side of the Ghats.

cards.front:
The NORTH-EAST (retreating) MONSOON is the main source of rainfall for:

(A) Kerala + Karnataka
(B) TAMIL NADU, COASTAL ANDHRA, RAYALASEEMA, Puducherry (Oct-Dec)
(C) Punjab
(D) Assam
cards.back:
(B) TAMIL NADU, COASTAL ANDHRA, RAYALASEEMA, Puducherry (Oct-Dec)

Climate & Monsoon — NE (RETREATING) MONSOON = WINTER MONSOON = post-monsoon season (October-December). As the ITCZ retreats southward, WINDS reverse from SW to NE, picking up moisture from the Bay of Bengal as they blow over it. Hits the EAST COAST of India. BENEFICIARIES: (1) TAMIL NADU — gets ~60% of its ANNUAL rainfall during NE monsoon (Nov-Dec); Chennai floods of Nov-Dec are a regular feature. (2) COASTAL ANDHRA PRADESH + RAYALASEEMA. (3) SOUTHERN KARNATAKA (coastal parts) + PUDUCHERRY. (4) SOUTH KERALA + SRI LANKA get some rain too. TAMIL NADU is UNIQUE — during SW monsoon it's in rain-shadow of the Western Ghats + gets very little rain, so it depends on NE monsoon + cyclones for water supply. CYCLONES — Oct-Dec is the peak season for Bay of Bengal cyclones hitting east coast (Tamil Nadu, AP, Odisha, WB, BD). WITHDRAWAL: NE monsoon wanes by early January; December is transitional. SW MONSOON = moist; NE MONSOON = drier overall (except coastal TN) because winds originate from cool, dry continental Asia (Siberian high). The NE monsoon phenomenon is called 'CHENNAI RAINS' colloquially. rain-shadow of SW monsoon.

cards.front:
EL NIÑO is a climatic phenomenon associated with:

(A) Strong monsoon rainfall in India
(B) Abnormal WARMING of Pacific Ocean surface waters
(C) Cooling of Atlantic Ocean
(D) Indian Ocean warming
cards.back:
(B) Abnormal WARMING of Pacific Ocean surface waters

Climate & Monsoon — EL NIÑO — Spanish for 'the little boy' / 'Christ child' (so named by Peruvian fishermen because it peaks around Christmas). Part of the ENSO (El Niño-Southern Oscillation) cycle. MECHANISM: Normally, TRADE WINDS blow east-to-west across the Pacific, piling warm water in the western Pacific (Indonesia + Philippines) + allowing cold water upwelling off Peru. In EL NIÑO years, trade winds WEAKEN/REVERSE, warm water sloshes eastward, Peruvian coast sees ANOMALOUS WARM surface temperatures (+0.5°C to +3°C). GLOBAL IMPACT: drought in Australia + Indonesia; floods in Peru + California; bleaches coral reefs (2016, 2023 bleaching events). INDIAN MONSOON LINK: El Niño → HADLEY + Walker cells disrupted → descending dry air over Indian subcontinent → WEAKER/DELAYED SW monsoon. 60% of El Niño years since 1900 have had below-normal Indian rainfall (drought). Recent El Niño years: 1997-98 (strong), 2015-16 (strongest on record), 2023-24 (moderate — led to 5% below-normal Indian rainfall). LA NIÑA (opposite) — Pacific cooling; STRENGTHENS Indian monsoon typically. 2020-22 was a rare 'triple-dip' La Niña → good monsoons. Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) — local analog; positive IOD offsets El Niño effect. typically WEAKENS the Indian SW monsoon; around Peru + Ecuador.

cards.front:
The 'BURSTING of the monsoon' refers to:

(A) Pre-monsoon thunderstorms (mango showers)
(B) The SUDDEN, heavy onset of SW monsoon rainfall, marking the transition from dry pre-monsoon to active monsoon regime
(C) Withdrawal of the monsoon
(D) A cyclonic disturbance
cards.back:
(B) The SUDDEN, heavy onset of SW monsoon rainfall, marking the transition from dry pre-monsoon to active monsoon regime

Climate & Monsoon — 'BURST OF MONSOON' — the SUDDEN + VIGOROUS arrival of the SW monsoon rains after weeks of oppressive pre-monsoon heat + humidity. Characterised by: (1) sharp drop in temperature (5-8°C overnight); (2) dark thunderclouds + torrential rain that can last days; (3) gusty winds from the SW; (4) sudden green-up of vegetation. Kerala experiences the FIRST BURST ~1 June. FROM the burst onwards, the monsoon is in 'active' mode. PRE-MONSOON SHOWERS (not the burst): (a) MANGO SHOWERS (Apr-May) — pre-monsoon thunderstorms in Kerala + Karnataka, helping ripen mangoes (hence the name). (b) BLOSSOM SHOWERS (Apr-May) — Karnataka coffee belt, help coffee flower. (c) KAAL BAISAKHI / NOR'WESTERS — violent thunderstorms in Bengal + Assam in April-May; called 'Bardoli Chheerha' in Assam; locally feared but beneficial for jute + rice. (d) LOO — hot dry WINDS (not rain) in N India during May-June; heat waves. (e) CHERRY BLOSSOM SHOWERS — Karnataka coffee. 'BREAKS IN MONSOON' (not burst) — dry spells within the active monsoon period; common + sometimes prolonged, can cause drought even in a 'normal' monsoon year.

cards.front:
The JET STREAM most relevant to Indian monsoon onset is the:

(A) Polar Jet Stream
(B) TROPICAL EASTERLY JET (TEJ)
(C) Pacific Jet Stream
(D) Antarctic Polar Vortex
cards.back:
(B) TROPICAL EASTERLY JET (TEJ)

Climate & Monsoon — JET STREAMS + INDIAN MONSOON: (1) SUBTROPICAL WESTERLY JET (STWJ) — winter jet at ~30°N, sits SOUTH of the Himalayas in winter; brings western disturbances (winter rain to N India). In May-June, STWJ MIGRATES NORTH of the Himalayas → low-level easterlies + SW monsoon can establish. The 'retreat' of STWJ is a KEY TRIGGER for monsoon onset (called the 'monsoon onset vortex'). (2) TROPICAL EASTERLY JET (TEJ) — summer jet; upper-tropospheric easterly at ~100-200 hPa, centered around 15°N; flows from SE Asia across India to Africa. Strong TEJ in June → strong divergence aloft → helps drive surface convergence + heavy rainfall. WEAK TEJ = weak monsoon. DISCOVERY: TEJ was first described by P. Koteswaram (1958), an IMD scientist. TIBETAN PLATEAU HEATING: reinforces TEJ by creating a warm anticyclone aloft over Tibet. MADDEN-JULIAN OSCILLATION (MJO) — eastward-moving tropical disturbance; modulates monsoon on 30-60 day timescale — 'active' + 'break' phases of monsoon partly driven by MJO passage. WALKER CELL + HADLEY CELL are zonal + meridional circulations, not jet streams per se. WESTERN DISTURBANCES come from Mediterranean via STWJ in winter.

cards.front:
The INDIAN OCEAN DIPOLE (IOD) when POSITIVE is associated with:

(A) Weaker Indian monsoon
(B) STRONGER Indian monsoon
(C) No impact on monsoon
(D) Caused by Pacific trade winds only
cards.back:
(B) STRONGER Indian monsoon

Climate & Monsoon — INDIAN OCEAN DIPOLE (IOD) — first identified in 1999 by scientists at JAMSTEC (Japan). Measured as SST (sea-surface temperature) difference between the WESTERN (off Somalia/Arabia) and EASTERN tropical Indian Ocean (off Sumatra). POSITIVE IOD (+IOD): west is ANOMALOUSLY WARM, east is COOLER than normal. Consequences: (a) warmer western Indian Ocean boosts moisture content near Indian subcontinent → STRENGTHENS SW monsoon; (b) drought-like conditions in Indonesia + Australia (2019 Australian bushfires linked to strong +IOD); (c) can OFFSET El Niño's weakening effect — e.g., 1997 saw concurrent strong El Niño + strong +IOD, India got NORMAL rainfall (El Niño alone would have caused drought). NEGATIVE IOD (-IOD) — opposite; typically weakens monsoon. INDICATOR: Dipole Mode Index (DMI) = SST(West) - SST(East); DMI > +0.4°C = positive IOD event. DURATION: IOD events last ~3-6 months, typically peak Aug-Oct; don't persist like ENSO. Other oceanic drivers of Indian monsoon: ENSO (Pacific), Atlantic Niño, Madden-Julian Oscillation, Indian Ocean Warm Pool. PREDICTION: IMD uses IOD forecast as one input in its monsoon forecast model. Positive IOD years: 1994, 1997, 2006, 2015, 2019, 2023. warmer western Indian Ocean (off Somalia/Arabia) + cooler eastern side (off Indonesia) → enhanced moisture transport to India.
cards.option3: Caused by Pacific trade winds only

cards.front:
MANGO SHOWERS are:

(A) Heavy rain that destroys mango crops
(B) PRE-monsoon thunderstorm showers in KERALA + coastal KARNATAKA (April-May) that help mangoes ripen
(C) A variety of shower trees in Kerala
(D) Post-monsoon drizzle in Tamil Nadu
cards.back:
(B) PRE-monsoon thunderstorm showers in KERALA + coastal KARNATAKA (April-May) that help mangoes ripen

Climate & Monsoon — MANGO SHOWERS (KERALA) / BLOSSOM SHOWERS (KARNATAKA) — PRE-MONSOON thunderstorms during April-May on the west coast of peninsular India. Triggered by: afternoon convective heating of land → rising hot air → condensation → brief but intense thunderstorms. EFFECT: help MANGO FRUITS ripen (hence 'mango showers') + help COFFEE BEANS flower ('blossom showers'). Similar pre-monsoon local thunderstorms elsewhere in India: (1) NOR'WESTERS / KAAL BAISAKHI — violent thunder-squalls in West Bengal + Assam (April-May), locally feared for damage but bring rain for rice + jute. In Assam also called 'BARDOLI CHHEERHA'. (2) LOO — hot dry continental winds (April-June) across N India + Pak; can be 45-50°C, cause heat-stroke. 'Loo' is NOT a shower. (3) CHERRY BLOSSOM SHOWERS — Karnataka coffee plantations. CATEGORY: all these are 'local winds + weather phenomena' — a favourite SSC/UPSC GS-1 category. Other LOCAL WINDS globally: Chinook (N America, 'snow-eater'), Foehn (Alps), Sirocco (Mediterranean), Mistral (France), Harmattan (W Africa), Bora (Adriatic), Santa Ana (California), Khamsin (Egypt), Brickfielder (Australia).

cards.front:
The three global WIND SYSTEMS are the Trade Winds, Westerlies, and Polar Easterlies. Which wind system is responsible for the Indian MONSOON?

(A) Polar Easterlies
(B) Trade Winds
(C) Jet streams only
(D) Westerlies
cards.back:
(B) Trade Winds

Climate & Monsoon — PERMANENT WINDS: (1) TRADE WINDS — blow from sub-tropical HIGH (30°N/S) towards the equatorial LOW (0°). Northeast Trades (N hemisphere) + Southeast Trades (S hemisphere). CORIOLIS EFFECT deflects them. Named 'Trade' because they helped sailing ships in colonial 'trade'. (2) WESTERLIES — blow from 30° to 60° latitude. Come from the west. Stronger in S hemisphere ('ROARING FORTIES', 'FURIOUS FIFTIES', 'SCREAMING SIXTIES' — due to fewer landmasses). (3) POLAR EASTERLIES — blow from polar highs toward sub-polar lows. INDIAN MONSOON = a DIFFERENTIAL HEATING phenomenon — in summer, the Indian subcontinent's massive landmass heats up faster than the Indian Ocean → LOW PRESSURE over land + HIGH PRESSURE over sea → the SE trades cross the equator (deflected to SW monsoon by Coriolis) and blow moist air onto the subcontinent (June-September). cards.front:
The 'LOO' is a hot, dry wind experienced in which region, during which season?

(A) Himalayan foothills; winter
(B) Northwest India (Rajasthan, Punjab, Haryana, UP, Delhi)
(C) Coastal Tamil Nadu; monsoon
(D) Central Maharashtra; spring
cards.back:
(B) Northwest India (Rajasthan, Punjab, Haryana, UP, Delhi)

Climate & Monsoon — LOO — a hot, dry, dusty wind blowing westerly/northwesterly over the PLAINS of northwestern India + Pakistan. Mostly May-June. Temperatures 45-50°C. Can cause heat strokes. Plants wilt; groundwater dries. Contrary to normal afternoon cooling, Loo afternoons are the hottest. Other LOCAL WINDS in India: (1) KALBAISAKHI / NORWESTERS — sudden violent thunderstorms in WB + Assam pre-monsoon (April-May). Also called 'Bardoli Chheerha' in Assam. Brings relief from heat + some rain for tea crops. (2) MANGO SHOWERS — pre-monsoon summer showers in KA, Kerala, Coastal AP (April-May) — help mango flowering, hence the name. (3) BLOSSOM / CHERRY BLOSSOM SHOWERS — Kerala, KA post-picking summer showers on coffee plantations (April-May — similar). (4) ANDHI — hot dust storms in Rajasthan. cards.front:
The CHINOOK wind — warm + dry, known as the 'SNOW-EATER' — blows down the leeward side of which mountain range?

(A) Alps in Europe
(B) Rocky Mountains in North America
(C) Andes in South America
(D) Himalayas
cards.back:
(B) Rocky Mountains in North America

Climate & Monsoon — CHINOOK — warm, dry wind on the EASTERN (leeward) slopes of the ROCKY MOUNTAINS in the USA + Canada. Can raise temperatures by 20-30°C within hours (especially in winter), melting snow rapidly — hence 'SNOW-EATER'. Forms when a moist Pacific air mass rises on the western slopes (loses moisture as rain/snow), then descends dry on the eastern slopes — compression heats it (adiabatic warming: ~10°C/km for dry air). Similar FOEHN WINDS occur worldwide on leeward sides: FOEHN (Alps — German original name, which 'chinook' loosely translates), CHINOOK (Rockies), BERG (South Africa), ZONDA (Andes). KATABATIC WINDS — cold winds flowing downhill by gravity (denser cold air) — include MISTRAL (Alps → Rhone valley → Mediterranean, cold NW, France), BORA (Dalmatia coast, cold NE from Balkans to Adriatic), FALL WINDS on Antarctic coast. HURRICANES / CYCLONES / TYPHOONS: region-specific names for the same phenomenon — tropical cyclones. Atlantic + NE Pacific = 'hurricane'; NW Pacific = 'typhoon'; Indian Ocean + South Pacific = 'cyclone'.

cards.front:
The CORIOLIS FORCE — an APPARENT force caused by Earth's rotation — deflects winds (and ocean currents) to the RIGHT in the Northern Hemisphere and to the LEFT in the Southern Hemisphere. Where is Coriolis effect ZERO?

(A) North Pole
(B) At the EQUATOR
(C) Tropic of Cancer
(D) At 45° latitude
cards.back:
(B) At the EQUATOR

Climate & Monsoon — CORIOLIS EFFECT — an apparent deflection of moving objects (air, water, projectiles) as observed from a rotating frame (Earth). Magnitude proportional to sin(latitude) × velocity × 2ω (ω = Earth's angular velocity). ZERO at the EQUATOR (latitude 0°). MAXIMUM at the POLES (latitude 90°). In N Hemisphere: deflects to the RIGHT. In S Hemisphere: deflects to the LEFT. CONSEQUENCES: (1) Tropical cyclones rotate counterclockwise in N and clockwise in S hemispheres; (2) They DON'T form within ~5° of the equator (too little Coriolis); (3) Trade winds deflect from northward/southward to become NE trades (N hem) + SE trades (S hem); (4) Bullet trajectories curve over long distances. Named after Gaspard-Gustave de Coriolis (French, 1835). Myth: toilet/sink water drains in opposite directions N vs S hemispheres — FALSE for small basins (effect too weak; drain direction depends on basin shape).

cards.front:
The Indian SUMMER MONSOON enters India from which direction, and which branch is formed by the Western Ghats' orographic effect?

(A) NE direction; Arabian Sea branch
(B) SOUTHWEST direction; ARABIAN SEA branch strikes Kerala first (~1 June), Western Ghats force uplift → heavy rain on windward slopes
(C) West direction; Bay of Bengal branch
(D) Easterly; from China
cards.back:
(B) SOUTHWEST direction; ARABIAN SEA branch strikes Kerala first (~1 June), Western Ghats force uplift → heavy rain on windward slopes

Climate & Monsoon — INDIAN SUMMER MONSOON (SW Monsoon, June-September) has TWO BRANCHES from the Indian Ocean: (1) ARABIAN SEA BRANCH — strikes Kerala coast first around 1 June (official 'monsoon onset'). Moves up the west coast, hits WESTERN GHATS which force it to rise → OROGRAPHIC / RELIEF RAIN on the windward (western) slopes — Mahabaleshwar, Amboli, Agumbe (Karnataka's 'Cherrapunji of the South' — ~7000 mm/year), Western Ghats spine. Rain shadow (leeward side) → Deccan plateau gets much less rain. (2) BAY OF BENGAL BRANCH — reaches NE India first, deflected by Arakan Yoma + Meghalaya hills → strikes Khasi Hills (MAWSYNRAM — Earth's wettest place, ~11,872mm/year; CHERRAPUNJI — #2). Then curves up Ganga plain from east to west. ONSET dates (normal): Kerala 1 June → Mumbai 10 June → Delhi 27 June → NW India/Punjab 1 July. WITHDRAWAL: reverse order, starting NW India early September to full withdrawal by mid-October. IMD officially records monsoon start/end dates every year.

cards.front:
The 'ROARING FORTIES', 'FURIOUS FIFTIES', and 'SCREAMING SIXTIES' refer to:

(A) Nautical miles per hour
(B) Strong WESTERLIES in the SOUTHERN HEMISPHERE between 40°-60° latitudes
(C) Speeds of Indian monsoon winds
(D) Colours of sea at different depths
cards.back:
(B) Strong WESTERLIES in the SOUTHERN HEMISPHERE between 40°-60° latitudes

Climate & Monsoon — 'ROARING FORTIES' (40-50°S), 'FURIOUS FIFTIES' (50-60°S), 'SCREAMING SIXTIES' (60-70°S) — strong westerly winds in the SOUTHERN HEMISPHERE Mid-latitudes. These winds are much more intense than their N hemisphere counterparts because: (1) less LAND in S hemisphere to create friction (90% of mid-latitude S hem is OCEAN — big open water bodies); (2) more uninterrupted fetch → winds build up. Sailors historically used Roaring Forties for SW Passage / fast east-bound voyages around the Cape of Good Hope (Africa) or Cape Horn (S America). Still dangerous for shipping. Home to many famous ocean disasters. In N hemisphere, the 40-60° zone is mostly LAND (Eurasia + N America), so winds are moderated. The ANTARCTIC CIRCUMPOLAR CURRENT (ACC) — driven by these westerlies — is the largest ocean current in the world (~125 Sverdrups). Also called the 'WEST WIND DRIFT'. No continents obstruct it.

cards.front:
The 'HORSE LATITUDES' refer to:

(A) Latitudes near the equator with no winds (Doldrums)
(B) SUBTROPICAL HIGH PRESSURE belts at ~30° N/S where winds are CALM / variable and descending air causes DRY conditions
(C) Latitudes where horses naturally migrate
(D) Polar regions
cards.back:
(B) SUBTROPICAL HIGH PRESSURE belts at ~30° N/S where winds are CALM / variable and descending air causes DRY conditions

Climate & Monsoon — HORSE LATITUDES — 30° N and 30° S latitudes — regions of SUBTROPICAL HIGH PRESSURE, where air descends (from equatorial ascent) and winds are CALM / light / variable. Descending air is COMPRESSED + WARMED → LOW HUMIDITY → clear skies + DRY conditions. Home to MOST of the world's great DESERTS: Sahara (Africa, 30°N), Thar (India), Arabian (Arabia), Gobi (Mongolia, slightly higher), Mexican, Great Victoria (Aus), Kalahari + Namib (S Africa, 30°S), Patagonian, Atacama (Chile). NAME ORIGIN: Sailing ships would be becalmed here for weeks — to save water, sailors threw HORSES (cargo) overboard. Also called the 'Calms of Cancer/Capricorn'. Adjacent zones: EQUATORIAL CALMS = DOLDRUMS / ITCZ (Intertropical Convergence Zone) — where trade winds meet, low pressure, ascending air, heavy rains (equatorial rainforests: Amazon, Congo, Indonesian). Polar regions also have SUBSIDING cold air → dry (Antarctica = technically largest desert). POLAR FRONTS at 60° latitude — low pressure, stormy — birthplace of mid-latitude cyclones. most deserts here.

cards.front:
The SAHARA DESERT in Africa is kept extremely dry due to which major atmospheric feature?

(A) Ocean currents only
(B) Subtropical HIGH PRESSURE belt at ~30°N (Horse Latitudes) causing descending dry air
(C) Rain shadow of the Rockies
(D) Polar vortex influence
cards.back:
(B) Subtropical HIGH PRESSURE belt at ~30°N (Horse Latitudes) causing descending dry air

Climate & Monsoon — SAHARA DESERT dryness: primarily due to the SUBTROPICAL HIGH PRESSURE BELT at ~30°N latitude (Horse Latitudes) — subsiding dry air from the HADLEY CELL circulation. Sahara sits right under this zone. Secondary factors: cold CANARY CURRENT off the west African coast (cold water → less evaporation → less rain over land); huge distance from moisture sources (interior Africa); Atlas Mountains + Red Sea create additional barriers. Sahara is ~9.2 million km² — larger than continental USA — and the 3rd-largest desert globally (after Antarctic + Arctic polar deserts). HOTTEST recorded temperature on Earth: Furnace Creek, Death Valley (56.7°C, 1913) — though some Sahara sites have come close. HADLEY CELL — tropical atmospheric circulation cell from 0° to ~30°; responsible for tropical rains AND subtropical deserts (0°=rising, 30°=sinking). FERREL CELL (30°-60°) + POLAR CELL (60°-90°) — other global circulation cells. IRONY of Sahara: used to be a lush savannah with lakes as recently as 6000 years ago (Holocene Green Sahara).

cards.front:
The concept of Biosphere Reserves is associated with which UNESCO programme?

(A) Operation Tiger
(B) Man and the Biosphere (MAB) Programme
(C) World Heritage Programme
(D) Ramsar Convention
cards.back:
(B) Man and the Biosphere (MAB) Programme

Soils, Forests & Biodiversity — MAB (Man and the Biosphere) Programme — UNESCO, launched 1971. Biosphere Reserves are 'science for sustainability' sites — combining biodiversity conservation with sustainable use. Three zones: (1) CORE — strictly protected, no human disturbance; (2) BUFFER — limited research, education, eco-tourism; (3) TRANSITION — communities live and work, sustainable practices. India has 18 designated biosphere reserves (national list); 12 of them are also part of the UNESCO World Network of Biosphere Reserves (WNBR). India joined WNBR with Nilgiri (2000).

Includes Bandipur, Mudumalai, Nagarhole, Mukurthi NPs and Wayanad WLS, Silent Valley NP. Ecologically rich — Western Ghats endemics (Lion-tailed macaque, Nilgiri tahr, Nilgiri langur). UNESCO WNBR 2000. Often confused with Nanda Devi (designated 1988, 2nd BR). Sequence of first 5 Indian BRs: Nilgiri (1986), Nanda Devi (1988), Nokrek (1988), Manas (1989), Sundarbans (1989).

cards.front:
The COLD DESERT Biosphere Reserve, located in Himachal Pradesh, includes which national park?

(A) Hemis (in Ladakh)
(B) Pin Valley National Park (Lahaul & Spiti)
(C) Great Himalayan National Park
(D) Khangchendzonga
cards.back:
(B) Pin Valley National Park (Lahaul & Spiti)

Khangchendzonga — Sikkim BR (UNESCO 2018, also a World Heritage Site). India's 18 BRs by approximate region: Western Ghats (4 — Nilgiri, Agasthyamala, NBR core, Gulf of Mannar coastal); Eastern Himalaya (4 — Nanda Devi, Khangchendzonga, Nokrek, Dibru-Saikhowa); NE (2 — Manas, Dehang Dibang); Central India (3 — Achanakmar-Amarkantak, Pachmarhi, Panna); Coastal/Islands (2 — Great Nicobar, Sundarbans); Cold Desert (1 — HP); Salt-marsh (1 — Kachchh, Gujarat); Aravalli (1 — Pachpadra/Sariska area as proposed) — totals approximate.

cards.front:
The Gulf of Mannar Biosphere Reserve, India's first MARINE biosphere reserve, lies along which coast?

(A) Coast of Gujarat
(B) Coast of Tamil Nadu (between India and Sri Lanka)
(C) Coast of Odisha
(D) Andaman & Nicobar Islands
cards.back:
(B) Coast of Tamil Nadu (between India and Sri Lanka)

Soils, Forests & Biodiversity — Gulf of Mannar BR — declared 1989; India's FIRST marine BR. Stretches ~140 km along Tamil Nadu coast from Rameswaram in the north to Kanyakumari in the south. 21 small islands; ~3,600 km² of coral reefs, mangroves, seagrass beds, salt marshes. Habitat of dugong (sea cow — endangered), corals, sacred chank, dolphins. UNESCO WNBR 2001. The Kachchh BR (Gulf of Kutch — 2008) is in Gujarat. Bhitarkanika in Odisha is a notable mangrove + olive ridley site but a Ramsar site / NP, not a BR.

(C) Panna Biosphere Reserve

cards.back:

(A) Nilgiri
(B) Gulf of Kachchh BR
(C) Cold Desert BR (~7,770 km², Lahaul-Spiti, Himachal Pradesh)

cards.back:

cards.front:
Which UNESCO-recognised Biosphere Reserve in the Northeast spans Sikkim and shares its territory with the world's third-highest mountain peak?

(A) Manas
(B) Khangchendzonga (Kanchenjunga) Biosphere Reserve, Sikkim
(C) Nokrek (Meghalaya)
(D) Dibru-Saikhowa (Assam)
cards.back:
(B) Khangchendzonga (Kanchenjunga) Biosphere Reserve, Sikkim

Soils, Forests & Biodiversity — Khangchendzonga BR — Sikkim. UNESCO WNBR 2018. Surrounds Mt Kanchenjunga (8,586 m, world's 3rd highest peak — India's highest peak; on India-Nepal border). The Khangchendzonga National Park within it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site (Mixed natural + cultural, 2016) — recognising both biodiversity (snow leopard, red panda, blue sheep) and the mountain's sacred status to the Lepcha people. Manas BR — Assam, royal Bengal tiger + golden langur + pygmy hog + hispid hare, also a UNESCO World Heritage Site (1985, originally listed as 'in danger' due to insurgency, removed from danger list in 2011). Nokrek — Meghalaya, citrus genetic diversity centre. Dibru-Saikhowa — Assam, river-island ecosystem.

cards.front:
India's TOTAL FOREST + tree cover is approximately what percent of geographical area?

(A) 10% forest + tree cover (very low)
(B) ~25% forest + tree cover (current)
(C) 50% forest + tree cover (way too high)
(D) 33% target by NFP (yet unmet)
cards.back:
(B) ~25% forest + tree cover (current)

Soils, Forests & Biodiversity — India's forest + tree cover (per India State of Forest Report 2023, FSI-MoEFCC): ~25.17% of total geographic area (forest cover ~21.7% + tree cover ~3.4%). NATIONAL FOREST POLICY 1988 TARGET: 33% (66% in hilly areas) — STILL UNMET after 35+ years. Top 5 forest-cover states by AREA: Madhya Pradesh > Arunachal Pradesh > Chhattisgarh > Odisha > Maharashtra. By PERCENTAGE OF AREA: Mizoram (highest, ~85%), Lakshadweep, A&N Islands, Arunachal Pradesh. Concerns: deforestation, tribal land rights (Forest Rights Act 2006), encroachment, mining. CO₂ ABSORPTION: forests absorb ~12% of India's emissions; key for climate goals (Paris commitment: 2.5-3 BtCO₂e additional sink by 2030).

cards.front:
TROPICAL EVERGREEN forests of India are mainly found in:

(A) Thar desert + Punjab plains
(B) Western Ghats + Andamans + NE India
(C) Deccan plateau + Maharashtra
(D) Himalayan high altitudes only
cards.back:
(B) Western Ghats + Andamans + NE India

Soils, Forests & Biodiversity — TROPICAL EVERGREEN — heavy rainfall (>200 cm), high temp + humidity. Multi-storied dense canopy; trees never shed all leaves at once. Areas: WESTERN GHATS (Kerala, southern Karnataka, Maharashtra, Goa); ANDAMAN + NICOBAR; NE INDIA (Assam, Meghalaya, Arunachal). KEY species: rosewood, mahogany, ebony, rubber, cinchona. Has 'wet evergreen' + 'semi-evergreen' subtypes. FOREST TYPES IN INDIA (Champion + Seth classification, 1968): (1) Tropical Evergreen + Semi-Evergreen; (2) Tropical Deciduous (LARGEST area — Sal, Teak); (3) Tropical Thorn / Scrub (arid Rajasthan); (4) Tidal / Mangrove (Sundarbans, Kutch coast); (5) Montane (Himalayan — sub-tropical, temperate, alpine). Each adapted to climate.

cards.front:
TEAK + SAL trees are found in which forest type?

(A) Mangrove forests on coasts
(B) Tropical deciduous (monsoon) forests
(C) Alpine + tundra Himalayan high zones
(D) Thorn scrub of Rajasthan deserts
cards.back:
(B) Tropical deciduous (monsoon) forests

Soils, Forests & Biodiversity — TROPICAL DECIDUOUS (MONSOON) FORESTS — India's MOST EXTENSIVE forest type (~38% of forest cover). Trees SHED leaves in dry season (winter / hot summer) to conserve water — adaptation to monsoon climate. RAINFALL: 70-200 cm/year. KEY SPECIES: TEAK (Tectona grandis) — premium timber, MP-Maharashtra; SAL (Shorea robusta) — Eastern + Central India; SANDALWOOD (Karnataka — state tree); BAMBOO; mahua, neem, sissoo, arjun, palash. SUBTYPES: MOIST DECIDUOUS (100-200 cm rain — TEAK) + DRY DECIDUOUS (70-100 cm — SAL). HUGE economic value: timber, fuel, bamboo, lac, gum, herbs. STATES: MP, Chhattisgarh, Maharashtra, Odisha — major teak/sal regions. FAST FACT: SAL is the dominant tree of Jharkhand + state tree of Chhattisgarh; TEAK is state tree of Maharashtra.

cards.front:
CHIPKO MOVEMENT (1973), to protect forests by HUGGING trees, started in:

(A) Bastar, Chhattisgarh's tribal area
(B) Reni village, Chamoli (Uttarakhand)
(C) Sundarbans of West Bengal
(D) Niyamgiri hills of Odisha
cards.back:
(B) Reni village, Chamoli (Uttarakhand)

Soils, Forests & Biodiversity — CHIPKO ('to embrace') — 26 March 1974, RENI VILLAGE (Chamoli, Uttarakhand). Women led by GAURA DEVI hugged trees to prevent loggers from cutting. Sparked nationwide environmental movement. KEY LEADERS: SUNDERLAL BAHUGUNA (Padma Vibhushan; coined 'ECOLOGY = PERMANENT ECONOMY'), CHANDI PRASAD BHATT (Magsaysay Award 1982). RESULT: 1980 BAN on commercial felling above 1000 m altitude in UP for 15 years. PRECURSOR: BISHNOI movement (1730, Khejarli, Rajasthan — Amrita Devi + 363 villagers killed protecting Khejri trees). LATER: APPIKO movement (1983, Karnataka — same idea in Western Ghats). NARMADA BACHAO ANDOLAN (Medha Patkar, 1985+). India has rich tradition of grassroots environmentalism.

NILGIRI BIOSPHERE RESERVE, India's first such reserve (1986), is in:

(A) Maharashtra (Western Ghats north)
(B) Tri-junction of TN, Karnataka, Kerala
(C) Andaman + Nicobar Islands area
(D) Sundarbans of West Bengal coast

(A) Mizoram (highest % cover but small area)
(B) Madhya Pradesh (largest area)
(C) Kerala (Western Ghats + plains)
(D) Odisha (eastern forests)
cards.back:
(B) Madhya Pradesh (largest area)

Soils, Forests & Biodiversity — MADHYA PRADESH — largest STATE forest area (~77,500 sq km). Reasons: large state size + Vindhya/Satpura hill ranges + sal-teak forests. MP alone has 11 NPs (Kanha, Bandhavgarh, Pench, Satpura — 'TIGER STATE' of India). FOREST POLICY 1988 set 33% target — far from achieved (~25%); main barriers = land hunger, mining demand, encroachment.

cards.front:
PROJECT TIGER (1973) was launched at which national park first?

(A) Kanha NP, in Madhya Pradesh here
(B) Jim Corbett NP (Uttarakhand) — first ever
(C) Bandhavgarh NP, in MP also here
(D) Ranthambore NP, in Rajasthan area
cards.back:
(B) Jim Corbett NP (Uttarakhand) — first ever

Soils, Forests & Biodiversity — PROJECT TIGER — launched 1 April 1973 at JIM CORBETT NATIONAL PARK (Uttarakhand) — also India's FIRST national park (1936, originally 'Hailey NP', renamed Jim Corbett 1957 after the British hunter-conservationist who saved Bengal tigers). INITIAL: 9 reserves, 268 tigers (1973 census). NOW: 55 tiger reserves, ~3682 tigers (2022 census — about 75% of world tiger population!). Indian govt's flagship conservation programme. NTCA (National Tiger Conservation Authority) since 2006. STATE WITH MOST TIGERS: Madhya Pradesh (~785 tigers) > Karnataka > Uttarakhand. Other ICONIC species programmes: PROJECT ELEPHANT (1992), PROJECT CHEETAH (2022 — 8 + 12 cheetahs from Namibia + S Africa to Kuno NP MP — first inter-continental large carnivore translocation), Project DOLPHIN, Hangul, etc.

cards.front:
The most widespread soil type in India, found in the northern plains, is:

(A) Black soil
(B) Alluvial soil
(C) Red soil
(D) Laterite soil
cards.back:
(B) Alluvial soil

Soils, Forests & Biodiversity — Alluvial soils cover about 40 % of India's land — deposited by the Ganga, Indus and Brahmaputra river systems and their tributaries. Very fertile; good for wheat, rice, sugarcane, jute. Two types: older Bhangar (on higher ground) and newer Khadar (on flood plains). Black cotton soil (regur) is next; red and laterite soils follow.

cards.front:
Black cotton soil (regur), ideal for cotton cultivation, is formed from the weathering of:

(A) Granite
(B) Basalt lava
(C) Limestone
(D) Sandstone
cards.back:
(B) Basalt lava

Soils, Forests & Biodiversity — Black cotton soil / regur — formed from the weathering of the Deccan Trap basalt lava flows. Found in Maharashtra, western MP, Gujarat, northern Karnataka, Telangana. Rich in calcium, potassium, magnesium; poor in nitrogen and organic matter. Retains moisture well — holds up well through the long dry season, which is why it suits cotton. Granite weathers to red soil.
