cards.front:
Red soils of India owe their colour to:

(A) Humus content
(B) Ferric oxide
(C) Calcium carbonate
(D) Potassium salts
cards.back:
(B) Ferric oxide

Soils, Forests & Biodiversity — Red soils get their colour from ferric (iron) oxide — formed in conditions of good aeration. They cover ~10 % of India — much of Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Andhra, parts of Odisha, Jharkhand, eastern MP. Relatively poor in nitrogen, phosphorus, humus; respond well to irrigation and fertilisers. Suit millets, groundnut, tobacco. Humus gives soil a dark-brown colour. iron oxide.

cards.front:
Laterite soils of India are formed in areas of:

(A) Cold and dry climate
(B) High temperature and heavy rainfall
(C) Semi-arid plateau climate
(D) Tropical desert climate
cards.back:
(B) High temperature and heavy rainfall

Soils, Forests & Biodiversity — Laterite soils — formed by intense leaching in high temperature + heavy rainfall. Silica is washed out, leaving iron and aluminium oxides. Found on the Western Ghats (Kerala, Karnataka, Maharashtra), Eastern Ghats (Odisha), NE hills, and the Malwa and Chhotanagpur plateaus. Poor in fertility; suited to cashew, tapioca, rubber, coffee, tea (with fertilisation). Laterite bricks are used in construction in Kerala and coastal Karnataka.

cards.front:
Which soil retains moisture for long periods, swells when wet and shrinks (forming cracks) when dry?

(A) Alluvial soil
(B) Black cotton soil (regur)
(C) Red soil
(D) Arid soil
cards.back:
(B) Black cotton soil (regur)

Soils, Forests & Biodiversity — Black cotton soil is rich in clay (montmorillonite) that absorbs water and swells; on drying, it shrinks and develops deep cracks — 'self-ploughing' nature. This helps it retain moisture and suits rain-fed cotton over long dry seasons. Alluvial soils drain more freely; red soils are coarser; arid soils are sandy with little clay.

cards.front:
Arid (desert) soils of Rajasthan are deficient in:

(A) Calcium and iron
(B) Nitrogen and humus
(C) Potassium and phosphate
(D) Sodium and potassium
cards.back:
(B) Nitrogen and humus

Soils, Forests & Biodiversity — Arid / desert soils are sandy (60-90 % sand), poor in nitrogen and humus (low organic matter because of sparse vegetation), but relatively rich in calcium and phosphates. They develop a calcareous kankar-hard pan below the surface. Can support crops like bajra, jowar, pulses where irrigated via canals like the Indira Gandhi Canal.

cards.front:
The most widely distributed soil in India by area is:

(A) Black (Regur) soil
(B) Alluvial soil
(C) Red soil
(D) Laterite soil
cards.back:
(B) Alluvial soil

Soils, Forests & Biodiversity — Alluvial soil — covers ~46% of India's total area. Two sub-types: Khadar (newer alluvium, fine-grained, fertile, replenished annually by floods) and Bhangar (older alluvium, contains kankar/calcareous nodules). Highly fertile — supports rice, wheat, sugarcane, oilseeds, pulses. Black soil is 2nd most extensive (~16%).

Black soil (Regur) is best suited for the cultivation of:

(B) Cotton — hence also called 'black cotton soil'
(C) Tea
(D) Coffee
cards.back:

Soils, Forests & Biodiversity — Black soil — formed from weathering of Deccan Trap basalts. Rich in iron, magnesium, lime, alumina; deficient in nitrogen, phosphorus, organic matter. Best for cotton, also good for jowar, wheat, sugarcane, oilseeds, citrus. Trap option Tea — actually grown on red/laterite soils; Coffee — laterite/red soils.

cards.front:
Laterite soil — typical of high-rainfall plateau regions — gets its red colour from:

(A) Manganese
(B) High iron oxide content
(C) Volcanic ash
(D) Calcium carbonate
cards.back:
(B) High iron oxide content

Found in Western Ghats (Kerala, Karnataka, Goa), Eastern Ghats (Odisha), parts of Assam, Meghalaya, Chhattisgarh. Generally infertile (low N, P, K), acidic; useful for cashew, rubber, coffee, tea, coconut. Hardens on exposure → used as building bricks. Same root word 'laterite' derives.

Match the soil type with its dominant region — which pairing is INCORRECT?

(A) Black soil — Deccan Plateau
(B) Mountain soil — Western Ghats / Himalayas
(C) Arid (desert) soil — Punjab plains
(D) Red soil — Eastern Ghats
cards.back:

Soils, Forests & Biodiversity — Arid / desert soil is found in RAJASTHAN (Thar desert), Haryana's southern parts, Gujarat's Kutch — NOT Punjab plains (which have rich alluvial soil from Indus tributaries). Desert soils are sandy, low in clay/humus, alkaline, saline; need irrigation + nitrogen. Indira Gandhi Canal has converted parts of western Rajasthan into productive agricultural land. Other major Indian soil types — peaty/marshy (Kerala backwaters, Sundarbans), forest soil (humus-rich on hills), saline-alkaline (Reh — UP, Haryana, dryland Maharashtra).

cards.front:
Khadar and Bhangar are sub-types of which soil?

(A) Black soil
(B) Alluvial soil
(C) Red soil
(D) Laterite soil
cards.back:

Khadar suits intensive cultivation; Bhangar is good for plantation / construction. Term Bhangar comes from 'bhang' meaning broken / weathered.

cards.front:
Soil erosion in India is most severe in which form?

(A) Wind erosion only
(B) Water erosion (sheet, rill, gully)
(C) Glacial erosion
(D) Coastal erosion
cards.back:
(B) Water erosion (sheet, rill, gully)

Soils, Forests & Biodiversity — Water erosion — main culprit (~75% of erosion-affected area in India). Forms: sheet (uniform thin layer removal), rill (small channels), gully (deep channels — Chambal-Yamuna ravines famous), riverbank, coastal. Wind erosion mostly in Rajasthan/Gujarat (~25% of total). Total degraded land in India ~30% (ICAR-IISWC). Mitigation — afforestation, contour bunding, terrace farming, gully plugging, check dams, mulching. Watershed development is the integrated approach.

cards.front:
ICAR's National Bureau of Soil Survey and Land-Use Planning (NBSS&LUP) is headquartered in:

(A) New Delhi
(B) Nagpur
(C) Hyderabad
(D) Bangalore
cards.back:
(B) Nagpur

Soils, Forests & Biodiversity — NBSS&LUP — Nagpur, Maharashtra. Established 1976 under ICAR (Indian Council of Agricultural Research). Mandate — soil surveys at various scales (1:1M for India, district-level), classification, mapping (Soil Resource Maps of India), land-use planning. Issues 'Soil Health Card' jointly with state agriculture departments. India also has the Soil Health Card scheme (launched 2015 by PM Modi) — every farmer gets a card with soil-test results + recommendations every 2 years.

cards.front:
JIM CORBETT NATIONAL PARK, India's first national park, is located in:

(A) Uttarakhand (Nainital district)
(B) Uttar Pradesh (further south)
(C) Madhya Pradesh (central area)
(D) Himachal Pradesh (further west)
cards.back:
(A) Uttarakhand (Nainital district)

Soils, Forests & Biodiversity — JIM CORBETT NATIONAL PARK — INDIA'S FIRST national park, established 1936 as 'Hailey National Park' (after then-Governor of UP Sir Malcolm Hailey). RENAMED to JIM CORBETT (1957) after the legendary British-Indian hunter-turned-conservationist who single-handedly stopped several man-eating tigers in the area, then became wildlife photographer/author ('Man-eaters of Kumaon'). LOCATION: NAINITAL + Pauri Garhwal districts, UTTARAKHAND. AREA: ~520 sq km core; ~1,300 sq km tiger reserve. FAUNA: ~250 BENGAL TIGERS (one of highest densities in India); leopard, elephant, sambar, chital, gharial, mahseer fish (in Ramganga river). FIRST 'PROJECT TIGER' RESERVE — 1973 (along with Bandipur, Kanha, Manas, Melghat, Palamau, Ranthambore, Simlipal, Sundarbans). RAMGANGA RIVER flows through. Visited by hundreds of thousands of tourists yearly. PROJECT TIGER stats (current): ~3,167 tigers in India (2022 census, ~71% of world's wild tigers), up from ~1,400 in 2006. INDIA'S FIRST NATIONAL PARK chronology: (1) Jim Corbett 1936. (2) Kanha NP 1955. (3) Tadoba 1955. (4) Sundarbans 1984. (5) Many more in 1980s-90s. PYQ FREQUENCY: Corbett-first-NP fact in SSC GA, UPSC, NDA — 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
KAZIRANGA NATIONAL PARK is famous for which UNESCO-listed flagship species?

(A) One-horned rhinoceros (Rhino unicornis)
(B) Royal Bengal tiger primarily
(C) Asiatic lion (Gir-only species)
(D) Asian elephant (multiple parks)
cards.back:
(A) One-horned rhinoceros (Rhino unicornis)

Soils, Forests & Biodiversity — KAZIRANGA NATIONAL PARK (Assam, ~430 sq km in core, ~1,000 sq km in greater Kaziranga). UNESCO World Heritage Site (1985). FLAGSHIP: GREAT INDIAN ONE-HORNED RHINOCEROS (Rhinoceros unicornis). Population: ~2,613 rhinos as per 2022 census — ~70% of WORLD'S population of this species. CONSERVATION SUCCESS: in 1900s, only ~12 rhinos left in Assam due to poaching for horn (used in Vietnamese/Chinese traditional medicine). Strict protection brought them back. ALSO HOSTS: Asian elephant, swamp deer (barasingha), water buffalo, Bengal tiger (~120 — highest density anywhere!), Hoolock gibbon, ~480 bird species. LANDSCAPE: alluvial floodplains of BRAHMAPUTRA river; tall elephant grass + marshes. PROBLEMS: (1) ANNUAL FLOODS — Brahmaputra inundates ~80% of park (June-September); animals drown or move to highways (vehicle collisions). (2) POACHING — though declining; horn smuggling remains. CONSERVATION TIMELINE: 1908 declared Reserve Forest by Curzon's wife Mary Curzon (after she heard about rhino disappearance); 1916 game sanctuary; 1974 NP. RHINO POPULATIONS in INDIA: Kaziranga (~2,600), Manas NP (~50, recovering), Pobitora WS (~100, highest density per area), Orang NP, Dudhwa (UP). PYQ FREQUENCY: Kaziranga-rhino in SSC, UPSC, NDA 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
GIR NATIONAL PARK is the only HOME of which big cat species in India?

(A) Asiatic Lion (Panthera leo persica)
(B) Royal Bengal Tiger (multiple parks)
(C) Indian Leopard (widely distributed)
(D) Snow Leopard (Himalayan species)
cards.back:
(A) Asiatic Lion (Panthera leo persica)

Soils, Forests & Biodiversity — GIR NATIONAL PARK (Junagadh, GUJARAT) — ~258 sq km core; ~1,400 sq km wildlife sanctuary. THE ONLY home of ASIATIC LION (Panthera leo persica) in INDIA — and indeed in the WILD globally (besides a few in Africa as African lion subspecies). POPULATION: ~675 lions (2020 census); up from ~12 in 1907 — incredible conservation comeback under the Nawabs of Junagadh and later Indian govt. ASIATIC vs AFRICAN LION: Asiatic slightly smaller, has folds of skin on belly (rare in African); MANES less prominent in Asiatic males (ears visible). HISTORY: lions once roamed across N. Africa, Middle East, Persia, India. By 1900s, only Gir remained. IUCN: Asiatic lion classified as ENDANGERED. CONSERVATION CHALLENGES: (1) Single-population RISK — disease (canine distemper killed 24 lions in 2018) could wipe them out. (2) Translocation to KUNO NATIONAL PARK (MP) was approved by SC 2013, but Gujarat resisted. KUNO eventually became home to AFRICAN CHEETAHS reintroduced in 2022. (3) Human-wildlife conflict — Maldhari pastoralists share habitat. ASIATIC LION SUBSPECIES status: classified as Panthera leo persica until 2017; now considered same as Panthera leo leo (Asiatic-North African subspecies). PYQ FREQUENCY: Gir-Lion in SSC, UPSC, NDA — 1× per cycle.

(3) Human-wildlife conflict — Maldhari pastoralists share habitat. ASIATIC LION SUBSPECIES status: classified as Panthera leo persica until 2017; now considered same as Panthera leo leo (Asiatic-North African subspecies). PYQ FREQUENCY: Gir-Lion in SSC, UPSC, NDA — 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
SUNDARBANS, the world's largest mangrove forest, is located in which Indian state?

(A) West Bengal (Bay of Bengal coast)
(B) Odisha (Mahanadi delta side)
(C) Tamil Nadu (eastern coast area)
(D) Andhra Pradesh (with Pulicat lake)
cards.back:
(A) West Bengal (Bay of Bengal coast)

Soils, Forests & Biodiversity — SUNDARBANS — WORLD'S LARGEST MANGROVE forest. Spans WEST BENGAL (India) + Khulna (BANGLADESH); total ~10,000 sq km, of which ~4,260 sq km in INDIA. Indian portion: SUNDARBANS NATIONAL PARK (1984), tiger reserve, biosphere reserve, UNESCO WORLD HERITAGE SITE (1987). NAME: 'Sundarbans' = 'beautiful forest' in Bengali (or possibly named after SUNDARI tree, Heritiera fomes — dominant mangrove species). HABITAT: complex network of tidal channels, mudflats, mangrove islands at the GANGA-BRAHMAPUTRA delta. FLAGSHIP: ROYAL BENGAL TIGER — UNIQUE 'SWIMMING TIGERS' that hunt in waist-deep water and prey on aquatic creatures; ~96 tigers in Indian portion. Famous for MAN-EATING incidents (~50 humans killed by tigers each year historically; now declining with conservation/awareness). OTHER SPECIES: estuarine crocodile, gharial, water monitor, Olive Ridley turtle, dolphins. CYCLONES: Sundarbans is regularly battered by Bay of Bengal cyclones (Aila 2009, Bulbul 2019, Amphan 2020) — mangroves provide CRUCIAL STORM PROTECTION for both coastlines. CLIMATE CHANGE: rising sea level threatens to submerge much of Sundarbans by 2100; some islands already lost (Lohachara, Bedford). PYQ FREQUENCY: Sundarbans in SSC, UPSC, NDA, NEET environment — 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
RANTHAMBORE NATIONAL PARK, famous for tiger sightings, is in which state?

(A) Rajasthan (Sawai Madhopur)
(B) Madhya Pradesh (Bandhavgarh near)
(C) Gujarat (close to Gir park)
(D) Karnataka (Bandipur Park area)
cards.back:
(A) Rajasthan (Sawai Madhopur)

Soils, Forests & Biodiversity — RANTHAMBORE NATIONAL PARK — Sawai Madhopur district, RAJASTHAN. Area: ~392 sq km core; ~1,400 sq km tiger reserve. TIGER POPULATION: ~75-80 (2022 census). FAMOUS FOR: (1) Spectacular RANTHAMBORE FORT inside the park — 10th-century AD; UNESCO Heritage. (2) MACHHALI THE TIGRESS (~1996-2016) — the most photographed tiger in the world; lived ~20 years; gave birth to 11 cubs, contributing significantly to RECOVERY of Indian tiger population. (3) Easy tiger sightings due to OPEN, semi-arid terrain (different from dense forests of Sundarbans/Manas). LANDSCAPE: dry deciduous forest + grasslands + lakes (Padam Talao). FAUNA: Bengal tiger, leopard, sloth bear, sambar, chital, blackbuck, mugger crocodile. ONE OF FIRST 9 PROJECT TIGER reserves (1973). KEY CONSERVATION: 'BUFFER ZONE' management, anti-poaching patrols, eco-tourism. RECENT CONCERNS: tiger MORTALITY due to occasional in-fighting + dispersal pressures. RANTHAMBORE is paired with KEOLADEO GHANA NP (Bharatpur, Rajasthan — UNESCO 1985, formerly bird sanctuary), TAL CHHAPAR (blackbuck sanctuary), DESERT NP (Jaisalmer area). RAJASTHAN's TIGER STATUS: ~88 tigers across Ranthambore, Sariska, Mukundra Hills (2022). PYQ FREQUENCY: Ranthambore-Rajasthan in SSC, UPSC, KAS — 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
PERIYAR NATIONAL PARK, famous for its boat safari and elephants, is in which state?

(A) Kerala (Idukki district)
(B) Tamil Nadu (the next state east)
(C) Karnataka (Western Ghats also)
(D) Andhra Pradesh (further north)
cards.back:
(A) Kerala (Idukki district)

Soils, Forests & Biodiversity — PERIYAR NATIONAL PARK — IDUKKI district, KERALA, in the Western Ghats. Core area: ~305 sq km; total tiger reserve: ~925 sq km. SPECIAL FEATURE: PERIYAR LAKE (artificial, formed by 1895 dam by British) lies INSIDE the park — visitors can take BOAT SAFARIS to spot wildlife along banks. FLAGSHIP: ASIAN ELEPHANT (Periyar has ~1,000 elephants — one of largest populations in S. India). Also Bengal tiger (~40), gaur (Indian bison), sambar deer, langur, lion-tailed macaque (endangered, endemic to W. Ghats). UNIQUE SPECIES: Nilgiri tahr (mountain goat, endemic to S. India W. Ghats). NEELAKURINJI flowers (Strobilanthes kunthiana) bloom every 12 YEARS — last big bloom 2018. PROJECT TIGER reserve (1978). LOCATION: ~190 km from Kochi airport; popular among S. Indian tourists. NEAR THEKKADY town. WESTERN GHATS — UNESCO Natural Heritage Site (2012); covers 39 sites, biodiversity hotspot, ~30% of India's flora and ~35% of fauna. KERALA WILDLIFE: also Wayanad WS, Silent Valley NP (Mathikettan Shola), Eravikulam NP (Munnar, where Neelakurinji blooms). PYQ FREQUENCY: Periyar-Kerala in SSC, UPSC, NDA 1× per cycle. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests state-park associations.

cards.front:
Which national park became HOME to AFRICAN CHEETAHS reintroduced to India in 2022?

(A) Kuno National Park (Madhya Pradesh)
(B) Ranthambore in Rajasthan area
(C) Bandipur in Karnataka also
(D) Gir in Gujarat (lions only)
cards.back:
(A) Kuno National Park (Madhya Pradesh)

Soils, Forests & Biodiversity — KUNO NATIONAL PARK (Sheopur district, MADHYA PRADESH) — became home to AFRICAN CHEETAHS reintroduced under PROJECT CHEETAH on 17 SEPTEMBER 2022 (PM Modi's birthday). FIRST BATCH: 8 cheetahs from Namibia (5 females + 3 males), released in special soft-release enclosures. SECOND BATCH (Feb 2023): 12 cheetahs from South Africa. CONTEXT: ASIATIC CHEETAH was DECLARED EXTINCT in India in 1952 (last 3 shot by Maharaja Ramanuj Pratap Singh of Korea, Chhattisgarh in 1947). African cheetahs are a different sub-species; introduced as 'free-living' for first time outside Africa. STATUS as of late 2024: ~25 cheetahs alive (incl. cubs born in India). MORTALITY: several cheetahs died (organ failure, infections, fights) — sparking criticism. ORIGINAL PLAN for KUNO: was supposed to be SECOND HOME for ASIATIC LIONS (Gir-only) per SC 2013 order; Gujarat resisted; eventually cheetahs were chosen instead. KUNO LANDSCAPE: dry deciduous forest, grasslands — similar to African savanna habitat. WATCHED: 'Sasha' (first cheetah to die in India, March 2023, kidney issue); 'Asha' (gave birth in 2023). RELATED: African vs Asiatic cheetah are genetically separate subspecies (Acinonyx jubatus jubatus vs A. j. venaticus). PYQ FREQUENCY: Project Cheetah is current-affairs but appears in PT 2024-26.

cards.front:
The 'Seven Sisters' of North-East India are Assam, Arunachal Pradesh, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland and:

(A) Sikkim
(B) Tripura
(C) West Bengal
(D) Bhutan
cards.back:
(B) Tripura

Soils, Forests & Biodiversity — The 'Seven Sisters' coined by journalist Jyoti Prasad Saikia (1972) refers to Assam, Arunachal, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland and Tripura. Sikkim was added to the NE Council in 2002 — popularly called the 'brother' of the Seven Sisters. Together, they are the 8 NE states. Total area: ~262,000 km² (8% of India); population ~46 million (~3.8%). Border with 5 countries: China, Bhutan, Myanmar, Bangladesh, Nepal.

cards.front:
Three NE states attained full statehood on the same day — 21 January 1972. They are:

(A) Manipur, Tripura, Meghalaya
(B) Mizoram, Arunachal Pradesh, Sikkim
(C) Assam, Nagaland, Manipur
(D) Manipur, Sikkim, Mizoram
cards.back:
(A) Manipur, Tripura, Meghalaya

Soils, Forests & Biodiversity — 21 January 1972 — Manipur, Tripura and Meghalaya all became full states (NE Areas Reorganisation Act, 1971). Earlier Manipur and Tripura were UTs; Meghalaya was carved out of Assam (autonomous state in 1970, then full state). Other NE statehood dates: Nagaland — 1 Dec 1963 (first to break away from Assam); Sikkim — 26 Apr 1975 (36th amendment); Arunachal Pradesh and Mizoram — 20 Feb 1987 (same day).

cards.back:

India's only Salt Lake (a UNESCO Ramsar site) is in which NE state?

(A) Manipur
(B) Sikkim — Tso Lhamo / Gurudongmar
(C) Loktak Lake — but it's freshwater
(D) None — there is no salt lake in NE India; Sambhar (Rajasthan) is India's largest

NE has many freshwater lakes — Loktak (Manipur, largest in NE), Tsomgo / Changu (Sikkim, glacial), Gurudongmar (Sikkim, sacred), Umiam (Meghalaya, man-made hydropower lake), Dawki / Umngot (Meghalaya, crystal-clear). cards.front:
Mawsynram — recognised as the wettest place on Earth — is in:

(A) Mizoram
(B) Meghalaya
(C) Assam
(D) Arunachal Pradesh
cards.back:
(B) Meghalaya

Soils, Forests & Biodiversity — Mawsynram (East Khasi Hills, Meghalaya) records ~11,872 mm of average annual rainfall — Guinness World Records confirms it as Earth's wettest. Cherrapunji (10 km away) was the previous holder. The hills act as a barrier to monsoon clouds rising over the Bay of Bengal, forcing them to dump moisture. State capital Shillong is also in the same district. 'Meghalaya' = 'abode of clouds' in Sanskrit.

cards.front:
The 'Apatani' tribe — famous for nose plugs and elaborate facial tattoos (now discouraged) — lives in which Indian state?

(A) Nagaland
(B) Arunachal Pradesh — Ziro Valley
(C) Manipur
(D) Sikkim
cards.back:
(B) Arunachal Pradesh — Ziro Valley

Soils, Forests & Biodiversity — Apatani tribe inhabits the Ziro Valley (Lower Subansiri district) of Arunachal Pradesh. Famous for distinctive face tattoos (younger women no longer practice; tradition was meant to make them less attractive to raiders), nose plugs (yapping hullo), and innovative paddy-cum-fish cultivation. The Ziro Valley itself is on UNESCO's tentative list. Apatani is one of ~26 major tribes of Arunachal — others include Adi, Galo, Mishmi, Nyishi, Monpa.

Among the eight NE states, which one borders the highest number of other Indian states?

(A) Assam — 7 Indian states
(B) Manipur — 4 Indian states

cards.back:

cards.front:
PROJECT TIGER was launched in INDIA in:

(A) 1973 (under PM Indira Gandhi)
(B) 1947 (right after independence)
(C) 1986 (Wildlife Protection Act)
(D) 2014 (Modi government era)
cards.back:
(A) 1973 (under PM Indira Gandhi)

Soils, Forests & Biodiversity — PROJECT TIGER — launched 1 APRIL 1973 by PM INDIRA GANDHI's government. INITIAL: 9 tiger reserves covering ~14,000 sq km — Corbett (Uttarakhand), Manas (Assam), Palamau (Jharkhand), Simlipal (Odisha), Bandipur (Karnataka), Melghat (Maharashtra), Kanha (MP), Ranthambore (Rajasthan), Sundarbans (WB). MOTIVATION: by 1972, Bengal tiger population had declined to ~1,800 from ~40,000 in 1900 — alarming poaching + habitat loss. NOW: 56 TIGER RESERVES (2024) covering ~78,000 sq km (~2.4% of India's land area). NATIONAL TIGER CONSERVATION AUTHORITY (NTCA, 2006) — statutory body under Wildlife Protection Act 1972 (amended 2006) to oversee Project Tiger. TIGER CENSUS by NTCA (every 4 years): (1) 2006: 1,411 tigers. (2) 2010: 1,706. (3) 2014: 2,226. (4) 2018: 2,967. (5) 2022: 3,167 (~71% of world's wild tigers). India hosts the WORLD'S LARGEST tiger population. FUNDING: ~₹400 crore/year central + state contribution. CONSERVATION SUCCESS: tiger population MORE THAN DOUBLED in 16 years (2006-2022). CHALLENGES: human-wildlife conflict, dispersal corridors, poaching pressure (still occurs). RECENT: 50 YEARS OF PROJECT TIGER celebration (April 2023, Mysuru) — PM Modi launched 'INTERNATIONAL BIG CATS ALLIANCE'. PYQ FREQUENCY: Project Tiger basics in UPSC, SSC, NDA — 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
BANDHAVGARH National Park, famous for high tiger density, is in which state?

(A) Madhya Pradesh (Umaria district)
(B) Rajasthan (Sawai Madhopur)
(C) Karnataka (Bandipur area)
(D) Maharashtra (Tadoba area)
cards.back:
(A) Madhya Pradesh (Umaria district)

Soils, Forests & Biodiversity — BANDHAVGARH NATIONAL PARK — UMARIA district, MADHYA PRADESH. Area: ~448 sq km core + ~820 sq km buffer = ~1,536 sq km tiger reserve. ESTABLISHED: 1968 NP, 1993 tiger reserve. TIGER DENSITY: among the HIGHEST in India — ~135 tigers as of 2022; ~7-8 tigers per 100 sq km. RAJOR ATTRACTIONS: BANDHAVGARH FORT — 2,000-year-old hilltop fort (cited in Ramayana — Lakshmana built it for his brother Bharata; 'Bandhav-garh' = brother's fort); HUNDREDS of CAVES from 1st century BCE-CE, with rock paintings; SHESHSHAYYA — sculpture of Vishnu reclining on serpent. WHITE TIGERS: discovered in WILD here — MOHAN (1951), captured by Maharaja Martand Singh of Rewa, became basis of all white tigers in zoos. Now no wild whites; in zoos only. MADHYA PRADESH — known as 'TIGER STATE OF INDIA'; hosts SIX tiger reserves: (1) BANDHAVGARH. (2) KANHA — inspiration for Kipling's 'Jungle Book' (Sher Khan's territory; Mowgli area). (3) PENCH — also Jungle Book setting. (4) SATPURA — central highlands. (5) PANNA — back from extinction (zero tigers in 2009; ~80 by 2022). (6) SANJAY-DUBRI. Plus RANTHAMBORE (Rajasthan) — for comparison. PYQ FREQUENCY: Bandhavgarh-MP in SSC GA, UPSC, NDA 1× per cycle.

TIGER DENSITY: among the HIGHEST in India — ~135 tigers as of 2022; ~7-8 tigers per 100 sq km. RAJOR ATTRACTIONS: BANDHAVGARH FORT — 2,000-year-old hilltop fort (cited in Ramayana — Lakshmana built it for his brother Bharata; 'Bandhav-garh' = brother's fort); HUNDREDS of CAVES from 1st century BCE-CE, with rock paintings; SHESHSHAYYA — sculpture of Vishnu reclining on serpent. WHITE TIGERS: discovered in WILD here — MOHAN (1951), captured by Maharaja Martand Singh of Rewa, became basis of all white tigers in zoos. Now no wild whites; in zoos only. MADHYA PRADESH — known as 'TIGER STATE OF INDIA'; hosts SIX tiger reserves: (1) BANDHAVGARH. (2) KANHA — inspiration for Kipling's 'Jungle Book' (Sher Khan's territory; Mowgli area). (3) PENCH — also Jungle Book setting. (4) SATPURA — central highlands. (5) PANNA — back from extinction (zero tigers in 2009; ~80 by 2022). (6) SANJAY-DUBRI. Plus RANTHAMBORE (Rajasthan) — for comparison. PYQ FREQUENCY: Bandhavgarh-MP in SSC GA, UPSC, NDA 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
Per the 2022 Tiger Census, INDIA had approximately HOW MANY wild tigers?

(A) 3,167 tigers (~71% of world's)
(B) 1,706 tigers (the 2010 figure)
(C) 5,000 tigers (over-estimate)
(D) 10,000 tigers (way over-shot)
cards.back:
(A) 3,167 tigers (~71% of world's)

Soils, Forests & Biodiversity — INDIA TIGER POPULATION (2022 census, results announced 9 April 2023): 3,167 tigers — approximately 71% of WORLD'S wild tiger population. World total: ~4,500-5,000. METHODOLOGY: M-STrIPES (Monitoring System for Tigers — Intensive Protection and Ecological Status) — combines camera traps, scat-DNA, footprint analysis, satellite imagery. Each tiger photographed by trap cameras has UNIQUE STRIPE PATTERN (like fingerprints) — counted individually. STATE-WISE: Madhya Pradesh ~785 (highest); Karnataka ~563 (2nd); Uttarakhand ~560 (3rd); Maharashtra ~444; Tamil Nadu ~306; Kerala ~213; Assam ~190. RECENT NEW RESERVES: Veerangana Durgavati (MP, 2023), Madhav Tiger Reserve (MP, 2025) — taking total to 56. WORLD TIGER DAY: 29 JULY (since 2010, St. Petersburg Tiger Summit, where 13 'tiger range' countries pledged to DOUBLE tigers by 2022 — TX2 GOAL — India achieved this 4 years early). 'TIGER RANGE COUNTRIES': India, Russia, China, Bangladesh, Nepal, Bhutan, Myanmar, Thailand, Vietnam, Laos, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia (extinct). KEY THREATS: poaching for skin/bones (Chinese traditional medicine), habitat fragmentation, human-wildlife conflict. SUCCESS PILLARS: protected areas + community-based conservation + cross-border cooperation. PYQ FREQUENCY: tiger census + WORLD share in UPSC, SSC GA — 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
NAGARHOLE NATIONAL PARK / Tiger Reserve is located in:

(A) Karnataka (Kodagu + Mysuru districts)
(B) Tamil Nadu (Mudumalai area)
(C) Kerala (Periyar adjacent area)
(D) Andhra Pradesh (Nallamala area)
cards.back:
(A) Karnataka (Kodagu + Mysuru districts)

Soils, Forests & Biodiversity — NAGARHOLE NATIONAL PARK — KARNATAKA, in KODAGU (Coorg) + MYSURU districts. Area: ~847 sq km. Original name: RAJIV GANDHI NATIONAL PARK (renamed for the former PM in 1992). NAME 'NAGARHOLE' = 'snake river' in Kannada (Naga + Hole = serpentine river that flows through the park). PART OF NILGIRI BIOSPHERE RESERVE — UNESCO heritage cluster: Nagarhole + Bandipur (Karnataka) + Wayanad (Kerala) + Mudumalai (Tamil Nadu) + Mukurthi (TN). Forms a CONTIGUOUS LANDSCAPE crucial for tiger + elephant connectivity. TIGERS at Nagarhole: ~150+ (one of highest densities in India). Other species: Asian elephant (~3,000+ in greater Nilgiri block, world's largest population), gaur, sambar, leopard, dhole (Indian wild dog), sloth bear. KABINI RESERVOIR within the park — winter dry season concentrates wildlife near water; great for safari. NATIVE COMMUNITIES: JENU KURUBA, BETTA KURUBA tribes traditionally lived here; relocated mostly outside park (some controversy over rehabilitation policies). PROJECT TIGER reserve since 1999. KARNATAKA tiger reserves: (1) Nagarhole. (2) Bandipur. (3) Bhadra. (4) Anshi-Dandeli. (5) BRT (Biligiri Ranganatha Temple). PYQ FREQUENCY: state-tiger reserve mapping in SSC GA, UPSC, KAS — 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
Which Indian tiger reserve is FAMOUS for its TIGERS THAT SWIM in saline waters and HUNT in mangroves?

(A) Sundarbans (West Bengal mangroves)
(B) Kaziranga (Assam grasslands)
(C) Bandipur (Karnataka jungles)
(D) Periyar (Kerala lake area)
cards.back:
(A) Sundarbans (West Bengal mangroves)

Soils, Forests & Biodiversity — SUNDARBANS TIGER RESERVE — UNIQUE among tiger habitats; the WORLD'S LARGEST mangrove forest, in WEST BENGAL (and continuing into Bangladesh). Area: ~2,585 sq km tiger reserve in Indian portion; ~10,000 sq km total ecosystem. UNESCO World Heritage 1987; Ramsar wetland; Biosphere Reserve. UNIQUE TIGER ADAPTATIONS: (1) SWIM regularly in tidal channels and saline water — only place in world where tigers swim daily (other tigers can swim but Sundarbans tigers do it as routine). (2) Hunt aquatic prey — fish, crabs, monitor lizards, deer crossing channels. (3) Drink BRACKISH water (low salinity tolerance). (4) Sometimes attack humans entering forest for honey, fish, wood — Sundarbans is the WORLD'S MOST DANGEROUS TIGER REGION for humans (~30-50 deaths/year historically; declining with awareness + protection). TIGER COUNT (2022): ~96 in Indian Sundarbans. CHALLENGES: (1) RISING SEA LEVELS — climate change threatens habitat. (2) CYCLONES — Aila 2009, Amphan 2020 devastated. (3) PROXIMITY TO HUMAN VILLAGES — conflict. CYCLONES + storm surges have submerged some islands (Lohachara, Bedford). NEIGHBORING fauna: estuarine crocodile, water monitor, Olive Ridley turtle, Gangetic dolphin (rare). HEAD MASKS worn by villagers (mask of human face on back of head — tigers attack from behind, mask deceives them) — partial success. PYQ FREQUENCY: Sundarbans-tiger uniqueness in UPSC, SSC, NDA 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
SARISKA Tiger Reserve, which famously had ZERO tigers in 2005, is in:

(A) Rajasthan (Alwar district)
(B) Madhya Pradesh (Indore zone)
(C) Gujarat (next to Gir park area)
(D) Haryana (Aravalli foothills)
cards.back:
(A) Rajasthan (Alwar district)

Soils, Forests & Biodiversity — SARISKA TIGER RESERVE — ALWAR district, RAJASTHAN (Aravalli hills). Area: 881 sq km; Project Tiger reserve since 1978. INFAMOUS FOR: 'TIGER WIPE-OUT' — by 2005, ALL tigers had been POACHED (last sighting 2003); officially confirmed ZERO tigers in 2005 — major embarrassment for Project Tiger; sparked policy reforms + creation of NTCA (2006). REINTRODUCTION (2008): tigers from Ranthambore translocated by helicopter — first ever such reintroduction in India. Slow recovery — ~25-30 tigers as of 2024. PROBLEMS faced: (1) POACHING gangs (organized crime, some allegedly with insider help). (2) HUMAN VILLAGES inside — ~25 villages (~5,000 people) still inside reserve; cattle grazing competes with prey species. (3) SARISKA HIGHWAY: NH-248A — passes through critical tiger habitat; nighttime traffic disrupts wildlife. KEY SITE: KANKWARI FORT (16th c.) — Aurangzeb imprisoned brother Dara Shikoh here; popular tourist spot WITHIN reserve. NEAR ATTRACTIONS: PANDUPOL HANUMAN TEMPLE (Mahabharata legend); Bhangarh Fort (haunted reputation). RECENT — VILLAGE RELOCATION: gradual (slow) relocation of villages; ~5 done; 20 remain. PROJECT TIGER REVIEW: Sariska episode triggered TIGER TASK FORCE (2005, headed by Sunita Narain) → recommendations led to: (1) NTCA establishment (2006). (2) M-STrIPES protocol for monitoring. (3) Larger buffer zones. PYQ FREQUENCY: Sariska story in UPSC, SSC.

cards.front:
WORLD TIGER DAY is observed annually on:

(A) 29 July (since 2010 St. Petersburg)
(B) 5 June (World Environment Day)
(C) 22 April (Earth Day mostly)
(D) 1 April (Project Tiger India)
cards.back:
(A) 29 July (since 2010 St. Petersburg)

Soils, Forests & Biodiversity — WORLD TIGER DAY — 29 JULY annually. ORIGIN: 2010 ST. PETERSBURG TIGER SUMMIT in Russia, where 13 TIGER RANGE COUNTRIES pledged to DOUBLE wild tiger population by 2022 (TX2 goal). India achieved this milestone EARLY (by 2018); other countries had mixed results. 13 TIGER RANGE COUNTRIES: India, Russia, China, Bangladesh, Bhutan, Nepal, Myanmar, Thailand, Vietnam, Laos, Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia. As of 2022 STATUS: India ~3,167 (largest); Russia ~600 (Amur tigers in Far East); Indonesia ~400 (Sumatran). EXTINCT in: Cambodia, Vietnam, Laos (functionally), Singapore (long ago), Bali, Java. KEY GLOBAL OBSERVANCES related to wildlife: (1) WORLD WILDLIFE DAY — 3 March. (2) WORLD ENVIRONMENT DAY — 5 June (PM Modi's 'Mission LiFE' launched on this day 2022). (3) WORLD TIGER DAY — 29 July. (4) WORLD ELEPHANT DAY — 12 August. (5) WORLD LION DAY — 10 August. (6) WORLD MIGRATORY BIRD DAY — 2nd Sat of May + Oct. INDIA-SPECIFIC: (a) PROJECT TIGER ANNIVERSARY — 1 April (1973). (b) PROJECT ELEPHANT — 1992. (c) PROJECT LION — 2018 (for Asiatic lions). PROJECT CHEETAH — 2022 (reintroduction at Kuno NP). NATIONAL ANIMAL: Bengal Tiger (since 1972, replaced lion which was prior). PYQ FREQUENCY: World Tiger Day in SSC GA, UPSC current affairs 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
KHARIF CROPS in India are sown around:

(A) Monsoon arrival (June-July) + harvested Sep-Oct
(B) Winter (October-November) and harvested March-April
(C) Pre-summer (March-April) and harvested July-August
(D) Year-round, irrigation-dependent farming
cards.back:
(A) Monsoon arrival (June-July) + harvested Sep-Oct

Agriculture & Industry — KHARIF (मानसूनी / monsoon) crops — sown JUNE-JULY (with SW monsoon onset), harvested SEP-OCT. Need warm + wet conditions. KEY KHARIF CROPS: rice (paddy), maize, jowar, bajra, ragi, cotton, jute, sugarcane, soybean, groundnut, pulses (arhar/tur, moong, urad). RABI crops — sown OCT-NOV, harvested MAR-APR. Need cool + dry conditions. KEY RABI CROPS: WHEAT (largest), barley, mustard, peas, gram (chana), masoor, linseed, oats. ZAID — short summer crops (March-June); watermelon, muskmelon, cucumber, vegetables, fodder. Indian agri = ~50% of workforce, ~17% of GDP. NORTHERN states (Punjab, Haryana, UP) — wheat-rice belt. SOUTHERN: rice + cotton + spices. EAST: rice + jute. MONSOON dependence is a key vulnerability.

cards.front:
India's LARGEST PRODUCER of WHEAT is:

(A) Uttar Pradesh (largest wheat producer)
(B) Punjab (highest yield per hectare)
(C) Madhya Pradesh (rapid riser)
(D) Haryana (early Green Revolution)
cards.back:
(A) Uttar Pradesh (largest wheat producer)

Agriculture & Industry — WHEAT PRODUCTION: UP (largest, ~30%), then Punjab + Haryana + MP. UP has largest TOTAL output due to size + Indo-Gangetic plain fertility. PUNJAB has HIGHEST YIELD per hectare ('granary of India'). Indian wheat output ~110 MT (FY24). India world's 2nd largest wheat producer (after CHINA, ~140 MT). RICE: largest = West Bengal, then UP, Punjab, Telangana. India world's 2nd largest rice producer (after CHINA), but LARGEST EXPORTER. SUGARCANE: UP largest, then Maharashtra. COTTON: Gujarat, Maharashtra. PULSES: MP largest. TEA: Assam (50%). COFFEE: Karnataka. SPICES: Kerala (cardamom), Andhra (chilli), Gujarat (cumin), Tamil Nadu (turmeric). ICAR — Indian Council of Agricultural Research, oversees research, sets standards.

cards.front:
India is world's LARGEST PRODUCER of which agricultural commodity?

(A) Milk + jute + pulses + spices (multiple firsts)
(B) Wheat (No. 2; China is No. 1) too alone
(C) Cotton (close, but China leads) too
(D) Rice (No. 2; China is No. 1) too alone
cards.back:
(A) Milk + jute + pulses + spices (multiple firsts)

Agriculture & Industry — INDIA — world's LARGEST producer of: MILK (~22% world share, ~230 MT/year — 'Operation Flood', AMUL); JUTE (~50% world); PULSES (~25%); SPICES (~75%); BANANAS, MANGOES, PAPAYAS; CASTOR; OKRA. India is 2ND in: rice, wheat, sugarcane, groundnut, cotton, FRUITS + VEGETABLES OVERALL (huge variety). Indian milk industry: white revolution (1970-90s) under VERGHESE KURIEN (founder of AMUL) revolutionised dairy — went from milk-deficit to surplus. AMUL = Anand Milk Union Ltd., Anand, Gujarat — world's largest dairy cooperative. NDDB (National Dairy Development Board) = institutional backer. India's per-capita milk consumption: ~440 g/day; rising over time. Globally: India ranks #1 in MILK above USA, China, Pakistan.

cards.option3: Rice (No. 2; China is No. 1) too alone

cards.front:
MSP (Minimum Support Price) is announced by:

(A) CACP (Commission for Agricultural Costs + Prices)
(B) RBI (regulator of banks alone) too alone
(C) FCI (Food Corp of India only buyer) too
(D) NABARD (rural development bank) too alone
cards.back:
(A) CACP (Commission for Agricultural Costs + Prices)

Agriculture & Industry — MSP — recommended by CACP (Commission for Agricultural Costs + Prices, attached to Min of Agri) → approved by CABINET COMMITTEE ON ECONOMIC AFFAIRS (CCEA). FCI (Food Corp of India) + state agencies BUY at MSP from farmers. Currently MSP for ~23 CROPS. KEY: WHEAT, RICE, BAJRA, JOWAR, MAIZE, TUR, MOONG, URAD, COTTON, MUSTARD, GROUNDNUT, SOYBEAN, SUNFLOWER, SUGARCANE (FRP, separate). MSP CALCULATION: A2 (cash costs); A2+FL (cash + family labour); C2 (full cost incl. land rent + capital interest). MSP currently = A2+FL × 1.5 (since 2018). DEMAND for legal MSP guarantee = key to farmer protests (esp. 2020-21). CONTROVERSY: only ~6% of farmers benefit (mostly Punjab/Haryana wheat-rice); rest face mandi prices.

cards.option2: FCI (Food Corp of India only buyer) too

cards.front:
TROPICAL CROP grown mainly in COASTAL STATES of India is:

(A) Coconut (Kerala, TN, Karnataka, Andhra)
(B) Wheat (Punjab + Haryana + UP)
(C) Apples (Himachal + Kashmir) too
(D) Saffron (Kashmir's Pampore area)
cards.back:
(A) Coconut (Kerala, TN, Karnataka, Andhra)

Agriculture & Industry — COCONUT — needs warm + humid + saline coastal climate. India's main coconut states: KERALA ('Kera' = coconut tree in Malayalam — state's name itself; ~37% national output), TAMIL NADU, KARNATAKA, ANDHRA PRADESH, ANDAMAN-NICOBAR. India is world's 3RD largest coconut producer (after Indonesia + Philippines). USES: copra, oil, water, fibre (coir, ropes, mats), shell. KERALA STATE TREE — coconut. KERALA also: spice exports (cardamom — 'queen of spices'; pepper — 'king'; cinnamon, clove). Compare: APPLES — temperate climate, HIMACHAL + J&K. SAFFRON — Kashmir (PAMPORE), only in India's Karewas (mid-altitude shelves) — world's most expensive spice (~₹2-3 lakh/kg).

KERALA also: spice exports (cardamom — 'queen of spices'; pepper — 'king'; cinnamon, clove). Compare: APPLES — temperate climate, HIMACHAL + J&K. SAFFRON — Kashmir (PAMPORE), only in India's Karewas (mid-altitude shelves) — world's most expensive spice (~₹2-3 lakh/kg).

cards.front:
BLACK SOIL (regur soil) is most suitable for which crop?

(A) Cotton (regur = 'black cotton soil')
(B) Tea (laterite + acidic soil)
(C) Apples (alluvial mountain soil)
(D) Coffee (laterite, Western Ghats)
cards.back:
(A) Cotton (regur = 'black cotton soil')

Agriculture & Industry — BLACK SOIL (REGUR) — formed from BASALTIC LAVA (Deccan trap area). Found in: MAHARASHTRA, GUJARAT, MADHYA PRADESH, parts of Karnataka + Andhra. RICH in calcium, magnesium, iron, potash; LOW in nitrogen + phosphorus. RETAINS MOISTURE well — good for DRY CROPS, esp. COTTON ('black cotton soil'). Also good for soybean, sugarcane, sorghum, pulses. EXPANDS when wet, CRACKS when dry → 'self-ploughing' soil. INDIAN SOIL TYPES: ALLUVIAL (most fertile, Indo-Gangetic plains, ~40% area; rice + wheat + sugarcane); BLACK / Regur; RED + YELLOW (Deccan plateau, less fertile; millets, pulses); LATERITE (heavy rain areas, SW + E coasts; tea, coffee, rubber, cashew); ARID (Rajasthan, low organic; bajra, drought-resistant); MOUNTAIN; PEATY + SALINE.

cards.front:
ICAR (Indian Council of Agricultural Research) headquarters is at:

(A) New Delhi (Pusa campus)
(B) Mumbai (financial capital)
(C) Bengaluru (tech capital)
(D) Hyderabad (CCMB area)
cards.back:
(A) New Delhi (Pusa campus)

Agriculture & Industry — ICAR — headquartered in NEW DELHI (Pusa campus, Krishi Bhavan). FOUNDED 1929 as Imperial Council of Agri Research; renamed 1946. Apex body for coordinating agricultural research + education in India. RUNS 100+ INSTITUTES + RESEARCH CENTRES across India. Key ones: IARI (Indian Agricultural Research Institute, Pusa, New Delhi — wheat varieties, GR development); IRRI (International Rice Research Institute, Philippines — Indian collaboration); NDRI (Karnal — dairy); IISR (Lucknow — sugarcane); CICR (Nagpur — cotton); IIVR (Varanasi — vegetables); CIFE (Mumbai — fisheries education); KVK (Krishi Vigyan Kendras) — district-level extension. NORMAN BORLAUG visited IARI; gave dwarf wheat. MS SWAMINATHAN was DG of ICAR (1972-79) + later Min of Agri's advisor + Rajya Sabha MP (2007).

cards.front:
GREEN REVOLUTION in INDIA started in which decade?

(A) 1960s (peak in late 60s-early 70s)
(B) 1990s (after liberalization)
(C) 1980s (mid-decade onwards)
(D) 1950s (pre-independence era)
cards.back:
(A) 1960s (peak in late 60s-early 70s)

Agriculture & Industry — GREEN REVOLUTION in INDIA: starts late 1960s. KEY ARCHITECT: M.S. SWAMINATHAN ('Father of Green Revolution in India', 1925-2023; Padma Shri, Padma Bhushan, Padma Vibhushan; first Indian to win World Food Prize 1987). KEY ELEMENTS: (1) HIGH-YIELDING VARIETY (HYV) seeds — wheat (NORMAN BORLAUG's IR-8 wheat dwarf varieties from CIMMYT, Mexico); rice (IR-8 from IRRI, Philippines). (2) IRRIGATION expansion — canals, tube-wells. (3) Chemical FERTILIZERS — N, P, K. (4) PESTICIDES + HERBICIDES. (5) MECHANIZATION — tractors, combines. (6) SUBSIDIES + price support (MSP). FOCUS REGIONS: PUNJAB, HARYANA, WESTERN UP — wheat. ANDHRA, TAMIL NADU, PUNJAB rice. RESULTS: (a) Food grain production: 1965 (~89 mt) → 1985 (~152 mt) → 2024 (~330 mt). (b) INDIA shifted from FOOD-IMPORT (PL-480 dependence) to FOOD-SURPLUS by 1970s. (c) Wheat production tripled by 1985. CRITICISMS: (i) Regional inequality (Punjab/Haryana booming; Bihar/eastern India lagging). (ii) Environmental degradation: groundwater depletion, soil salinity, pesticide pollution. (iii) Inequality: large farmers benefited more; small farmers debt. (iv) Monoculture, biodiversity loss. (v) High-input dependency. SECOND GREEN REVOLUTION (proposed): focus on RAINFED areas, eastern India, pulses + oilseeds + millets. EVERGREEN REVOLUTION (Swaminathan term): sustainable, climate-resilient agriculture. UPSC angle: GREEN REVOLUTION + sustainability tradeoffs in GS-3 economics + GS-3 environment. PYQ FREQUENCY: Green Revolution + Swaminathan in UPSC, MPSC, SSC 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
WHICH state is the LARGEST producer of WHEAT in INDIA?

(A) Uttar Pradesh (~30% of national)
(B) Punjab (with high productivity)
(C) Haryana (smaller area)
(D) Madhya Pradesh (a close 2nd)
cards.back:
(A) Uttar Pradesh (~30% of national)

Agriculture & Industry — UTTAR PRADESH — LARGEST PRODUCER of wheat in India (~30%). PRODUCTIVITY-WISE PUNJAB has the highest wheat productivity (~5,500 kg/hectare vs UP's ~3,500 kg/ha) — hence PUNJAB is INDIA's TOP-PRODUCTIVITY agriculture state per area. WHEAT TOP STATES (rough share): (1) UP — ~30% national production. (2) MP — ~17%. (3) Punjab — ~16%. (4) Haryana — ~11%. (5) Rajasthan — ~10%. WHEAT BELT: Indo-Gangetic Plain (Punjab, Haryana, UP, MP). RICE TOP STATES: WB (~13%), Punjab (~10%), UP, AP, TN, Bihar. SUGARCANE TOP: UP (~50% — largest!), Maharashtra, Karnataka. COTTON TOP: Maharashtra (~25%), Gujarat (~24%), Telangana, AP. PULSES TOP: MP (~25%), Rajasthan, Maharashtra. OILSEEDS: MP, Rajasthan, Maharashtra (groundnut, mustard, soybean). MILLETS (Bajra, Jowar, Ragi): Karnataka, Rajasthan, Maharashtra. FRUITS: TOP banana = TN; TOP mango = UP; TOP grapes = MH; TOP apple = HP/J&K. SPICES: TOP tea = Assam (~50%) + WB; TOP coffee = Karnataka (~70%); TOP black pepper = Kerala. INDIA RANKS GLOBALLY: 2nd in WHEAT (after China), 2nd in RICE (after China), 1st in MILK (since 1998 — Operation Flood, Verghese Kurien), 1st in PULSES, 2nd in SUGARCANE (after Brazil), 1st in MANGO, 2nd in TEA. UPSC angle: agricultural geography + regional economic patterns. PYQ FREQUENCY: top crop-state pairings in SSC, UPSC, NDA 2-3× per cycle.

cards.front:
MSP (MINIMUM SUPPORT PRICE) is announced by:

(A) Government of India based on CACP
(B) RBI on banking interest rates
(C) World Trade Organization (WTO)
(D) State assemblies independently
cards.back:
(A) Government of India based on CACP

Agriculture & Industry — MINIMUM SUPPORT PRICE (MSP): price GUARANTEED by GOI to farmers; Govt commits to PURCHASE crops at MSP if market price falls below. AIM: protect farmers from market collapses; ensure remunerative prices. RECOMMENDATION: by COMMISSION FOR AGRICULTURAL COSTS AND PRICES (CACP) — set up 1965 under Min of Agriculture & Farmers Welfare. ANNOUNCED: by GOI based on CACP recommendation (often slight upward adjustment). MSP COVERS 23 CROPS (since 2018-19): (1) 7 CEREALS — paddy, wheat, jowar, bajra, maize, ragi, barley. (2) 5 PULSES — tur (arhar), moong, urad, gram, lentil. (3) 7 OILSEEDS — groundnut, sunflower, soybean, sesame, niger, safflower, rapeseed-mustard. (4) 4 COMMERCIAL — cotton, copra, jute, sugarcane (FRP for sugarcane — different from MSP). MSP CALCULATION FACTORS: (a) Cost A2 (paid-out costs only). (b) Cost A2+FL (Family Labour). (c) Cost C2 (comprehensive cost incl. imputed values). M.S. SWAMINATHAN COMMITTEE (2004-2006) — recommended MSP = C2 × 1.5 (50% profit margin). MODI GOVT (2018) committed MSP = A2+FL × 1.5 (less than Swaminathan). KEY INSTITUTIONS: (1) FCI (Food Corporation of India) — main procurement agency. (2) NAFED (National Agricultural Cooperative Marketing Federation) — pulses, oilseeds. (3) Cotton Corporation of India — cotton. UPSC angle: 2020-21 FARM LAWS + farmer protests; MSP legalization debate ongoing. KEY: MSP is NOT a legal right; only an administrative announcement. PYQ FREQUENCY: MSP basics in UPSC, MPSC, SSC 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
WHITE REVOLUTION in INDIA refers to the dramatic increase in:

(A) Milk production (Operation Flood)
(B) Egg production (poultry sector)
(C) Cotton production fabric quality
(D) Pearl + diamond gem production
cards.back:
(A) Milk production (Operation Flood)

Agriculture & Industry — WHITE REVOLUTION ('OPERATION FLOOD') — programme launched 1970 by VERGHESE KURIEN (1921-2012, 'FATHER OF WHITE REVOLUTION'); transformed India from MILK-DEFICIT country to LARGEST MILK-PRODUCER in the world (since 1998). PROGRAMME: developed COOPERATIVE-DAIRY MODEL — farmers organized in village cooperatives → district cooperatives → state cooperatives → national federation (NDDB — National Dairy Development Board). KEY: AMUL (Anand Milk Union Limited) in Gujarat — pioneer cooperative; founder TRIBHUVANDAS PATEL + Verghese Kurien. NUMBERS: India's milk production: 1950 ~17 mt → 1970 ~21 mt (Operation Flood begins) → 2024 ~230 mt (largest globally; ~22% of world output). AMUL pattern replicated as Mother Dairy (Delhi), Vijaya (AP), Aavin (TN), Nandini (Karnataka), etc. KEY INSTITUTION: National Dairy Development Board (NDDB) — set up 1965 by KURIEN; HQ in Anand, Gujarat. OTHER 'COLOR REVOLUTIONS' in Indian agriculture (memorize): (1) GREEN — food grains (Swaminathan). (2) WHITE — milk (Kurien). (3) YELLOW — oilseeds (1986 onwards; Technology Mission on Oilseeds). (4) BLUE — fish/aquaculture. (5) PINK — onion + meat/poultry. (6) ROUND — potato. (7) GOLDEN — fruits/horticulture. (8) RED — meat + tomato. (9) GREY — wool + fertilizer. (10) RAINBOW — sustainable agriculture combining several. UPSC angle: agricultural diversity + Verghese Kurien (PADMA VIBHUSHAN, World Food Prize 1989). PYQ FREQUENCY: White Revolution + Kurien in UPSC, SSC, MPSC 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
KHARIF crops are sown in which season?

(A) Monsoon (June-July, harvest Sep-Oct)
(B) Winter (October-November sowing)
(C) Summer (March-April sowing)
(D) Pre-monsoon (April-May only)
cards.back:
(A) Monsoon (June-July, harvest Sep-Oct)

Agriculture & Industry — KHARIF (खरीफ) season — SOWN at start of MONSOON (June-July); HARVESTED in autumn (September-October). 'Kharif' means autumn (Arabic origin). KHARIF CROPS need: (a) HEAT + plenty of WATER (during growing). (b) Examples: RICE, MAIZE, COTTON, SOYBEAN, GROUNDNUT, JOWAR, BAJRA, RAGI, PULSES (MOONG, URAD, ARHAR), JUTE, SUGARCANE. RABI (रबी) season — SOWN in WINTER (October-November); HARVESTED in SPRING (March-April). 'Rabi' means spring. RABI CROPS need: (a) Cool growing season + warm to ripen. (b) Examples: WHEAT, BARLEY, MUSTARD, GRAM, PEAS, OATS, LENTILS. ZAID — minor third season; March-June (between Rabi harvest + Kharif sowing). Crops: WATERMELON, CUCUMBER, MUSKMELON, FODDER, MOONG (some). KEY INSIGHT: India's TWO MAIN crop seasons (Kharif + Rabi) ride the MONSOON cycle. SOUTHWEST MONSOON (June-September) brings ~75% of annual rainfall — drives Kharif. Northeast Monsoon (Oct-Dec, mainly Tamil Nadu coast) — secondary. KHARIF FAILURES — common in DROUGHT YEARS (2002, 2009, 2014); cause distress + farmer suicides. RABI more reliable due to assured irrigation in major belts. UPSC angle: AGRO-CLIMATIC zones + crop calendar; agriculture insurance schemes (PMFBY — Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana). PYQ FREQUENCY: Kharif vs Rabi in SSC, UPSC, NDA 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
Which is the LARGEST source of IRRIGATION in INDIA today?

(A) Tubewells / groundwater (~60%)
(B) Canal irrigation (about 25%)
(C) Tanks (with declining share)
(D) Rainwater harvesting only
cards.back:
(A) Tubewells / groundwater (~60%)

Agriculture & Industry — TUBEWELLS / GROUNDWATER — LARGEST source of irrigation in India today: ~60% of irrigated area. SHIFT HISTORY: in 1950, CANALS were dominant (~40%) + TANKS (~20%); GROUNDWATER (~30%). By 2020: GROUNDWATER (~60%) + canals (~25%) + tanks (~5%) + others (~10%). REASONS for groundwater dominance: (1) Subsidized electricity for tubewell pumps (especially Punjab, Haryana, UP, AP, Karnataka). (2) Canal water unreliable in many areas. (3) Easier to install than canal infrastructure. (4) Farmer-controlled. PROBLEM — GROUNDWATER DEPLETION: India is the LARGEST GROUNDWATER USER globally (~25% of world's extraction!). Punjab, Haryana, Western UP — STAGE-IV depletion (Central Ground Water Board classification — over-exploited). Some areas: water table dropping ~1 m/year. CONSEQUENCES: drying wells, requiring deeper drilling, energy costs rising, soil salinization. SOLUTIONS proposed: (a) MICRO-IRRIGATION (drip + sprinkler) — used in Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu, AP. (b) PRADHAN MANTRI KRISHI SINCHAYEE YOJANA (PMKSY, 2015) — 'Per Drop More Crop'. (c) Rainwater harvesting MANDATORY in some states. (d) Crop diversification — shift from water-intensive (rice, sugarcane) to less water-intensive (millets, pulses). NATIONAL WATER POLICY: 2002, revised 2012; emphasizes integrated water management. UPSC angle: water security, food-water nexus, climate change. PYQ FREQUENCY: irrigation sources in UPSC, SSC, geography 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
PM-KISAN (since 2019) provides INCOME SUPPORT to landholding farmers of:

(A) ₹6,000 per year (in 3 installments)
(B) ₹2,000 per year (under-estimate)
(C) ₹12,000 per year (over-estimate)
(D) ₹20,000 per year (much over)
cards.back:
(A) ₹6,000 per year (in 3 installments)

Agriculture & Industry — PM-KISAN (Pradhan Mantri Kisan Samman Nidhi) — Direct Income Support scheme launched 24 February 2019; effective from 1 December 2018. AMOUNT: ₹6,000 per year per landholding farmer family, paid in THREE INSTALLMENTS of ₹2,000 each (April-July, Aug-Nov, Dec-March). KEY INSTALLMENTS to date: ~17-18 installments released by April 2025; total ~₹3 lakh crore disbursed. ELIGIBILITY: ALL LANDHOLDING FARMERS, including SMALL + MARGINAL (initial 2018 design was only SMALL+MARGINAL; expanded in 2019). EXCLUSIONS: (1) Constitutional post holders (current/former). (2) Senior bureaucrats (Group A + Group B). (3) Income tax payers. (4) Central/state govt employees (sections of). (5) Pensioners with monthly pension > ₹10,000. (6) Professionals (doctors, lawyers, etc.). KEY: payment via DBT (Direct Benefit Transfer) to bank accounts; AADHAAR-linked for transparency. NUMBERS as of 2024-25: ~9.7 crore farmers benefited; major reach. CONTRAST WITH OTHER SCHEMES: (1) PRADHAN MANTRI FASAL BIMA YOJANA (PMFBY, 2016) — crop insurance, partially subsidized premium. (2) PMKSY (Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana) — irrigation. (3) E-NAM (electronic National Agricultural Market) — online unified market. (4) SOIL HEALTH CARD scheme. (5) NATIONAL MISSION ON SUSTAINABLE AGRICULTURE. CRITICISM: ₹6,000/yr is INSUFFICIENT for distress; should be expanded; AGRARIAN CRISIS (farmer suicides) continues. STATES like TELANGANA had RYTHU BANDHU before PM-KISAN. UPSC angle: agricultural income support + welfare schemes. PYQ FREQUENCY: PM-KISAN in UPSC, MPSC current affairs 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
India's THREE main cropping seasons are:

(A) Summer, winter, monsoon
(B) Kharif, Rabi, Zaid
(C) Tropical, temperate, boreal
(D) Spring, autumn, winter
cards.back:
(B) Kharif, Rabi, Zaid

Agriculture & Industry — KHARIF — sown June-July (with monsoon), harvested Oct-Nov. Crops: rice, maize, jowar, bajra, ragi, soybean, cotton, groundnut. RABI — sown Oct-Nov (winter), harvested March-April. Crops: wheat, barley, mustard, gram, peas, oats. ZAID — short summer season (March-June). Crops: watermelon, cucumber, fodder. Names from Urdu/Arabic — Kharif = autumn harvest, Rabi = spring harvest. India's agricultural calendar still revolves around these three.

cards.front:
India's largest producer state of WHEAT is:

(A) Punjab
(B) Uttar Pradesh
(C) Madhya Pradesh
(D) Haryana
cards.back:
(B) Uttar Pradesh

Agriculture & Industry — UP — largest wheat producer (~33-34 MT, ~30% share). Punjab — 2nd largest by output but #1 in YIELD per hectare. MP — 3rd. Together UP+Punjab+Haryana+MP make ~75% of national wheat production (most rabi). Largest RICE producer — West Bengal (or UP, varies year on year). Largest cotton producer — Maharashtra. Largest sugarcane producer — UP. Largest tea producer — Assam. Largest coffee producer — Karnataka.

cards.front:
MSP (Minimum Support Price) is announced by the Centre on the recommendation of:

(A) Niti Aayog
(B) Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices (CACP)
(C) RBI
(D) Finance Commission
cards.back:
(B) Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices (CACP)

Agriculture & Industry — CACP — formed 1965 (then Agricultural Prices Commission, renamed 1985). Statutory body under MoA. Recommends MSPs for 23 crops — 7 cereals (paddy, wheat, maize, ragi, jowar, bajra, barley), 5 pulses, 7 oilseeds, 4 commercial crops (sugarcane FRP, cotton, jute, copra). MSP intended to provide assured income (M.S. Swaminathan formula MSP = C2 + 50% margin — ie cost + 50%). Paddy + wheat have most active procurement (FCI). M.S. Swaminathan is called 'Father of Green Revolution in India' (received Bharat Ratna posthumously, 2024).

cards.front:
The 'Green Revolution' in India during the late 1960s primarily focused on:

(A) Tropical fruits
(B) High-Yielding Variety (HYV) wheat and rice — particularly in Punjab, Haryana, western UP
(C) Cash crops only
(D) Tea and coffee
cards.back:
(B) High-Yielding Variety (HYV) wheat and rice — particularly in Punjab, Haryana, western UP

Agriculture & Industry — Green Revolution — late 1960s, led by M.S. Swaminathan (Indian) + Norman Borlaug (American, Nobel Peace 1970). Imported HYV wheat (Mexican dwarf varieties — Sonora 64, Lerma Rojo) + rice (IR-8 from Philippines). Combined with assured irrigation, fertilisers, pesticides, MSP, FCI procurement — transformed India from food-deficient (1965-66 famine fears) to self-sufficient by 1975. Focus on Punjab-Haryana-W.UP because of irrigation infrastructure. Side effects — soil exhaustion, water-table depletion, pesticide use, regional inequality.

cards.front:
India's 'White Revolution' (Operation Flood) — making India the largest milk producer globally — was launched by:

(A) M.S. Swaminathan
(B) Verghese Kurien (under National Dairy Development Board)
(C) Norman Borlaug
(D) C.D. Deshmukh
cards.back:
(B) Verghese Kurien (under National Dairy Development Board)

Agriculture & Industry — Verghese Kurien — 'Father of White Revolution'. Operation Flood launched 1970 by NDDB, Anand, Gujarat (HQ of Amul). Created a national milk grid linking producers across India to consumers in cities; cooperative dairy model based on Amul (Anand Milk Union Limited). India became #1 milk producer 1998; current ~22% of global milk output. Bharat Ratna posthumously to Kurien (in pipeline; not yet conferred). His birthday 26 November is National Milk Day. Operation Flood often called 'world's largest dairy development programme'.

cards.front:
India's 'Pink Revolution' refers to the rapid growth in:

(A) Pulses production
(B) Meat (especially poultry / pork) and processed-meat exports
(C) Floriculture
(D) Fruits like dragon fruit
cards.back:
(B) Meat (especially poultry / pork) and processed-meat exports

Agriculture & Industry — Multiple 'colour revolutions' in India. WHITE — milk; YELLOW — oilseeds; BLUE — fisheries / aquaculture; GREEN — food grains; PINK — meat (also onion / shrimp in some sources); GOLDEN — fruits / honey; SILVER — eggs / cotton; GREY — fertilisers; ROUND — potatoes; BROWN — cocoa / leather. India is now the largest exporter of buffalo meat. The 'Rainbow Revolution' is the umbrella term for pursuing all these together — agricultural diversification.

cards.front:
PM-KISAN scheme provides direct cash transfer to farmers of:

(A) ₹3,000/year
(B) ₹6,000/year — paid in 3 installments of ₹2,000
(C) ₹10,000/year
(D) ₹5,000/year
cards.back:
(B) ₹6,000/year — paid in 3 installments of ₹2,000

Agriculture & Industry — PM-KISAN (Pradhan Mantri Kisan Samman Nidhi) — launched 24 February 2019. ₹6,000/year via DBT to all eligible landholding farmer families, in 3 four-monthly installments of ₹2,000. Earlier ceiling of 2 hectares removed in June 2019. Excluded: institutional landowners, current/former MPs/MLAs/ministers, professionals (doctors, CAs etc), pension >₹10,000/month. ~10 crore farmers receive benefits. ₹3+ lakh crore transferred since launch.

cards.front:
In India, rice, maize and jute are primarily grown during which cropping season?

(A) Rabi
(B) Kharif
(C) Zaid
(D) Winter
cards.back:
(B) Kharif

Agriculture & Industry — Kharif (monsoon) crops are sown with the onset of the SW monsoon in June and harvested in October-November. Examples: rice, maize, jowar, bajra, ragi, cotton, jute, groundnut. Rabi (winter) crops are sown in October-November and harvested in March-April — wheat, barley, gram, mustard, peas. Zaid is the short summer season (March-June) for cucumber, musk-melon, moong, fodder.

cards.front:
India's largest producer of wheat — the grain belt of the country — is:

(A) Punjab
(B) Uttar Pradesh
(C) Haryana
(D) Madhya Pradesh
cards.back:
(B) Uttar Pradesh

Agriculture & Industry — Uttar Pradesh is India's largest wheat producer by volume (~30 % of national output). In terms of yield per hectare, Punjab and Haryana lead — thanks to irrigation, short-duration HYV seeds, and Green Revolution inputs. Madhya Pradesh has become the second-largest producer in recent years, overtaking Punjab.

cards.front:
India's largest producer of tea is:

(A) West Bengal
(B) Assam
(C) Tamil Nadu
(D) Kerala
cards.back:
(B) Assam

Agriculture & Industry — Assam produces about 50 % of India's tea — chiefly in the Brahmaputra valley. West Bengal (Darjeeling, Dooars, Terai) is second; Tamil Nadu (Nilgiris) third. India is the world's second-largest tea producer after China. Assam tea is robust and malty; Darjeeling tea (WB) is floral and is often called the 'champagne of teas'.

cards.front:
The 'Green Revolution' in India during the 1960s-70s was driven primarily by the introduction of:

(A) Drip irrigation
(B) High-Yield Variety (HYV) seeds
(C) Satellite remote sensing
(D) Electric tractors
cards.back:
(B) High-Yield Variety (HYV) seeds

Agriculture & Industry — The Green Revolution was led by M. S. Swaminathan in India and Norman Borlaug globally (Borlaug won the 1970 Nobel Peace Prize). It relied on HYV seeds — especially dwarf wheat (from CIMMYT, Mexico) and IR-8 rice (IRRI, Philippines) — combined with chemical fertilisers, pesticides and assured irrigation. Drip irrigation became widespread much later. It boosted yields but produced regional concentration (Punjab, Haryana, western UP) and environmental concerns like ground-water depletion.

India's largest producer of sugarcane is:

India is the world's largest sugarcane producer and second-largest sugar producer after Brazil. Karnataka and Tamil Nadu are smaller but important.

cards.front:
Which of the following crops requires the most water for cultivation per hectare?

(A) Wheat
(B) Rice (paddy)
(C) Millets
(D) Pulses
cards.back:
(B) Rice (paddy)

Agriculture & Industry — Paddy rice is grown in flooded fields and typically needs 1,100-1,250 mm of water per crop cycle — far more than wheat (~400-500 mm), millets (300-400 mm) or pulses (which are often rain-fed). This is one reason rice cultivation in water-scarce Punjab and Haryana is being rethought in favour of less thirsty crops.

cards.front:
India's first iron and steel plant in the modern era — Tata Iron and Steel Co. (TISCO) — was set up in 1907 at:

(A) Burnpur, West Bengal
(B) Sakchi, later renamed Jamshedpur (Jharkhand)
(C) Bhilai, Chhattisgarh
(D) Bokaro, Jharkhand
cards.back:
(B) Sakchi, later renamed Jamshedpur (Jharkhand)

Agriculture & Industry — Tata Iron and Steel Co. (TISCO, now Tata Steel) — incorporated 1907 by Jamsetji Tata; first ingot rolled February 1912 at Sakchi, Bihar. Sakchi renamed Jamshedpur (1919) after Jamsetji's death. Located at confluence of Subarnarekha + Kharkai — proximity to iron ore (Mayurbhanj/Singhbhum), coal (Jharia), water, port (Calcutta). Other public-sector steel plants — Rourkela (1959, Odisha, German collaboration), Bhilai (1959, Chhattisgarh, Soviet), Durgapur (1959, WB, British), Bokaro (1972, Jharkhand, Soviet), Salem (TN), Vizag (AP), Vijayanagar (Bellary, Karnataka). SAIL (Steel Authority of India Ltd) — 1973.

cards.front:
India's COTTON textile industry historically concentrated in:

(A) Punjab and Haryana
(B) Maharashtra (Mumbai) and Gujarat (Ahmedabad)
(C) West Bengal (Kolkata)
(D) Tamil Nadu only
cards.back:
(B) Maharashtra (Mumbai) and Gujarat (Ahmedabad)

Agriculture & Industry — First Indian cotton mill: Bombay Spinning Mill (1854) by Cawasji Davar, Mumbai. Mumbai-Ahmedabad belt led the industry through 19th-20th century — proximity to cotton belt (Maharashtra-Gujarat black soil), port access (Mumbai), capital (Parsis, Marwaris), labour. Also Coimbatore (TN) — 'Manchester of South India'. Modern industry has spread — Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Andhra. India is world's #1 cotton producer (some years) + 2nd largest exporter of cotton textiles. Jute industry, by contrast, was concentrated in Bengal (Hooghly basin).

cards.front:
India's largest sugar-producing state (typically) is:

(A) Maharashtra
(B) Uttar Pradesh — vast sugar belt across Doab
(C) Karnataka
(D) Tamil Nadu
cards.back:
(B) Uttar Pradesh — vast sugar belt across Doab

Agriculture & Industry — UP — largest sugar producer historically (long stable yield, traditional jaggery industry, dense Doab cane). Maharashtra (sugar cooperatives — Pune-Kolhapur belt) sometimes overtakes UP in lean monsoon years. Top 3: UP, Maharashtra, Karnataka (~80% of total). Sugarcane requires 75-150 cm rainfall + 21-27 °C — suits subtropical North India + Deccan plateau. India is world's 2nd largest sugar producer (after Brazil) and largest consumer. Surplus exported (~7-8 MT in 2024-25). Ethanol blending push (E20 by 2025) is diverting cane to ethanol production.

Total capacity ~1.36 million barrels/day — world's LARGEST refining complex at a single location. India is the 4th largest refiner globally (~5 million bpd total). cards.front:
KHARIF crops in India are sown in:

(A) October-November (winter)
(B) JUNE-JULY (with the onset of SW monsoon) + harvested in SEPT-OCT; includes rice, maize, bajra, jowar, cotton, sugarcane, tur
(C) March-April
(D) Year-round
cards.back:
(B) JUNE-JULY (with the onset of SW monsoon) + harvested in SEPT-OCT; includes rice, maize, bajra, jowar, cotton, sugarcane, tur

Agriculture & Industry — AGRICULTURAL SEASONS in India: (1) KHARIF (monsoon) — sown June-July with SW monsoon arrival; harvested SEPT-OCT; water-intensive crops; includes PADDY/RICE (dominant), MAIZE, JOWAR (sorghum), BAJRA (pearl millet), RAGI (finger millet), GROUNDNUT, COTTON, SUGARCANE, SOYABEAN, TUR (arhar/pigeon pea), URAD, MOONG, JUTE. (2) RABI (winter) — sown OCT-NOV (post-monsoon, using soil moisture + winter rains); harvested MARCH-APRIL; includes WHEAT (dominant), BARLEY, GRAM/CHANA, MUSTARD/RAPESEED, PEAS, LENTIL/MASOOR, LINSEED, ONION, POTATO. (3) ZAID (summer) — sown MARCH-APRIL, harvested MAY-JUNE; short-duration crops; WATERMELON, MUSKMELON, CUCUMBER, VEGETABLES, MOONG, FODDER CROPS. MSP (Minimum Support Price): announced for 23 crops (14 Kharif + 6 Rabi + others) by CACP recommendations, approved by CCEA. NAMES: Kharif from Arabic 'autumn' (these crops ready in autumn); Rabi from Arabic 'spring' (harvested in spring). TOP RICE STATES: WB, UP, Punjab, AP, Telangana, Bihar, TN. TOP WHEAT STATES: UP, Punjab, Haryana, MP, Rajasthan. MP has surpassed Punjab in wheat production recently. INDIA is the 2nd largest producer globally of rice + wheat (China is 1st for rice; China 1st, India 2nd wheat). LARGEST producer of PULSES + MILK + SPICES + JUTE globally.

cards.front:
The 'GREEN REVOLUTION' in India, launched in the 1960s-70s, primarily increased the production of:

(A) Pulses + oilseeds
(B) WHEAT + RICE
(C) Fruits + vegetables
(D) Coffee + tea
cards.back:
(B) WHEAT + RICE

Agriculture & Industry — GREEN REVOLUTION — transformation of Indian agriculture from 1965-66 onwards; made India from 'ship-to-mouth' food importer to self-sufficient + exporter. DRIVERS: (1) HYV SEEDS — especially high-yielding wheat varieties developed by NORMAN BORLAUG (Nobel Peace Prize 1970) at CIMMYT Mexico, brought to India in 1965; Indian scientist MS SWAMINATHAN adapted them (Sonora-64, Lerma Rojo); (2) CHEMICAL FERTILISERS (urea, DAP, potash); (3) PESTICIDES + herbicides; (4) IRRIGATION infrastructure (Bhakra Nangal, tube wells); (5) MECHANISATION (tractors, harvesters, threshers); (6) MSP + procurement via FCI (1965 establishment) + state mandis; (7) INSTITUTIONAL CREDIT (bank nationalisation 1969, NABARD 1982). GEOGRAPHIC CONCENTRATION: PUNJAB, HARYANA, Western UP — became 'WHEAT BOWL'. Rice component later in AP, TN, Punjab. KEY CROPS: WHEAT (fastest growth), RICE. OTHER revolutions followed: (a) WHITE Revolution — MILK — Verghese Kurien + Amul's OPERATION FLOOD (1970s-90s); India now world's LARGEST milk producer. (b) YELLOW Revolution — OILSEEDS — 1986-90. (c) BLUE Revolution — FISH — 1985 onwards. (d) PINK Revolution — MEAT + POULTRY; or alternatively prawns/shrimps. (e) SILVER Revolution — eggs. (f) RAINBOW Revolution — holistic agri-growth. CRITIQUES: bypassed dryland farmers + pulses + millets; caused GROUNDWATER depletion (Punjab); soil degradation; fertiliser overuse; regional inequality. M.S. SWAMINATHAN ('Father of Indian Green Revolution') died 2023; Bharat Ratna 2024. through HYVs (High-Yielding Varieties), fertilisers, irrigation, MSP; concentrated in Punjab, Haryana, W. UP.

Match the crop with its LARGEST PRODUCER (state) in India (2022-23 data): (1) SUGARCANE; (2) COTTON; (3) TEA; (4) COFFEE.

(B) UTTAR PRADESH; GUJARAT; ASSAM; KARNATAKA

Agriculture & Industry — LARGEST PRODUCING STATES (commercial + plantation crops): (1) SUGARCANE — UTTAR PRADESH (≈45% of national production); followed by Maharashtra + Karnataka + TN. UP grows it in the GANGETIC PLAINS; Maharashtra + Karnataka use it more intensively for sugar + ethanol. India = world's 2nd largest sugarcane producer (Brazil 1st). Chikmagalur, Coorg, Hassan); also Kerala (Wayanad) + TN (Nilgiris). India = world's 7th largest coffee producer. ARABICA + ROBUSTA grown. cards.front:
The BLACK COTTON SOIL (REGUR) is best suited for COTTON cultivation. It is MAINLY found in:

(A) Gangetic plains
(B) DECCAN TRAP region
(C) Himalayan foothills
(D) Coastal Kerala
cards.back:
(B) DECCAN TRAP region

Agriculture & Industry — BLACK COTTON SOIL / REGUR — a residual black soil derived from DECCAN TRAPS (weathered BASALT + volcanic lava of Cretaceous age). COVERS ~16% of India's geographic area. DISTRIBUTION: MAHARASHTRA (largest area), MADHYA PRADESH, GUJARAT, KARNATAKA (northern), ANDHRA PRADESH (western), TAMIL NADU (Coimbatore, Salem), Chhattisgarh (parts). CHARACTERISTICS: (1) RICH in calcium, potassium, magnesium, iron, lime; POOR in nitrogen, phosphorus, humus. (2) Very FINE TEXTURE → retains moisture well (good for dry Kharif crops under rain-fed conditions). (3) Develops DEEP CRACKS in summer (self-ploughing) + swells when wet → can damage foundations, roads. (4) Deep black → absorbs heat, warms soil fast. (5) DARK COLOUR from titanium + iron compounds. SUITABLE CROPS: COTTON (primary), wheat, jowar, linseed, pulses, tobacco, sugarcane, soyabean, groundnut, sunflower. SIX MAJOR INDIAN SOIL TYPES (ICAR classification): (1) ALLUVIAL (~40% — Indo-Gangetic plain, coastal plains; most fertile; khadar + bhangar subtypes); (2) BLACK/Regur; (3) RED + YELLOW (peninsular India, derived from metamorphic rocks); (4) LATERITE (areas of high rainfall + temp — Kerala, Karnataka, Odisha, hills of NE + Eastern + Western Ghats); (5) ARID/DESERT (Rajasthan, Gujarat); (6) FOREST/Mountain (Himalayan slopes). Other: Saline/Alkaline (Punjab's reh); Peaty + Marshy (Kerala's Kuttanad, Sundarbans). Maharashtra, MP, Gujarat, Karnataka, AP; derived from basalt + volcanic lava.

The 'WHITE REVOLUTION' (Operation Flood) that made India the world's LARGEST MILK PRODUCER was led by:

(A) M.S. Swaminathan
(B) Dr VERGHESE KURIEN ('Father of White Revolution' / 'Milkman of India') via AMUL + NDDB from 1970
(C) Norman Borlaug
(D) C. Subramaniam
cards.back:
(B) Dr VERGHESE KURIEN ('Father of White Revolution' / 'Milkman of India') via AMUL + NDDB from 1970

Agriculture & Industry — OPERATION FLOOD / WHITE REVOLUTION — launched 13 January 1970 by the NATIONAL DAIRY DEVELOPMENT BOARD (NDDB, est. 1965, Anand, Gujarat). ARCHITECT: Dr VERGHESE KURIEN (1921-2012) — 'Milkman of India' / 'Father of the White Revolution'; Founder-Chairman of NDDB (1965); Founding Chairman of AMUL (Anand Milk Union Limited, est. 1946 by Tribhuvandas Patel). AMUL MODEL: 3-tier cooperative — (1) VILLAGE-level milk producers' societies; (2) DISTRICT-level unions (e.g., Kaira District Co-op Milk Producers' Union, AMUL); (3) STATE-level federations (Gujarat Co-op Milk Marketing Federation, GCMMF, markets the AMUL brand). Motto: 'farmer owned, farmer run'. 3 PHASES of Operation Flood (1970-96): Phase I (1970-80) — 18 milksheds, 'Anand Pattern' replicated; Phase II (1981-85) — Operation spread nationwide; Phase III (1985-96) — consolidation. RESULT: India surpassed USA as world's largest MILK producer in 1998; today ~24% of global milk. Per-capita milk availability: ~430 grams/day (2022) — above WHO minimum. KURIEN AWARDS: Padma Vibhushan (1999), World Food Prize (1989), Magsaysay Award (1963). HIS OTHER achievement: HE PIONEERED milk powder FROM BUFFALO milk (previously thought impossible; developed at Amul's Anand lab by engineers Dalaya + Kurien) — this made India's buffalo-heavy dairy viable. 26 NOVEMBER (Kurien's birthday) celebrated as NATIONAL MILK DAY.

cards.front:
INDIA's largest producer of PULSES is:

(A) Uttar Pradesh
(B) MADHYA PRADESH
(C) Punjab
(D) Kerala
cards.back:
(B) MADHYA PRADESH

Agriculture & Industry — PULSES — India is the WORLD'S LARGEST producer, consumer + importer of pulses. TOP STATES: (1) MADHYA PRADESH — ~25% of national output (3.5-5 MT/yr); main crops = GRAM/chana + tur/arhar + urad + moong + masoor. MP is also largest producer of SOYABEAN. (2) RAJASTHAN — ~17%; desert + semi-arid areas are pulse-friendly. (3) MAHARASHTRA — ~14%; tur heartland, Vidarbha. (4) UP — ~9%; (5) Karnataka, AP, Bihar follow. INDIA IMPORTS pulses despite being largest producer — demand outpaces supply due to rising population + vegetarianism + low productivity (~700-800 kg/ha vs Canada's 2,000+). MAJOR IMPORT sources: CANADA (yellow peas + lentils), Myanmar (urad/tur), Mozambique + Tanzania + Sudan + Malawi (tur); long-term deals signed with Mozambique. ICRISAT (Hyderabad) leads pulse research. NATIONAL PULSES MISSION + PM Annadata Aay Sanrakshan Abhiyan (PM-AASHA) for procurement. MSP hikes 2014-2024 (chana, tur, urad, moong, masoor). Pulses nitrogen-fix soil (legumes — Rhizobium bacteria) → sustainable. NATIONAL FOOD SECURITY Act 2013 covers pulse distribution via PDS in some states. INDIAN PULSES: CHANA (Cicer arietinum, gram), TUR/ARHAR (Cajanus cajan, pigeon pea), URAD (Vigna mungo, black gram), MOONG (Vigna radiata, green gram), MASOOR (Lens culinaris, red lentil), rajma (kidney bean), lobia (cowpea), matar (field pea). 2016 = International Year of Pulses (UN, proposed by India). ~25% of national production; gram (chana), tur, urad, moong, masoor; state gets 'Krishi Karman' Awards often.

cards.front:
The MINIMUM SUPPORT PRICE (MSP) for agricultural crops is RECOMMENDED by:

(A) Finance Commission
(B) CACP
(C) RBI
(D) NITI Aayog
cards.back:
(B) CACP

Agriculture & Industry — MSP (MINIMUM SUPPORT PRICE) — a guarantee-floor price by the Indian government to protect farmers from post-harvest price crash + incentivise production of target crops. PROCESS: (1) CACP (Commission for Agricultural Costs + Prices) — an attached office of Ministry of Agriculture + Farmers' Welfare (est. 1965 as APC, renamed CACP 1985). Recommends MSPs based on: A2 (paid-out costs), A2+FL (paid-out + imputed family labour), C2 (comprehensive cost incl. rent + interest on owned assets). (2) CACP submits PRICE POLICY REPORTS for Kharif + Rabi crops to the government. (3) CCEA (Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs, chaired by PM) — APPROVES the MSPs. (4) FCI (Food Corporation of India, est. 1965) — the MAIN procurement agency for WHEAT + RICE; state agencies also procure in some states (Markfed in Punjab etc.). CROPS COVERED: 23 — 14 KHARIF (paddy, jowar, bajra, ragi, maize, tur/arhar, moong, urad, groundnut, sunflower seed, soyabean, sesamum, nigerseed, cotton) + 6 RABI (wheat, barley, gram, masoor, rapeseed/mustard, safflower) + 2 others (jute + copra) + sugarcane (FRP — Fair + Remunerative Price — by CCEA). SWAMINATHAN COMMISSION (2004-06): recommended MSP = C2 + 50%; partially implemented from 2018 as A2+FL + 50%. FARM LAW PROTESTS (2020-21): one key demand was LEGAL GUARANTEE of MSP; farm laws repealed Nov 2021; MSP committee set up 2022; recent 2024 protests continue. PROCUREMENT heavily skewed — WHEAT + RICE dominate; Punjab + Haryana farmers benefit most; pulse + oilseed procurement weaker.

cards.front:
The PM-KISAN SAMMAN NIDHI scheme provides INCOME SUPPORT to farmers of:

(A) Only marginal farmers (<1 ha)
(B) ALL landholding farmers
(C) Only farmers above 60 years
(D) Only organic farmers
cards.back:
(B) ALL landholding farmers

Agriculture & Industry — PM-KISAN SAMMAN NIDHI — CENTRAL-SECTOR scheme (100% Centre-funded) launched 1 FEBRUARY 2019 (Interim Budget), effective RETROSPECTIVELY from 1 DECEMBER 2018; 1st instalment disbursed Feb 24, 2019 by PM Modi at Gorakhpur. BENEFICIARIES (post-1 Jun 2019 expansion): ALL LANDHOLDING farming families (previously only <2ha holders); EXCLUSIONS: former + current constitutional post-holders; MPs/MLAs/MLCs; retired govt officials; income-tax payers in preceding year; pensioners >₹10000/month; professionals (doctors, lawyers, CAs); INSTITUTIONAL landholders. AMOUNT: ₹6000/year per family in 3 EQUAL INSTALMENTS of ₹2000 — April-July, Aug-Nov, Dec-March. DBT directly to bank accounts via AADHAAR-seeded banking (NPCI). BUDGET: ~₹60,000 crore/year; total ~9.5+ crore beneficiary farmers; launched via PM-KISAN portal (pmkisan.gov.in). RELATED farmer schemes: (1) PMFBY — Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (2016, crop insurance; premium 1.5-2% Kharif, Rabi); (2) PM-KMY — PM Kisan Maandhan Yojana (2019, pension scheme; ₹3000/month post-60); (3) Soil Health Card (2015); (4) e-NAM (National Agriculture Market, 2016, online mandi integration); (5) Kisan Credit Card (1998); (6) PM Matsya Sampada Yojana (fisheries 2020); (7) PMKSY — PM Krishi Sinchayee Yojana (irrigation 2015); (8) PDMC (Per Drop More Crop). STATE variants: Andhra PM-Kisan top-up (₹13,500); TELANGANA Rythu Bandhu (₹10,000/acre/year 2018); Odisha KALIA; WB Krishak Bandhu. DOUBLING FARMER INCOME — target for 2022 (goal partially met). ₹6000/year in 3 installments of ₹2000 each — direct benefit transfer (DBT) to Aadhaar-linked accounts.

cards.front:
India is the LARGEST PRODUCER in the world of:

(A) Wheat + rice
(B) MILK, PULSES, JUTE, SPICES, COTTON
(C) Soyabean + corn
(D) Coffee + cocoa
cards.back:
(B) MILK, PULSES, JUTE, SPICES, COTTON

Agriculture & Industry — INDIA'S WORLD-#1 AGRICULTURAL PRODUCTS (as of 2023 FAO + APEDA data): (1) MILK — #1, 24% of global; ~230 MT/yr. (2) PULSES — #1, 25% of global; ~27 MT/yr. (3) JUTE — #1, 55% of global; ~10 MT/yr (mostly WB). (4) SPICES — #1, 70% of production + consumption; major exports of chilli, turmeric, cumin, coriander, pepper; India is 'Spice Bowl of the World'. (5) COTTON — #1 in production as of 2015 (overtook China) — ~6-6.5 MT/yr. (6) BANANA — #1 by far, ~26% global. (7) MANGO — #1, 40% global (Alphonso, Dasheri, Langra, Chausa, Totapuri). (8) PAPAYA, CUSTARD APPLE, GUAVA, CHIKOO — #1. (9) CASHEW — #1 producer (historically; now China comes close). (10) CASTOR OIL — #1. (11) GINGER — #1. (12) OKRA — #1. (13) BUFFALO MEAT — #1. INDIA'S WORLD #2 products: WHEAT (after China), RICE (after China), SUGARCANE (after Brazil), ONION (after China), POTATO (after China), GROUNDNUT (after China), TEA (after China), FISH (after China), SILK (after China). #3: COFFEE in Robusta; TOBACCO. INDIA'S WORLD #1 CONSUMER of: tea, pulses, spices. INDIA'S LARGEST EXPORTS in agriculture: rice (basmati + non-basmati, #1 rice exporter globally — ~40% market share), sugar, buffalo meat, spices, cotton, tea. TOTAL AGRI EXPORTS ~$50 billion. KRISHI UDAN YOJANA + APEDA promote exports. all 5 are world-#1 categories for India.
