cards.front:
The 'SUGAR BOWL' of India refers to the belt of which state?

(A) Maharashtra
(B) UTTAR PRADESH
(C) Gujarat
(D) Punjab
cards.back:
(B) UTTAR PRADESH

Agriculture & Industry — 'SUGAR BOWL OF INDIA' — nickname for UTTAR PRADESH, which accounts for ~45% of India's sugarcane production + ~35-40% of sugar production. MAIN SUGARCANE BELT: western UP districts — MUZAFFARNAGAR, MEERUT, BULANDSHAHR, BIJNOR, SAHARANPUR, BAGHPAT, SHAMLI; central UP — Bareilly, Shahjahanpur, Sitapur, Lakhimpur Kheri. Home to many of India's oldest sugar mills (Triveni, Bajaj Hindusthan, Balrampur Chini, DCM Shriram). NATURAL FAVORS: (1) fertile alluvial soil of Gangetic plain; (2) warm humid summers + mild winters; (3) abundant irrigation (Ganga, Yamuna canal systems, tubewells); (4) Ganga-Yamuna doab = one of world's most productive agricultural zones. TROPICAL vs SUBTROPICAL belts of sugarcane in India: (a) SUBTROPICAL = UP, BIHAR, PUNJAB, HARYANA, UTTARAKHAND — 60% of area but LOWER yield (~65 tonnes/ha); lower sucrose content. (b) TROPICAL = MAHARASHTRA, KARNATAKA, AP, TELANGANA, TAMIL NADU, GUJARAT — HIGHER yield (~85-100 tonnes/ha); higher sucrose (12%+); longer growing season. Despite lower area, TROPICAL belt has HIGHER productivity; Maharashtra + Karnataka contribute ~60% of India's SUGAR production (not cane). INDIA = world's 2nd-largest sugarcane producer + 2nd-largest sugar producer (Brazil leads). Sugarcane = a key source of BIOETHANOL (target 20% blending by 2025-26; currently ~12%). SUGAR MILL payments to farmers are a perennial political issue — state-level FRP + SAP differences. especially the Ganges basin of the western + central UP — Muzaffarnagar, Meerut, Bijnor, Shahjahanpur, Sitapur belts.

cards.front:
The JUTE industry of India is concentrated in:

(A) Maharashtra
(B) West Bengal
(C) Gujarat
(D) Andhra Pradesh
cards.back:
(B) West Bengal

Agriculture & Industry — Hugli basin in WB has ~90% of India's jute mills. Reasons: abundant jute crop in Bengal delta + humid climate needed for fibre-softening + Kolkata port + cheap waterway transport + Bihar/Jharkhand coal for power historically. India is the world's largest raw-jute producer.

cards.front:
The 'GREEN REVOLUTION' in India was primarily associated with:

cards.front:
Consider the following statements about INDIAN MONSOON. 1. The south-west monsoon arrives at Kerala around 1 June. 2. The retreating (north-east) monsoon brings heavy rainfall to Tamil Nadu in October-December. 3. The 'break in the monsoon' occurs when the monsoon trough shifts closer to the Himalayan foothills. 4. El Niño events tend to DEPRESS the Indian monsoon, while La Niña tends to ENHANCE it. Which are correct?

(A) 1, 2 and 4 only
(B) 1, 2, 3 and 4
(C) 1 and 3 only
(D) 2 and 4 only
cards.back:
(B) 1, 2, 3 and 4

Agriculture & Industry — All four correct. Official monsoon onset at Kerala: long-term mean 1 June. NE monsoon (Oct-Dec) brings 48% of TN's annual rainfall. 'Break in monsoon' is a documented phenomenon when the monsoon trough shifts north. El Niño (warm Eastern Pacific) weakens Indian monsoon rainfall; La Niña strengthens it.

cards.front:
Which of the following is the LARGEST soil type of India (by area)?

(A) Red soil
(B) Alluvial soil
(C) Black soil (Regur)
(D) Laterite soil
cards.back:
(B) Alluvial soil

cards.front:
INDIA's LARGEST producer of IRON ORE is:

(A) Karnataka
(B) ODISHA
(C) Jharkhand
(D) Chhattisgarh
cards.back:
(B) ODISHA

Minerals & Resources — IRON ORE in INDIA — world's 4TH LARGEST producer after Australia + Brazil + China. Total production ~260 MT/yr (2023-24). India has among the world's best quality HEMATITE reserves + large magnetite reserves. STATE-WISE TOP PRODUCERS: (1) ODISHA — ~55% national production (2023-24). Main belts: KEONJHAR (Barbil-Joda — world's largest iron ore mining town), SUNDARGARH (Banspani-Daitari), MAYURBHANJ (Gorumahisani-Badampahar). KIRIBURU + MEGHAHATUBURU (Jharkhand border) major mines. TISCO + SAIL + NMDC key players. (2) CHHATTISGARH — ~18%; BAILADILA range in DANTEWADA (MAOIST-affected area), ~14 deposits, NMDC-operated. BAILADILA exports iron ore pellets. (3) KARNATAKA — ~14%; BELLARY-HOSPET (Sandur schist belt), KUDREMUKH (magnetite, mining stopped 2005 per SC order), Chitradurga, Tumkur. (4) JHARKHAND — ~8%; NOAMUNDI, GUA, CHIRIA, MANOHARPUR (Singhbhum district) — Tata Steel leases + SAIL. (5) Other: Goa (pre-ban), Maharashtra, AP, Rajasthan. IRON ORE GRADES: (a) HEMATITE (Fe₂O₃) — deep red/black, 60-70% Fe, FRIABLE HIGH-GRADE (DANTEWADA, Keonjhar). (b) MAGNETITE (Fe₃O₄) — black, magnetic, 70% Fe (Kudremukh, Salem). (c) LIMONITE + SIDERITE — less common. MAJOR STEEL PLANTS: TATA STEEL (Jamshedpur, 1907, private), SAIL (Bhilai, Bokaro, Durgapur, Rourkela, Burnpur, Salem), RINL-VIZAG (public), JSW (Vijayanagar, Dolvi), Jindal (Angul, Raigarh, Toranagallu), Essar (Hazira, now JSW). INDIA is world's 2ND LARGEST crude steel producer (behind China) since 2019 — ~140 MT/yr. EXPORTS of iron ore PELLETS big to China, Japan, Korea. 'GOA BAN' (2012 onwards, Shah Commission) halted illegal mining. NMDC (PSU, HQ Hyderabad) = largest iron ore miner publicly. ~55% of India's iron ore production; major mines at Barbil-Joda-Bonai-Keonjhar-Sundargarh belt.

cards.front:
INDIA's largest COAL-PRODUCING state is:

(A) West Bengal
(B) JHARKHAND (coal)
(C) Tamil Nadu
(D) Kerala
cards.back:
(B) JHARKHAND (coal)

Minerals & Resources — COAL in INDIA — world's 2nd LARGEST producer (after China) + 2nd LARGEST CONSUMER + 3rd LARGEST reserves (after USA + Russia). Power source for ~55-60% of India's electricity (though falling with renewables surge). ANNUAL PRODUCTION (FY 2023-24): ~1 BILLION TONNES (milestone crossed by COAL INDIA LIMITED + captive + commercial miners). STATE RANKINGS: (1) JHARKHAND ~25%; (2) ODISHA ~24%; (3) CHHATTISGARH ~21%; (4) MADHYA PRADESH ~11%; (5) TELANGANA ~8%; (6) MAHARASHTRA ~6%; (7) West Bengal ~3%. MAJOR COALFIELDS: (1) JHARIA (Jharkhand, Dhanbad) — India's LARGEST coal reserves + only COKING COAL (used in steel making); underground fires raging since 1916 — a ecological disaster + affects 500,000 people. (2) RANIGANJ (West Bengal, Asansol) — OLDEST coalfield; first discovered 1774 by Sumner + Heatly of EIC. (3) BOKARO (Jharkhand) — non-coking. (4) KARANPURA + GIRIDIH (Jharkhand). (5) SINGRAULI (MP-UP border). (6) TALCHER (Odisha). (7) KORBA (Chhattisgarh). (8) GODAVARI VALLEY (Telangana) — Singareni. (9) NEYVELI (Tamil Nadu) — LIGNITE (brown coal). COAL TYPES: (a) Anthracite (highest, ~95% C, rare in India — mostly J&K); (b) BITUMINOUS (60-80% C, most Indian coal); (c) SUB-BITUMINOUS; (d) LIGNITE (brown, 30-40%, Neyveli TN, Rajasthan, Gujarat). CHIEF PRODUCER: COAL INDIA LIMITED (CIL) — PSU with 8 subsidiaries (CCL, NCL, SECL, WCL, MCL, ECL, BCCL, CMPDIL); world's LARGEST coal-mining company. 2020 AUCTIONS — commercial coal mining opened to PRIVATE sector (previously nationalised 1973). CAPTIVE mines to steel + power companies. CLIMATE: India committed to NET ZERO by 2070 (Glasgow COP26); COAL PHASE-DOWN (not phase-out per India's insistence). RENEWABLES now ~42% of installed capacity. ~25% of national production; Dhanbad district has INDIA's largest coal reserves (Jharia + Bokaro fields).

cards.front:
MUMBAI HIGH, India's largest OFFSHORE OIL FIELD, is located in the:

(A) Bay of Bengal
(B) ARABIAN SEA, ~160 km off Mumbai coast
(C) Gulf of Mannar
(D) Indian Ocean south of Kanyakumari
cards.back:
(B) ARABIAN SEA, ~160 km off Mumbai coast

Minerals & Resources — MUMBAI HIGH (earlier called BOMBAY HIGH) — India's LARGEST OIL FIELD + offshore giant in the Arabian Sea, ~160 km west off Mumbai coast. DISCOVERED: 19 Feb 1974 by ONGC's jack-up rig SAGAR SAMRAT (leased from USSR); first oil flowed 21 May 1976. OWNED + operated by ONGC (Oil + Natural Gas Corporation, est. 14 Aug 1956 as a Commission, became Corporation 1994). COMPOSITION: (a) Mumbai High North + Mumbai High South (carbonate reservoirs, Miocene era); (b) linked to smaller fields — Neelam, Heera, Bassein, B-193 (all Bombay Offshore Basin). Total offshore oil: ~200+ platforms. PEAK PRODUCTION: ~22 MT/yr in 1990s. Today declining; ~10-12 MT/yr. Still accounts for ~40% of India's domestic crude. DISASTER: MUMBAI HIGH NORTH FIRE on 27 July 2005 — fire on Bombay High North platform killed 22; platform destroyed; set back production. OTHER INDIAN OIL FIELDS: (1) ONSHORE — ASSAM (Digboi est. 1889 — India's oldest oil field; Naharkatiya, Moran, Rudrasagar; Numaligarh refinery), GUJARAT (Ankleshwar, Kalol, Lunej — Cambay basin), RAJASTHAN (Barmer — Mangala field, discovered 2004 by Cairn, now Vedanta). (2) OFFSHORE — MUMBAI HIGH, Krishna-Godavari basin (KG-D6 block of Reliance — discovered 2002; disputed/declining gas), Cauvery basin (TN), Bengal basin. REFINERIES: India has 23 — Jamnagar (Reliance, world's largest complex — ~70 MT/yr), IOCL (Mathura, Barauni, Haldia, Panipat, Gujarat), BPCL, HPCL. INDIA imports ~85% of crude — world's 3rd largest oil importer (after China + US). MAJOR SUPPLIERS: Iraq, Saudi Arabia, UAE, Russia (post-2022, discounted due to Ukraine war), USA, Nigeria. SPR (Strategic Petroleum Reserve): Visakhapatnam, Mangaluru, Padur — ~5 MT crude, ~10 days of imports backup (adding more). REFINERY MAJORS of India: IOCL (largest public), RELIANCE (largest private), BPCL, HPCL. discovered 1974 by ONGC + operational from 1976; ~70% of India's domestic crude oil historically.

cards.front:
The KOLAR GOLD FIELDS (now closed) were located in:

(A) Andhra Pradesh
(B) KARNATAKA
(C) Rajasthan
(D) Jharkhand
cards.back:
(B) KARNATAKA

Minerals & Resources — KOLAR GOLD FIELDS (KGF) — located in Kolar district, KARNATAKA, ~100 km east of Bengaluru (Bangalore). Operated 1880 (by John Taylor + Sons, British) — 2001 when BHARAT GOLD MINES LTD (BGML, successor PSU) closed them due to depletion + losses. PEAK: once among world's 2nd DEEPEST mines (~3.2 km deep at Champion Reef; deepest was South Africa's Mponeng at 4 km). KGF's 'town' was a company town, often called 'Mini England' due to British architecture + English-speaking workforce. OVER ~120 YEARS: produced ~800 TONNES of gold; a legendary mining community. MOVIE: 'KGF' (2018-22) the Kannada/PAN-Indian film franchise directed by PRASHANTH NEEL starring YASH — based on KGF lore (fictional). After closure, the town lost jobs + population; many went to Chennai, Bangalore. CURRENT gold mining in INDIA (reduced): (1) HUTTI (Raichur, Karnataka) — ONLY significant gold mine operational today; run by Hutti Gold Mines Ltd (Karnataka PSU). ~2-3 tonnes/yr. (2) RAMAGIRI (Anantapur, AP) — small. (3) SONBHADRA (UP) — recent reports of reserves. (4) LAVA KA BAAS (Rajasthan), Bundelkhand (MP). India PRODUCES only ~1.5-2 tonnes/yr but CONSUMES ~700-900 tonnes/yr (world's LARGEST gold consumer along with China) — mostly IMPORTS. PROCESSING: MMTC-PAMP in Mewat (Haryana) refines imported doré + recycles old gold. SOVEREIGN GOLD BONDS (2015) launched to reduce gold import demand. OTHER LINKED minerals: SILVER in India — mostly by-product of lead-zinc mining (Hindustan Zinc's Zawar/Rampura Agucha, Rajasthan); world's largest silver mine in Mexico (Fresnillo). GOLD RESERVES of RBI: ~800+ tonnes (Jun 2024); used for currency management. ~100 km east of Bangalore; operated 1880-2001; once world's 2nd DEEPEST mine (~3.2 km); closed due to depletion + losses.

cards.front:
Which state is India's LARGEST producer of BAUXITE (aluminium ore)?

(A) Madhya Pradesh
(B) ODISHA
(C) Kerala
(D) Assam
cards.back:
(B) ODISHA

Minerals & Resources — BAUXITE — primary ore of ALUMINIUM (Al₂O₃ + hydrates + impurities). India has world's 5th LARGEST bauxite reserves (~650 MT). STATE-WISE LARGEST PRODUCERS: (1) ODISHA ~50% — Koraput district (PANCHPATMALI mines of NALCO, world's largest Alumina-Aluminium complex). Also Rayagada, Kalahandi (NIYAMGIRI hills — Dongria Kondh tribe's struggle against Vedanta's mining plans, famous environmental case; rejected in 2013 after Gram Sabha vote — UN/ICCPR hailed the tribal veto). (2) GUJARAT ~15% — Kutch + Jamnagar-Devbhumi-Dwarka region. (3) JHARKHAND ~10% — Gumla, Lohardaga; Hindalco mines. (4) MAHARASHTRA ~8% — Kolhapur, Sindhudurg. (5) Madhya Pradesh — Balaghat, Mandla; minor. ALUMINIUM PRODUCTION (India = 2nd largest producer globally): NALCO (National Aluminium, PSU, Odisha) — integrated miner + smelter (Damanjodi refinery, Angul smelter, Panchpatmali mines); HINDALCO (Aditya Birla group) — largest private + global (after Novelis acquisition); VEDANTA / BALCO (Korba) + VEDANTA Jharsuguda (smelter). MAJOR ALUMINIUM SMELTERS: Hirakud, Renukoot (Hindalco UP), Mettur (Vedanta TN), Angul (NALCO), Jharsuguda (Vedanta), Korba (BALCO). cards.front:
India's ONLY TIN-producing state is:

(A) Bihar
(B) CHHATTISGARH
(C) Kerala
(D) Uttarakhand
cards.back:
(B) CHHATTISGARH

Minerals & Resources — TIN (Sn) in INDIA — extremely SCARCE; India relies on imports for ~90%+ of tin needs. ONLY producing state: CHHATTISGARH — DANTEWADA district (BASTAR region). Mineral: CASSITERITE (SnO₂). Producer: HINDUSTAN ZINC (Vedanta) — small-scale operations. BIHAR earlier claims + Jharkhand potential. USES of tin: (a) TINPLATE (tin-coated steel) — cans, soldering; (b) BRONZE (Cu + Sn alloy) — classical alloy; (c) PEWTER (Sn + Sb + Cu). Industrial + consumer goods. WORLD's major tin producers: China, Indonesia, Myanmar, Peru, Bolivia, Malaysia. OTHER RARE / STRATEGIC MINERALS in INDIA: (1) URANIUM — JADUGUDA (Jharkhand — India's only operating uranium mine by UCIL); also Tummalapalle (AP), Turamdih (Jharkhand). Reserves in Meghalaya + Karnataka. (2) THORIUM — Kerala (Manavalakurichi) + Odisha (Chhatrapur) — MONAZITE sands. India has 25% world's thorium reserves → 3-STAGE NUCLEAR program (Bhabha): U-238 → Pu-239 → Th-232 for reactors. (3) RARE EARTH ELEMENTS (REEs) — Kerala + AP beach sands; IREL (Indian Rare Earths Ltd) PSU. China dominates globally. (4) LITHIUM — SALAL-HAIMANA block in REASI, J&K — 5.9 MT inferred REE resources found 2023 (significant for EV batteries). Also explored in Karnataka + Andhra Pradesh. Demand skyrocketed with EV + battery transition. Argentina, Chile, Australia, Bolivia are 'Lithium Triangle' giants. (5) COBALT — explored in Odisha, Jharkhand; also trace in copper ores. (6) GRAPHITE — ANDHRA PRADESH + ODISHA + Jharkhand + Tamil Nadu; India is 4th/5th largest producer (after China, Brazil, Mozambique, Madagascar). (7) MICA — JHARKHAND (Koderma — 'Mica Capital of World' historically), Rajasthan, AP; India is world's 2nd largest producer of mica. 'KOR' metals discovery: India's critical minerals list (2023) notifies 30 critical minerals — lithium, REE, cobalt, graphite, germanium, indium, niobium etc. DANTEWADA district (Bailadila-Bastar region) is India's only tin producer.

cards.front:
Which of these is not a MANGANESE-producing state of India?

(A) Madhya Pradesh (Balaghat)
(B) Maharashtra (Nagpur-Bhandara)
(C) Odisha (Sundargarh-Keonjhar)
(D) PUNJAB — has no significant manganese deposits
cards.back:
(D) PUNJAB — has no significant manganese deposits

Minerals & Resources — MANGANESE in INDIA — 7th largest producer globally. MAIN states: (1) MADHYA PRADESH ~34% — BALAGHAT district (largest manganese mine in India, MOIL-operated). (2) MAHARASHTRA ~25% — NAGPUR-BHANDARA-GONDIA belt (MOIL's underground Dongri Buzurg mine). (3) ODISHA ~20% — SUNDARGARH-KEONJHAR-KORAPUT. (4) KARNATAKA ~10% — North Kanara, Shimoga, Chitradurga, Bellary. (5) ANDHRA PRADESH — Srikakulam, Vizianagaram. (6) JHARKHAND — Singhbhum. (7) RAJASTHAN — Banswara. Also Gujarat + Telangana. MOIL LTD (Manganese Ore India Ltd, Nagpur HQ) — public sector, 45% of India's production. USES of MANGANESE: (1) STEEL making — 90% of world's manganese goes into steelmaking (ferromanganese, silicomanganese alloys) to improve strength, hardness, resistance to wear, workability. Essential in rails, construction, auto-body. (2) DRY CELL BATTERIES — MnO₂ (manganese dioxide) as cathode in Zn-C batteries. (3) ALUMINIUM alloys — manganese improves corrosion resistance (aluminium cans, aircraft). (4) MMT (methylcyclopentadienyl manganese tricarbonyl) — petrol octane enhancer (gasoline additive, partially replaced lead; controversial in US). PUNJAB — DOES NOT HAVE significant manganese deposits. Same for most Indo-Gangetic plain states (Haryana, Punjab, UP plains) — because they're on ALLUVIAL soils (not the Peninsular Plateau where most metallic minerals of India are concentrated). OTHER metallic minerals largely absent in Gangetic plains: iron ore, copper, bauxite, chromite. Punjab has SAND + GRAVEL (important for construction), gypsum (a bit), + some limestone. INDIA's NON-METALLIC minerals: LIMESTONE (Rajasthan, MP, Chhattisgarh, Karnataka, AP, Gujarat — ~220 MT/yr); MICA (Jharkhand, Rajasthan, AP); DOLOMITE (Chhattisgarh); GYPSUM (Rajasthan, J&K, Gujarat — Jaisalmer, Bikaner); ASBESTOS (Andhra Pradesh, Rajasthan); SALT (Gujarat — Kutch, Rann; Rajasthan — Sambhar Lake; TN — Marakkanam); DIAMONDS (Panna, MP — only).

cards.front:
The only DIAMOND-producing mine still active in India is in:

(A) Golconda, Hyderabad
(B) PANNA, Madhya Pradesh
(C) Jaipur, Rajasthan
(D) Surat, Gujarat
cards.back:
(B) PANNA, Madhya Pradesh

Minerals & Resources — DIAMONDS in INDIA — HISTORIC global leader (until South Africa + Russia + Australia discoveries of 19th-20th c.). Ancient sources: (1) GOLCONDA kingdom (around Hyderabad) — produced legendary diamonds from mines along the Krishna River: KOH-I-NOOR ('Mountain of Light', 105.6 carats now in British Crown, part of Queen Mother's Crown; India's ongoing repatriation demand), HOPE DIAMOND (45.5 carats, dark blue, Smithsonian DC), DARYA-I-NOOR ('Sea of Light', Iranian crown jewels), REGENT (140 carats, Louvre Paris), ORLOV (189 carats, Kremlin) — many were found at Kollur mines Andhra. (2) In MEDIEVAL times, Golconda was WORLD'S ONLY diamond source until 18th c. Today only OPERATING diamond mine is at PANNA, Madhya Pradesh — MAJHGAWAN mine (kimberlite pipe, discovered 1960s), operated by NMDC (Nat Mineral Dev Corp, PSU). Produces ~30,000-40,000 carats per year. Small volume globally (world produces ~130 million carats/year). Other Panna-area mines private via auction. INDIA is now world's LARGEST CUTTER + POLISHER + EXPORTER OF DIAMONDS — not PRODUCER. ~90% of world's cut diamonds are processed in INDIA — mainly SURAT, Gujarat (~500,000 workers, 'Diamond City'; Surat diamond bourse inaugurated Dec 2023 — world's largest office complex). Indian POLISHERS import ROUGH diamonds from De Beers, Alrosa, Rio Tinto — cut them into brilliant form + export as POLISHED diamonds worth ~$22-25B annually. FAMOUS INDIAN diamond merchants: Jatin Mehta (Winsome), Nirav Modi (fled), Mehul Choksi (Gitanjali, fled), Savji Dholakia (Hari Krishna Exports, Surat — famous for giving employees cars + homes as Diwali bonus). Recent shift towards LAB-GROWN DIAMONDS (CVD-process) — India also emerging player. Natural diamond prices dropping 30-40% since 2022 due to LGD competition. Majhgawan mine operated by NMDC; produces ~30,000 carats annually.

cards.front:
NMDC, INDIA's largest IRON ORE producing company, is headquartered in:

(A) Bhubaneswar
(B) HYDERABAD (Telangana)
(C) Raipur
(D) Ranchi
cards.back:
(B) HYDERABAD (Telangana)

Minerals & Resources — NMDC (NATIONAL MINERAL DEVELOPMENT CORPORATION) — India's largest iron-ore producer. ESTABLISHED: 1958. HEADQUARTERS: HYDERABAD (Telangana). Navratna CPSE (Central Public Sector Enterprise). Operates 4 integrated production facilities: BAILADILA sectors in CHHATTISGARH (Kirandul, Bacheli — ~35 MT/yr combined) + DONIMALAI in KARNATAKA. Total iron ore production: ~45 MT/yr — largest by tonnage in India. Also produces DIAMONDS (Panna, MP — Majhgawan mine, India's ONLY operating diamond mine), phosphorite, limestone, dolomite. Constructed NMDC STEEL LTD (Nagarnar, Chhattisgarh 3 MTPA steel plant, demerged 2022, being privatised). OTHER MAJOR PSU MINERS: (1) COAL INDIA LIMITED (CIL) — Kolkata HQ; world's largest coal miner. 8 subsidiaries + CMPDIL research. Listed 2010, largest IPO then. (2) ONGC — Delhi/Dehradun HQ; oil + gas. (3) SAIL — Delhi HQ; integrated steel. (4) NALCO — Bhubaneswar HQ; aluminium. (5) HINDUSTAN COPPER (HCL) — Kolkata HQ; copper ore + smelting. Main mines: Khetri (Rajasthan), Malanjkhand (MP), Singhbhum (Jharkhand). (6) HINDUSTAN ZINC (Vedanta) — Udaipur HQ; world's 2nd largest zinc miner. Zawar + Rampura Agucha (Rajasthan). (7) URANIUM CORP (UCIL) — Jaduguda HQ; uranium. (8) MOIL — Nagpur HQ; manganese. (9) ECL, BHEL, REC, NTPC in energy. INDIAN MINING CONTRIBUTES ~2.5% of GDP; employment ~1 million direct. REGULATED by: MINISTRY OF MINES, MINES + MINERALS (DEVELOPMENT + REGULATION) ACT (MMDR Act 1957), AMENDMENTS 2015 (auction-based allocation) + 2021 + 2023 (private sector opening for critical minerals + atomic). Indian Bureau of Mines (IBM, Nagpur) regulates. STATE Mines + Geology departments allocate minor minerals.

cards.front:
JADUGUDA, India's only operating URANIUM mine, is in:

(A) Jharkhand (Singhbhum)
(B) Andhra Pradesh
(C) Meghalaya
(D) Karnataka
cards.back:
(A) Jharkhand (Singhbhum)

Minerals & Resources — JADUGUDA — India's FIRST + LONGEST-operating URANIUM MINE. LOCATION: Jaduguda (Jadugoda) in EAST SINGHBHUM district of JHARKHAND, ~35 km from Jamshedpur. MINING started 1967 by UCIL (URANIUM CORPORATION of INDIA LTD — PSU under Dept of Atomic Energy, DAE). Additional mines in the Singhbhum region: Bhatin, Narwapahar, Turamdih, Bagjata, Banduhurang, Mohuldih, Kamar PC. Grade ~0.06% U₃O₈ (low compared to world avg). Uranium from Jaduguda goes to the mill at Jaduguda → yellowcake (U₃O₈) → to Hyderabad's Nuclear Fuel Complex (NFC) for enrichment + fuel fabrication → ultimately to nuclear power plants. ENVIRONMENTAL + HEALTH CONCERNS: villages around Jaduguda have reported higher rates of birth defects + cancers — extensively documented by journalists + NGO studies. UCIL + DAE contest the link. Tailings ponds. TUMMALAPALLE, ANDHRA PRADESH — India's LARGEST uranium deposit (sedimentary, ~1.5 lakh tonnes U₃O₈; massive reserve by world standards). Operational since 2012. Processing plant runs but grade is low (~0.05%). MEGHALAYA — exploration deposits (Domiasiat); tribal opposition blocked mining. Karnataka + Chhattisgarh + Rajasthan — exploration. RAJASTHAN's Rohil deposit (Sikar district) found ~2007. India's total uranium reserves: ~2.7 lakh tonnes (as of 2024 DAE estimates). INDIA IS NOT signatory to NPT (Non-Proliferation Treaty); until 2008 INDO-US NUCLEAR DEAL (123 agreement + NSG waiver), India couldn't import uranium — forced reliance on domestic Jaduguda. Post-2008 — India signed civil nuclear cooperation with USA, France, Russia, Kazakhstan, Mongolia, Canada, Australia, Argentina, Namibia — now imports uranium from KAZAKHSTAN (main), France, Russia, Canada, Australia. India's 3-STAGE NUCLEAR PROGRAMME (Bhabha Plan): (1) Pressurised Heavy Water Reactors (PHWRs) on natural U — most current reactors; (2) Fast Breeder Reactors on Pu (from spent fuel) — Kalpakkam PFBR; (3) Thorium reactors using U-233 (from Th-232 converted in FBRs) — long-term self-sufficiency via India's huge thorium reserves.

India's largest producer of COAL is:

(A) Odisha
(B) Jharkhand
(C) Chhattisgarh
(D) West Bengal
cards.back:

The LARGEST iron-ore-producing state in India is:

(A) Jharkhand

cards.front:
Rocks formed by the cooling and solidification of MAGMA or LAVA are called:

(A) Sedimentary rocks, formed by deposition of sediments over time
(B) Igneous rocks, formed when molten material cools and solidifies
(C) Metamorphic rocks, formed under heat and pressure
(D) Loose sediments, like sand and clay layers in deltas
cards.back:
(B) Igneous rocks, formed when molten material cools and solidifies

Minerals & Resources — IGNEOUS rocks (Latin 'ignis' fire) — cooled magma (intrusive, slow-cooled, large crystals — granite) or lava (extrusive, fast-cooled, small crystals — basalt). The Deccan Traps are basalt flows (~65 million years old). SEDIMENTARY (Distractor 1) — formed by accumulation + cementation of particles (sandstone, limestone). METAMORPHIC (Distractor 3) — pre-existing rocks transformed by heat / pressure (limestone → marble, shale → slate, granite → gneiss).

cards.option2: Metamorphic rocks, formed under heat and pressure
cards.option3: Loose sediments, like sand and clay layers in deltas

cards.front:
MARBLE is the metamorphic form of which sedimentary rock?

(A) Sandstone, formed from compacted sand grains
(B) Limestone, formed mainly from calcium carbonate
(C) Shale, a fine-grained clay-rich rock
(D) Conglomerate, a coarse rock of rounded pebbles
cards.back:
(B) Limestone, formed mainly from calcium carbonate

Minerals & Resources — Marble = metamorphosed LIMESTONE (CaCO₃). Heat + pressure recrystallise the calcite grains into a denser, harder rock. Famous Indian marbles — Makrana (Rajasthan), used in Taj Mahal. Other parent → metamorphic pairs: SANDSTONE → quartzite; SHALE → slate (then phyllite, schist, gneiss with increasing grade); GRANITE → gneiss; LIMESTONE → marble; coal → graphite → diamond (with extreme P + T).

cards.front:
The most ABUNDANT element in the Earth's continental crust by weight is:

(A) Iron, the major component of Earth's core
(B) Oxygen, present in nearly all silicate minerals
(C) Carbon, the basis of life and organic compounds
(D) Hydrogen, the lightest and most common in oceans
cards.back:
(B) Oxygen, present in nearly all silicate minerals

Minerals & Resources — Earth's crust composition (by mass): Oxygen ~46%, Silicon ~28%, Aluminium ~8%, Iron ~5%, Calcium ~4%, Sodium ~3%, Potassium ~3%, Magnesium ~2%, others ~1%. Most rock-forming minerals are SILICATES (containing SiO₄ tetrahedra) — quartz, feldspar, mica, pyroxene, amphibole. Iron is abundant in the CORE but only ~5% of the crust. Distractor 1 confuses crust with core. Distractor 3 — carbon is rare in crust (~0.1%). Distractor 4 — hydrogen is abundant in oceans/atmosphere but minor in crust.

cards.front:
The hardest naturally-occurring substance — a 10 on the Mohs scale — is:

(A) Quartz, found in many sedimentary rocks
(B) Diamond, the high-pressure form of carbon
(C) Corundum, the gem family with sapphire and ruby
(D) Topaz, a silicate gemstone of pale colour
cards.back:
(B) Diamond, the high-pressure form of carbon

Minerals & Resources — Mohs hardness scale (1-10): TALC 1, GYPSUM 2, CALCITE 3, FLUORITE 4, APATITE 5, ORTHOCLASE FELDSPAR 6, QUARTZ 7, TOPAZ 8, CORUNDUM 9, DIAMOND 10. Diamond is the hardest known natural substance (carbon atoms in tetrahedral covalent network). Synthetic substances — wurtzite boron nitride, lonsdaleite — even harder. Mineral hardness measures resistance to scratching, not toughness (diamond can shatter from impact). Industrial diamond is used in cutting tools, drill bits, abrasives.

The major ORE of ALUMINIUM is:

(B) Bauxite, a hydrated aluminium oxide ore
(C) Galena, the chief lead-bearing mineral
(D) Cinnabar, the principal mercury ore
cards.back:
(B) Bauxite, a hydrated aluminium oxide ore

Minerals & Resources — BAUXITE — Al₂O₃·xH₂O (hydrated aluminium oxide). Major aluminium ore. Refined to alumina via the Bayer process; alumina then electrolysed (Hall-Héroult process) to yield aluminium. India is among the top 5 bauxite producers; major reserves in Odisha (Panchpatmali, Kalahandi), AP, Jharkhand, Gujarat, Maharashtra. Distractor 1 — hematite is iron ore (Fe₂O₃). Distractor 3 — galena is lead ore (PbS). Distractor 4 — cinnabar is mercury ore (HgS). Other ore-element pairs to know: pyrite/iron, magnetite/iron, chalcopyrite/copper, sphalerite/zinc, monazite/thorium-rare earths.

cards.front:
BASALT, the dark volcanic rock that covers much of the Deccan plateau, is an:

(A) Intrusive coarse-grained igneous rock cooling slowly underground
(B) Extrusive fine-grained igneous rock from cooling lava on the surface
(C) Sedimentary rock made of compacted volcanic ash and dust
(D) Metamorphic rock formed from limestone under intense pressure
cards.back:
(B) Extrusive fine-grained igneous rock from cooling lava on the surface

Minerals & Resources — BASALT — extrusive (volcanic), mafic, fine-grained because it cools rapidly when erupted onto the surface. Deccan Traps in central + western India: ~65 million years ago, vast lava flows from a hot-spot eruption (linked to the K-Pg mass extinction along with the Chicxulub impact). Cover ~500,000 km², forming distinctive 'trap' (staircase) topography in Maharashtra, Gujarat, MP. Also major in mid-ocean ridges, oceanic crust, ocean islands like Hawaii. Distractor 1 = granite (intrusive felsic). Distractor 3 = tuff. Distractor 4 = marble.

cards.option2: Sedimentary rock made of compacted volcanic ash and dust
cards.option3: Metamorphic rock formed from limestone under intense pressure

cards.front:
The ROCK CYCLE describes how:

(A) Rocks remain unchanged in their original form indefinitely
(B) Each rock type can transform into the others over geological time
(C) Sedimentary rocks are formed only at the equator regions
(D) Igneous rocks always remain igneous after their formation
cards.back:
(B) Each rock type can transform into the others over geological time

Minerals & Resources — Rock cycle — geological process by which the three rock types interconvert: IGNEOUS rocks weather and erode → sediments → SEDIMENTARY rocks; sedimentary rocks subjected to heat + pressure → METAMORPHIC; metamorphic rocks melt → magma → IGNEOUS again. Time scale — typically millions of years. Driving forces: plate tectonics, volcanism, weathering, erosion, deposition. Sedimentary rocks form anywhere sediments accumulate (river deltas, sea floors, lakebeds, deserts) — NOT just at the equator.

(B) Sahara, spanning much of north Africa

Spans 11 countries — Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, Libya, Egypt, Western Sahara, Mauritania, Mali, Niger, Chad, Sudan. Largest desert overall is ANTARCTICA (cold desert, ~14 million km²). Distractor 1 = Kalahari (southern Africa). Distractor 3 = Namib (Namibia, Atlantic coast). Distractor 4 = Atacama (driest desert, Chile/Peru).

cards.front:
The LONGEST river in Africa (and one of the longest in the world) is the:

(A) Congo River, of central African basin
(B) Nile River, flowing through 11 African countries
(C) Niger River, of west African region
(D) Zambezi River, of southern African region
cards.back:
(B) Nile River, flowing through 11 African countries

World Geography — Nile — ~6,650 km. Often listed as the LONGEST river in the world (Amazon contests this; modern measurements suggest Amazon may be longer). Two main tributaries: WHITE NILE (origin Lake Victoria; primary source) + BLUE NILE (origin Lake Tana, Ethiopia; carries most sediment + water during rains). Joins at Khartoum, Sudan; flows through Egypt; delta at Mediterranean. Civilisations along Nile — Ancient Egypt, Nubia. Aswan High Dam (1970, USSR-aided, Egypt). Distractor 1 = Congo (~4,700 km, 2nd longest). Distractor 3 = Niger (~4,180 km). Distractor 4 = Zambezi (~2,693 km).

cards.front:
The GREAT RIFT VALLEY, a major geological feature, runs through:

(A) Western Africa, from Senegal to Nigeria
(B) Eastern Africa, from Mozambique to the Red Sea
(C) Northern Africa, across the Sahara region
(D) Southern Africa, around the Cape of Good Hope
cards.back:
(B) Eastern Africa, from Mozambique to the Red Sea

World Geography — East African Rift — ~6,400 km long, from Mozambique through Malawi, Tanzania, Kenya, Ethiopia, into the Red Sea + Jordan Valley. Caused by Africa SPLITTING into two tectonic plates (Nubian + Somali) at ~6-7 mm/year — eventually a new ocean will form (millions of years). Hosts the AFRICAN GREAT LAKES — Tanganyika, Malawi, Turkana, Albert. Active volcanoes — Kilimanjaro, Kenya, Nyiragongo. Hominid fossil sites — Olduvai Gorge (Tanzania), Hadar (Ethiopia, Lucy). Distractors are wrong regions.

(B) Mount Kilimanjaro, in northern Tanzania

(D) Mount Cameroon, in west African Cameroon
cards.back:

Distractor 3 = Mt Stanley / Margherita Peak (Rwenzori, Uganda-DRC, 5,109 m, 3rd). Distractor 4 = Mount Cameroon (4,040 m, active volcano).

cards.front:
VICTORIA FALLS, one of the world's largest waterfalls, lies on the border between:

(A) Egypt and Sudan, on the Nile River
(B) Zambia and Zimbabwe, on the Zambezi River
(C) Kenya and Uganda, between two lakes
(D) Nigeria and Cameroon, on the Niger River
cards.back:
(B) Zambia and Zimbabwe, on the Zambezi River

World Geography — Victoria Falls — on the ZAMBEZI river, ZAMBIA-ZIMBABWE border. Local name 'Mosi-oa-Tunya' = 'The Smoke that Thunders'. Width 1,708 m, height 108 m. Discovered + named (after Queen Victoria) by David Livingstone in 1855. Volume: 1 km wide × 100 m high curtain of water — among world's largest by combined width × height. UNESCO World Heritage Site. Compare: Niagara (US-Canada, 51 m high but high volume), Iguazu (Brazil-Argentina, ~80 m, very wide), Angel Falls (Venezuela, world's tallest at 979 m).

cards.front:
The imaginary line that divides the Earth into the Northern and Southern Hemispheres is called the:

(A) Tropic of Cancer
(B) Equator
(C) Prime Meridian
(D) Arctic Circle
cards.back:
(B) Equator

World Geography — The Equator (latitude 0°) is the great circle equidistant from the poles — divides Earth into Northern and Southern Hemispheres. The Prime Meridian (longitude 0°, through Greenwich) divides East and West Hemispheres. Other key parallels — Tropic of Cancer (23.5° N), Tropic of Capricorn (23.5° S), Arctic Circle (66.5° N), Antarctic Circle (66.5° S).

cards.front:
The 'Tropic of Cancer' passes through how many Indian states?

(A) Six
(B) Eight
(C) Ten
(D) Five
cards.back:
(B) Eight

World Geography — The Tropic of Cancer (23.5° N) passes through eight Indian states — from west to east — Gujarat, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Tripura, Mizoram. A popular mnemonic: 'Go Race Mom Cha-Cha Ju Who-a Tells Mi' or simply memorise the order west-to-east: Gu-Ra-MP-CG-JH-WB-TR-MZ.

cards.front:
Indian Standard Time (IST) is based on the 82.5° E longitude, which passes through:

(A) Mumbai (Maharashtra)
(B) Mirzapur (Uttar Pradesh)
(C) Kolkata (West Bengal)
(D) Chennai (Tamil Nadu)
cards.back:
(B) Mirzapur (Uttar Pradesh)

World Geography — IST is GMT+5:30 — derived from longitude 82.5° E (since 15° of longitude = 1 hour; 82.5 × 4 min/° = 330 min = 5:30 hours). The 82.5° E meridian passes through Mirzapur (UP) and is called the Standard Meridian of India. It also passes through AP and parts of Odisha. Only ONE time zone for the whole country; debated periodically (NE states lose early daylight).

cards.front:
The difference in time between Gujarat (westernmost India) and Arunachal Pradesh (easternmost India) is approximately:

(A) 1 hour
(B) 2 hours
(C) 3 hours
(D) 30 minutes
cards.back:
(B) 2 hours

World Geography — India spans longitudes ~68° E (Gujarat) to ~97° E (Arunachal Pradesh) — about 29° of longitude. Time difference = 29° × 4 min/° ≈ 116 min ≈ ~2 hours. Because India uses a single IST, 'sunrise' in Arunachal is nearly 2 hours before Gujarat. This is why debates on dual-time-zones (IST-1 for NE, IST for the rest) keep recurring.

cards.front:
A point at latitude 0°, longitude 0° would be located in:

(A) Greenland
(B) Gulf of Guinea (off West Africa)
(C) Mid-Pacific Ocean
(D) Antarctic coast
cards.back:
(B) Gulf of Guinea (off West Africa)

World Geography — The intersection of 0° latitude (Equator) and 0° longitude (Prime Meridian) lies in the Gulf of Guinea, off the west coast of Africa — roughly south of Ghana. There's no land at exactly this point. The nearest named location is 'Null Island' — a virtual landmark popular in GIS / navigation datasets when something 'falls through' coordinate checks.

cards.front:
Each degree of longitude corresponds to a time difference of:

(A) 1 minute
(B) 4 minutes
(C) 10 minutes
(D) 60 seconds
cards.back:
(B) 4 minutes

World Geography — Earth rotates 360° in 24 hours → 360°/24 = 15° per hour → 15°/60 min = 1° per 4 minutes. So every 1° of longitude eastward adds 4 minutes to local time (and westward subtracts 4 minutes). 15° difference = 1 hour — the basis of standard time zones. Knowing this converts any longitude difference to a time difference.

cards.front:
The southernmost point of the Indian mainland is:

(A) Indira Point
(B) Kanyakumari (Cape Comorin)
(C) Rameswaram
(D) Thiruvananthapuram
cards.back:
(B) Kanyakumari (Cape Comorin)

World Geography — Kanyakumari (Cape Comorin) at ~8°4′ N is the southernmost tip of the Indian MAINLAND. The southernmost point of Indian TERRITORY is Indira Point on Great Nicobar Island (~6°45′ N). Indira Point was partially submerged by the 2004 tsunami. The northernmost point is Indira Col in the Siachen / Karakoram area.

The INDIAN STANDARD TIME (IST) is based on the meridian at:

(A) 77.5° E

The EQUATOR divides the Earth into:

(A) Eastern and Western hemispheres
(B) Northern and Southern hemispheres
(C) Arctic and Antarctic
(D) Old and New Worlds
cards.back:
(B) Northern and Southern hemispheres

World Geography — Equator (0° latitude) — divides Earth into Northern and Southern hemispheres. The Prime Meridian (0° longitude through Greenwich) + International Date Line (~180°) divide Eastern and Western hemispheres. Equator is ~40,075 km long.

cards.front:
The WORLD has how many STANDARD TIME ZONES?

(A) 12
(B) 24
(C) 15
(D) 360
cards.back:
(B) 24

World Geography — 24 main time zones (360°/15° each = 24, since Earth rotates 360° in 24 hr → 15°/hour). Some countries use half-hour / 45-min offsets (India = +5:30; Nepal = +5:45; Iran = +3:30). Russia: 11 zones. China: single zone despite wide longitude.

cards.front:
The INTERNATIONAL DATE LINE is approximately along:

(A) 0° longitude
(B) 180° longitude
(C) 23.5° N
(D) 66.5° S
cards.back:
(B) 180° longitude

World Geography — IDL — roughly 180° meridian, zig-zagging to keep island groups and countries on the same calendar date (Kiribati line, Chukotka). Cross IDL going east → lose a day. Going west → gain a day. with kinks to avoid splitting countries.

cards.front:
Which of the following pairs a WARM ocean current with its ocean correctly?

(A) Gulf Stream — North Pacific Ocean
(B) Kuroshio Current — North Pacific Ocean
(C) Benguela Current — North Atlantic Ocean
(D) Humboldt Current — Indian Ocean
cards.back:
(B) Kuroshio Current — North Pacific Ocean

World Geography — The Kuroshio Current (Japanese for 'Black Stream') is a warm current flowing north along the east coast of Japan in the NORTH PACIFIC — the Pacific analogue of the Gulf Stream. Distractors: Gulf Stream is in the North ATLANTIC (not Pacific); Benguela is a COLD current along South Africa in the South ATLANTIC (not North); Humboldt/Peru Current is a COLD current along South America in the PACIFIC (not Indian). Memorising the big 10-12 ocean currents by name, ocean, and temperature is a high-ROI Geography drill.

cards.front:
The Coriolis effect — arising from Earth's rotation — deflects ocean currents and wind patterns:

(A) To the LEFT in the Northern Hemisphere and to the RIGHT in the Southern Hemisphere
(B) To the RIGHT in the Northern Hemisphere and to the LEFT in the Southern Hemisphere
(C) To the right in both hemispheres
(D) Toward the equator in both hemispheres
cards.back:
(B) To the RIGHT in the Northern Hemisphere and to the LEFT in the Southern Hemisphere

World Geography — Coriolis deflection: RIGHT in the Northern Hemisphere, LEFT in the Southern Hemisphere. This is why gyres (large circular current systems) rotate CLOCKWISE in the N Hemisphere (North Atlantic, North Pacific) and ANTI-CLOCKWISE in the S Hemisphere (South Atlantic, South Pacific, Indian). This effect is stronger at higher latitudes and vanishes at the Equator (where the Coriolis parameter is zero). Useful mnemonic: 'Right-Northern' — R-N.

cards.option2: To the right in both hemispheres
cards.option3: Toward the equator in both hemispheres

cards.front:
Which of the following is a COLD ocean current flowing along the western coast of South America, known for supporting one of the world's most productive fisheries due to UPWELLING?

(A) Brazil Current
(B) Falkland (Malvinas) Current
(C) Peru (Humboldt) Current
(D) Canary Current
cards.back:
(C) Peru (Humboldt) Current

World Geography — The Peru Current (also called the Humboldt Current, after Alexander von Humboldt) is a COLD current flowing north along the western coast of South America. Easterly trade winds push surface water offshore, triggering upwelling of nutrient-rich deep water — this supports anchovy, sardine, and tuna fisheries. Peru is historically one of the world's top anchovy producers. During El Niño events, the upwelling weakens and the fishery collapses. Distractors: Brazil Current is a warm current on the EAST coast of South America; Falkland is cold but flows on the East (Atlantic) side too; Canary is off the West African coast.

cards.front:
Which of the following regions is known as 'Grand Banks' — one of the world's richest fishing grounds — and what oceanographic feature explains its productivity?

(A) Off the coast of California; meeting of the Alaska and California currents
(B) Off the coast of Newfoundland; confluence of the warm Gulf Stream and cold Labrador Current
(C) Off the coast of Peru; Humboldt Current upwelling alone
(D) Off the Great Australian Bight; meeting of the East Australian and West Australian currents
cards.back:
(B) Off the coast of Newfoundland; confluence of the warm Gulf Stream and cold Labrador Current

World Geography — The Grand Banks lies off the southeast coast of Newfoundland (Canada), where the warm Gulf Stream meets the cold LABRADOR Current. The temperature contrast creates nutrient mixing + plankton blooms that feed cod, halibut, haddock. The meeting also creates persistent fog (the 1912 Titanic struck an iceberg carried south by the Labrador Current in this zone). Peru supports a productive fishery from upwelling alone (option C), but it's a different geographic region. Options A and D describe plausible-sounding but incorrect current-pairings.

cards.option2: Off the coast of Peru; Humboldt Current upwelling alone
cards.option3: Off the Great Australian Bight; meeting of the East Australian and West Australian currents

cards.front:
Five major subtropical ocean gyres exist worldwide. Which of the following lists them CORRECTLY?

(A) North Atlantic, South Atlantic, North Pacific, South Pacific, Indian Ocean
(B) North Atlantic, Arctic, North Pacific, South Pacific, Southern Ocean
(C) Gulf of Mexico, Caribbean, Mediterranean, Red Sea, Indian Ocean
(D) North Atlantic, North Pacific, Indian Ocean, Antarctic, Arctic
cards.back:
(A) North Atlantic, South Atlantic, North Pacific, South Pacific, Indian Ocean

World Geography — The five major subtropical gyres are: North Atlantic, South Atlantic, North Pacific, South Pacific, and Indian Ocean (note: only ONE gyre in the Indian Ocean since it's bounded to the north by the Asian landmass — no North-Indian gyre as such). Arctic and Southern Oceans have their own circulation patterns but not the classical subtropical gyres. These gyres trap floating debris — the 'Great Pacific Garbage Patch' forms in the North Pacific Gyre. Knowing the five by name is a Geography GK staple.

cards.front:
Match each cold current with the continent whose coast it flows along, and select the correct pairing:
(i) Labrador Current — North America (east coast)
(ii) California Current — North America (west coast)
(iii) Benguela Current — Africa (west coast)
(iv) West Australian Current — Australia (west coast)

(A) Only (i) and (ii)
(B) Only (i), (ii), and (iii)
(C) All four (i), (ii), (iii), (iv)
(D) Only (ii) and (iv)
cards.back:
(C) All four (i), (ii), (iii), (iv)

World Geography — ALL four pairings are correct. Cold currents typically flow from the poles towards the equator along WESTERN coasts of continents (with Labrador as an exception — it flows along the NE coast of N. America). Memorisation pattern: Labrador (NA east) + California (NA west) + Peru/Humboldt (SA west) + Benguela (Africa west) + Canary (Africa west, N. hemisphere) + West Australian (Australia west) + Oyashio (east Russia/NE Asia). Pairing them with 'western coast of continent' gives students a rule rather than rote memorization.

cards.front:
The thermohaline circulation — or 'global ocean conveyor belt' — is driven primarily by variations in:

(A) Wind stress alone
(B) Water temperature (thermo-) and salinity (-haline)
(C) Tidal forces of the Moon and Sun
(D) Submarine volcanic activity
cards.back:
(B) Water temperature (thermo-) and salinity (-haline)

World Geography — 'Thermo-' (temperature) + 'haline' (salt content) — the name directly tells you the drivers. Cold, salty water (denser) sinks in polar regions (especially the North Atlantic near Greenland and the Southern Ocean near Antarctica); warm, less-salty water flows to replace it at the surface. This creates a slow (~1000-year cycle) global circulation connecting all the oceans. Wind-driven currents are a DIFFERENT system — they mainly affect the upper ~400m. Tidal and volcanic forces produce local effects but don't drive the global conveyor. Collapse of this system (e.g. from Arctic ice melt diluting N. Atlantic salinity) is a major climate-change concern.
cards.option2: Tidal forces of the Moon and Sun

cards.front:
The ENGLISH CHANNEL — specifically the Dover Strait — has one of the highest TIDAL RANGES in the world. What oceanographic phenomenon primarily causes this?

(A) The North Atlantic Drift flowing across it at high speed
(B) The funnel-shape of the Channel that amplifies tidal amplitudes as water is constrained laterally
(C) Constant submarine volcanic activity beneath the Channel
(D) The Coriolis effect alone at that latitude
cards.back:
(B) The funnel-shape of the Channel that amplifies tidal amplitudes as water is constrained laterally

World Geography — Tidal range is amplified where coastal geometry FUNNELS water — the Bay of Fundy (Canada) has the world's highest tidal range (~16m) for this reason; the English Channel narrowing into the Dover Strait similarly amplifies tides. As the tidal wave's cross-sectional area shrinks, its amplitude rises to conserve energy. The North Atlantic Drift warms the British Isles but does NOT cause tides. No volcanic activity in the Channel. Coriolis affects the shape of gyres but is not the primary driver of tidal range.

cards.option2: Constant submarine volcanic activity beneath the Channel
cards.option3: The Coriolis effect alone at that latitude

cards.front:
A SPRING TIDE — with the highest tidal range — occurs when:

(A) The Sun, Earth, and Moon are in a right angle (first and third quarter)
(B) The Sun, Earth, and Moon are in alignment (new moon or full moon)
(C) The Moon is farthest from Earth (apogee)
(D) Only during the spring equinox (20 March)
cards.back:
(B) The Sun, Earth, and Moon are in alignment (new moon or full moon)

World Geography — Spring tides occur when the Sun, Earth, and Moon are roughly in a straight line — at NEW MOON (syzygy) and FULL MOON. The Sun's tidal pull ADDS to the Moon's → higher high tides and lower low tides → maximum tidal range. NEAP tides occur when Sun-Earth-Moon form a right angle (first/third quarter) → solar pull CANCELS part of lunar pull → minimum tidal range. 'Spring' has nothing to do with the season; it refers to 'jumping up' (Old English). Apogee is when the Moon is farthest — reduces tidal amplitude (vs perigee, when the Moon is closest, amplifying it — 'perigean spring tides' are the highest of all).

cards.option2: The Moon is farthest from Earth (apogee)
cards.option3: Only during the spring equinox (20 March)

cards.front:
The Sargasso Sea — a unique area of the North Atlantic bounded by CURRENTS (not by land) — is enclosed by:

(A) The Gulf Stream, North Atlantic Current, Canary Current, and North Equatorial Current
(B) The Gulf Stream and Labrador Current only
(C) The Kuroshio and California Currents
(D) The Agulhas and Benguela Currents
cards.back:
(A) The Gulf Stream, North Atlantic Current, Canary Current, and North Equatorial Current

World Geography — The Sargasso Sea is bounded entirely by the four currents that make up the North Atlantic Gyre: Gulf Stream (west), North Atlantic Current (north), Canary Current (east), and North Equatorial Current (south). It's famous for: (i) floating Sargassum seaweed (its namesake); (ii) the spawning ground of Atlantic and European eels — they migrate thousands of km to spawn here; (iii) being the sea without a shore. Option B, C, D list currents from different gyres. Worth memorising as Geography's prime example of a sea defined by currents alone.

cards.front:
UPWELLING zones — where deep, cold, nutrient-rich water rises to the surface — typically occur along:

(A) EASTERN coasts of continents in the trade-wind belt
(B) WESTERN coasts of continents where trade winds push surface water offshore
(C) Middle of open oceans, far from any coast
(D) Polar coasts of Antarctica and Greenland only
cards.back:
(B) WESTERN coasts of continents where trade winds push surface water offshore

World Geography — Coastal upwelling occurs along the WESTERN coasts of continents in the trade-wind belt — Peru, California, Northwest Africa (Canary), Southwest Africa (Benguela), Western Australia. Trade winds (blowing equatorward along these coasts) combined with Ekman transport move surface water offshore, allowing deep cold water to replace it. These become exceptional fisheries and — less happily — are also regions of strong climate variability (El Niño, for instance, disrupts Peruvian upwelling). There ARE polar-ocean upwellings (Southern Ocean), but the classical coastal-upwelling pattern is the trade-wind-belt western-continent pattern.

cards.front:
El Niño — the periodic warming of the central/eastern tropical Pacific — DISRUPTS which ocean current, with major fisheries consequences?

(A) Kuroshio Current
(B) Peru (Humboldt) Current
(C) Agulhas Current
(D) North Atlantic Drift
cards.back:
(B) Peru (Humboldt) Current

World Geography — El Niño weakens the trade winds that normally drive upwelling along the Peru coast. The Peru/Humboldt Current — usually cold and nutrient-rich — is overlaid by a warm layer, suppressing upwelling and collapsing the anchovy fishery. The name 'El Niño' ('the boy child' in Spanish, referring to the Christ child) comes from Peruvian fishermen who noticed the warming usually peaked around Christmas. 'La Niña' is the opposite — intensified cold upwelling. Kuroshio, Agulhas, and North Atlantic Drift operate in different basins and aren't the primary El Niño target (though teleconnections exist — e.g. Indian monsoon variability).

cards.front:
Which of the following warm-water current systems is primarily responsible for the comparatively MILD winters of Northwestern Europe (compared with regions at the same latitude in North America)?

(A) Gulf Stream and its extension
(B) Kuroshio Current
(C) East Australian Current
(D) Agulhas Current
cards.back:
(A) Gulf Stream and its extension

World Geography — The Gulf Stream carries warm tropical water northward from the Gulf of Mexico; at around 40°N it becomes the North Atlantic Drift/Current, which warms air masses reaching Western Europe. This is why Britain (latitude ~55°N) has winters comparable to much milder latitudes in North America. Labrador (same latitude, eastern Canada) has a frigid winter due to cold Labrador Current. The Kuroshio warms Japan; East Australian warms NZ's east coast; Agulhas warms SE Africa — all parallel climate effects on their respective continents. the North Atlantic Drift (Current).

cards.front:
Which of the following is INCORRECT about ocean tides?

(A) The Sun's tidal influence is about 46% as strong as the Moon's
(B) Most coasts experience TWO high tides and two low tides approximately every 24 hours 50 minutes (semi-diurnal tides)
(C) The tidal wave moves at exactly the same speed as the Earth's rotation, maintaining alignment with the Moon at all times
(D) The Bay of Fundy in Canada records the world's highest tidal range (~16 m)
cards.back:
(C) The tidal wave moves at exactly the same speed as the Earth's rotation, maintaining alignment with the Moon at all times

World Geography — Statement C is INCORRECT — the tidal bulge does NOT keep perfect alignment with the Moon. Earth rotates faster than the tidal wave can travel (due to continents, friction, ocean depth), causing the bulge to lead the Moon by roughly 12° — this is why high tide often occurs a bit AFTER the Moon's highest point in the sky. Statements A, B, D are all correct: Sun's tidal force is ~46% of the Moon's (this is why spring tides are only ~20% higher than average, not doubled); semi-diurnal tides have a period of 24h 50min = lunar day; Bay of Fundy records 16.3m range — world's highest.

cards.front:
The Agulhas Current — flowing along the east coast of southern Africa — is notable in oceanography because it:

(A) Is the coldest current in the world
(B) Retroflects (curves back on itself) near the southern tip of Africa, occasionally shedding warm-water 'Agulhas rings' into the South Atlantic
(C) Flows from Antarctica to the Equator continuously without interruption
(D) Is responsible for the ice cover over Greenland
cards.back:
(B) Retroflects (curves back on itself) near the southern tip of Africa, occasionally shedding warm-water 'Agulhas rings' into the South Atlantic

World Geography — The Agulhas Current is a WARM, fast-flowing current along the southeast coast of Africa. It's famous for 'Agulhas retroflection' — near the southern tip of Africa, it curves sharply back eastward (rather than continuing into the South Atlantic), and occasionally sheds large eddies called 'Agulhas rings' that DO cross into the South Atlantic, carrying warm tropical water that contributes to the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation. This is an active research topic for climate models. Options A, C, D are fiction.

cards.option3: Is responsible for the ice cover over Greenland

cards.front:
The planetary winds that blow from SUB-TROPICAL HIGH toward the EQUATORIAL LOW are called:

(A) Westerlies
(B) Trade winds
(C) Polar easterlies
(D) Doldrums
cards.back:
(B) Trade winds

World Geography — Trade winds — NE trades (Northern Hemisphere) and SE trades (Southern Hemisphere) driven by Coriolis. Converge at ITCZ (Intertropical Convergence Zone) near equator = the Doldrums. Westerlies blow from 30°-60° toward the polar low. Polar easterlies from 90° toward 60°.

cards.front:
The deflection of winds and ocean currents due to Earth's rotation is caused by the:

(A) Gravitational force
(B) Coriolis force
(C) Centripetal force
(D) Magnetic force
cards.back:
(B) Coriolis force

World Geography — Coriolis effect — apparent force due to Earth's rotation. Deflects moving objects TO THE RIGHT in Northern Hemisphere, TO THE LEFT in Southern. Strongest at poles, zero at equator. Explains trade winds, cyclone rotation.

The meeting of warm and cold ocean currents near Newfoundland creates ideal conditions for:

(B) Dense fog and one of the world's richest fishing grounds

cards.back:

cards.front:
Under UNCLOS (1982), a coastal state's Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) extends from its shore baseline to a maximum of:

(A) 12 nautical miles (the territorial-sea limit)
(B) 200 nautical miles (about 370 km from the baseline)
(C) 350 nautical miles (only continental-shelf claim)
(D) 500 nautical miles (no such limit in UNCLOS)
cards.back:
(B) 200 nautical miles (about 370 km from the baseline)

World Geography — UNCLOS (United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, 1982) — defines maritime zones. Territorial sea: 12 nm (full sovereignty). Contiguous zone: 24 nm (limited control). EEZ: 200 nm (sovereign rights over economic resources — fishing, oil, gas, mining). Continental shelf: 200 nm or further if naturally extending (max 350 nm). India's EEZ ~ 2.3 million km² — among the world's largest. Distractor 1 = territorial sea. Distractor 3 = extended shelf claim cap. Distractor 4 = invented.

cards.front:
POLYMETALLIC NODULES on the deep-ocean floor are commercially valuable mainly for their content of:

(A) Gold, silver, platinum traces only
(B) Manganese, nickel, copper, cobalt
(C) Lithium, sodium, potassium salts
(D) Uranium and rare-earth elements only
cards.back:
(B) Manganese, nickel, copper, cobalt

World Geography — Polymetallic / manganese nodules — potato-sized rocks scattered on abyssal plains (~4-6 km depth). Composition: ~30% manganese, 1.3% nickel, 1.1% copper, 0.2% cobalt, plus iron + traces. Critical for batteries (Ni, Co), stainless steel (Mn), electronics. India has been allotted a 75,000 km² PMN exploration site in the Central Indian Ocean Basin (CIOB) by the International Seabed Authority — first developing country to get such allotment (1987). Deep-sea mining is technically feasible but environmentally controversial — ISA has not yet finalised commercial-extraction rules.

India's MAJOR offshore oil and gas field, accounting for ~40% of domestic production, is the:

The world's most productive marine fishing grounds typically occur where:

(B) Cold and warm currents meet over a continental shelf
(C) An equatorial current flows steadily eastward
(D) Coral reefs form along tropical island shores

Distractor 4 — coral reefs are biodiverse but small in total fish biomass compared to temperate shelves.

(A) South Atlantic Ocean near Antarctica
(B) Western Pacific Ocean east of the Philippines
(C) North Indian Ocean near Sri Lanka
(D) Arctic Ocean near the North Pole region
cards.back:

Other deep trenches: Tonga (~10,800 m), Philippine (~10,500 m), Java/Sunda (~7,400 m, deepest in Indian Ocean), Puerto Rico (~8,400 m, deepest in Atlantic).

cards.front:
The 'GARBAGE PATCH' in the North Pacific is primarily made up of:

(A) Floating logs from large-scale rainforest deforestation
(B) Tiny plastic fragments accumulated by ocean gyre currents
(C) Toxic chemical sludge from offshore oil-rig leaks
(D) Sunken cargo from container-ship spills near Hawaii
cards.back:
(B) Tiny plastic fragments accumulated by ocean gyre currents

World Geography — Great Pacific Garbage Patch — between Hawaii and California; ~1.6 million km² (~3× the size of France). Composed mostly of MICROPLASTICS (1-5 mm fragments) plus larger plastic debris, fishing nets, bottles. Concentrated by the North Pacific subtropical gyre — converging currents trap floating debris. The water is not solid garbage as often imagined; it's a 'plastic soup' with high concentrations. Five major ocean gyres globally — each has a similar garbage patch (Indian Ocean, North Atlantic, South Pacific, South Atlantic). Plastic enters the food chain via marine animals; ~80% of marine plastic comes from land-based sources, primarily rivers in developing countries.

Mercury also has 'Morning Star'/'Evening Star' visibility but is much dimmer and harder to spot.

cards.front:
Why is Mercury the hottest planet during the day but not on average?

(A) Because it rotates very slowly, but has no atmosphere to retain heat at night
(B) Because its orbit is elliptical and it is sometimes very far from the Sun
(C) Because it has thick clouds that reflect heat away
(D) Because it is made of ice
cards.back:
(A) Because it rotates very slowly, but has no atmosphere to retain heat at night

World Geography — Mercury has virtually NO atmosphere (exosphere only). So during the day, its surface reaches ~430°C (closer to Sun). At night, without any atmosphere to retain heat, temperatures plunge to ~−180°C. VENUS, despite being farther from the Sun, is the HOTTEST planet on average (surface ~465°C) due to its extreme CO₂ greenhouse effect. Mercury has very slow rotation (1 Mercury-day = 59 Earth-days) exposing each side to extreme temperatures.

cards.front:
When and why was Pluto reclassified as a 'dwarf planet'?

(A) In 2006 by IAU, because it failed to clear its orbital neighborhood of other objects
(B) In 1990 by NASA, because Voyager-2 found no atmosphere
(C) In 2012 by UN Space Committee, because of its small size alone
(D) In 2019 by Hubble Space Telescope, because of its elliptical orbit
cards.back:
(A) In 2006 by IAU, because it failed to clear its orbital neighborhood of other objects

World Geography — In August 2006, the International Astronomical Union (IAU) established three criteria for PLANET status: (1) orbits the Sun; (2) sufficient mass for hydrostatic equilibrium (spherical); (3) has cleared the neighborhood around its orbit. Pluto satisfies (1) and (2) but NOT (3) — its orbit is dominated by other Kuiper Belt objects, some larger than Pluto (e.g., Eris). It was thus reclassified as a 'dwarf planet'. Other dwarf planets: Eris, Haumea, Makemake, Ceres.

cards.front:
Which planet has a day (rotation) longer than its year (revolution)?

(A) Mercury
(B) Venus
(C) Mars
(D) Saturn
cards.back:
(B) Venus

World Geography — Venus's rotation period (sidereal day) is ~243 Earth-days, while its orbital period (year) is ~225 Earth-days. So a VENUSIAN DAY is LONGER than a VENUSIAN YEAR! Venus also rotates RETROGRADE (opposite to most planets) — meaning the Sun rises in the west and sets in the east on Venus. Mercury has a day of 59 Earth-days and year of 88 Earth-days (day < year).

The asteroid belt in our solar system lies between which two planets?

(A) Earth and Mars
(B) Mars and Jupiter
(C) Jupiter and Saturn
(D) Saturn and Uranus
cards.back:
(B) Mars and Jupiter

Jupiter's gravity prevented material in this region from coalescing into a planet. The KUIPER BELT (beyond Neptune) is a separate belt of icy bodies and the OORT CLOUD is a spherical shell of comets far beyond.

cards.front:
Which planet tilts on its side (axial tilt ~98°), causing extreme seasonal variations?

(A) Mars
(B) Neptune
(C) Uranus
(D) Saturn
cards.back:
(C) Uranus

World Geography — Uranus's axial tilt is ~98°, meaning its rotation axis is nearly in the plane of its orbit. As a result, each pole receives ~42 years of continuous sunlight followed by ~42 years of darkness — extreme seasons. Hypothesis: a massive early collision may have knocked Uranus on its side. Earth's tilt is 23.5°; Mars 25°; Saturn 27°; Neptune 28°.

cards.front:
The world's HIGHEST peak (8,848.86 m) and its location:

(A) K2 — Karakoram
(B) Mount Everest (Sagarmatha / Chomolungma) — Mahalangur Himal of the Himalayas, Nepal-China (Tibet) border
(C) Kanchenjunga — Sikkim-Nepal
(D) Mont Blanc — Alps
cards.back:
(B) Mount Everest (Sagarmatha / Chomolungma) — Mahalangur Himal of the Himalayas, Nepal-China (Tibet) border

World Geography — Mount Everest — height 8,848.86 m (revised from 8,848 m by joint Nepal-China survey, December 2020). Border peak — Sagarmatha (Nepali, head in the sky) / Chomolungma (Tibetan, mother goddess). Named after Sir George Everest (Surveyor General of India 1830-43). First confirmed summit — Edmund Hillary + Tenzing Norgay, 29 May 1953. K2 (Karakoram, Pakistan-China) — 8,611 m, 2nd highest, technically harder. Kanchenjunga — 8,586 m, India's HIGHEST peak (Sikkim-Nepal). Mont Blanc — Alps, only 4,807 m. 14 peaks > 8,000 m globally — all in Himalaya-Karakoram.

cards.front:
The LONGEST mountain range above sea level (~7,000 km along S America's western edge) is the:

(A) Himalayas
(B) Andes — runs through 7 countries (Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia, Chile, Argentina)
(C) Rockies
(D) Atlas
cards.back:
(B) Andes — runs through 7 countries (Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia, Chile, Argentina)

World Geography — Andes — longest continental range, ~7,000 km, S American Pacific coast. Highest peak — Aconcagua (Argentina, 6,961 m, highest outside Asia + tallest in Western Hemisphere). Born from convergence of Nazca + South American plates. Many active volcanoes (Cotopaxi, Chimborazo, Llaullaillaco). Longest UNDERWATER mountain range — the Mid-Atlantic Ridge (~16,000 km, mostly submerged). Rockies — ~4,800 km, N America. Himalayas — ~2,400 km only. Tallest mountain measured base-to-summit — Mauna Kea (Hawaii, 10,200 m from ocean floor).

cards.front:
The Himalayas are an example of:

(A) Block (fault) mountains
(B) Fold mountains (formed by collision of Indian + Eurasian plates ~50 Ma)
(C) Volcanic mountains
(D) Residual / dome mountains
cards.back:
(B) Fold mountains (formed by collision of Indian + Eurasian plates ~50 Ma)

World Geography — Fold mountains — sedimentary layers on the seabed get crumpled when continental plates collide. Indian plate began separating from Africa-Antarctica ~150 Ma, drifted north at ~15 cm/yr. Collided with Eurasian plate ~50 Ma — Tethys Sea closed; sediments piled up to form Himalayas. Still rising ~5 mm/year! Other fold mtns: Andes, Alps, Atlas, Urals, Rockies. BLOCK mountains — rift / horst-graben (Vosges, Rhine valley). VOLCANIC — Mount Fuji, Vesuvius, Kilimanjaro. RESIDUAL — Aravallis (oldest fold mtn, now eroded to remnants). DOME — Black Hills (Dakota).

cards.front:
The HIGHEST mountain in Africa, also a free-standing volcano:

(A) Mount Kenya
(B) Mount Kilimanjaro (5,895 m, in Tanzania) — dormant volcano
(C) Mount Ras Dashen (Ethiopia)
(D) Mount Stanley (Rwenzori)
cards.back:
(B) Mount Kilimanjaro (5,895 m, in Tanzania) — dormant volcano

World Geography — Kilimanjaro — Tanzania, 5,895 m. Stratovolcano with three cones (Kibo, Mawenzi, Shira). Largest free-standing mountain (rises ~5 km from surrounding plain). Snow-capped summit (the icecap is shrinking due to climate change — could disappear by 2040). Mount Kenya — 2nd highest in Africa, 5,199 m. Other notable peaks: Mt Damavand (Iran, 5,610 m, highest in Middle East); Vinson Massif (Antarctica, 4,892 m); Mt Kosciuszko (Australia, 2,228 m, highest in Australia mainland; 'Seven Summits' challenge sometimes uses Mt Carstensz Pyramid in Indonesia at 4,884 m as the Oceania peak).

cards.front:
K2 (the world's 2nd highest peak) is in which mountain range?

(A) Himalayas
(B) Karakoram (Pakistan-administered Kashmir / Xinjiang border)
(C) Alps
(D) Hindu Kush
cards.back:
(B) Karakoram (Pakistan-administered Kashmir / Xinjiang border)

World Geography — K2 (Mt Godwin-Austen / Chhogori) — 8,611 m, in the Karakoram range. India claims it as part of its territory (Pak-occupied Kashmir, Gilgit-Baltistan). 'K2' from the British Survey of India numbering — K1 = Masherbrum, K3 = Broad Peak. First summited 1954 (Italian expedition Lacedelli + Compagnoni). One of the deadliest 8000ers — climber fatality rate ~25%. Karakoram = 4 of the 14 eight-thousanders (K2, Gasherbrum I, II, Broad Peak). Plus Nanga Parbat (Himalaya, Gilgit-Baltistan), Kanchenjunga, Lhotse, Makalu, Annapurna … all 14 are in Pakistan, India, Nepal, China, with 8 in Nepal.

cards.front:
The Aravalli range — running ~700 km from Gujarat through Rajasthan to Delhi — is famous as:

(A) World's youngest mountain range
(B) One of the oldest fold mountain ranges on Earth (~3.5 billion years)
(C) Active volcanic chain
(D) Block mountains
cards.back:
(B) One of the oldest fold mountain ranges on Earth (~3.5 billion years)

World Geography — Aravallis — formed in the Proterozoic (~3.5 Ga, earlier estimates 700 Ma), ancient Precambrian fold mountains. Have eroded substantially — current highest peak Guru Shikhar (Mt Abu, 1,722 m). Function as a critical biogeographic barrier — separating Thar Desert from Gangetic plains. Acts as 'green wall' protecting NCR. Mining + sand quarrying in Rajasthan — major environmental damage; SC banned mining in protected stretches. Compare Western Ghats (~150 Ma, much younger), Eastern Ghats (similar age to Aravallis but different orogeny), Himalayas (~50 Ma, youngest).

(A) Mount Aconcagua — South America

Reinhold Messner's list uses Carstensz; original Bass list uses Kosciuszko.

cards.front:
The largest ocean in the world (by area) is the:

(A) Atlantic Ocean
(B) Pacific Ocean
(C) Indian Ocean
(D) Arctic Ocean
cards.back:
(B) Pacific Ocean

World Geography — Pacific Ocean covers ~165 million km² — larger than all land on Earth combined. Five recognised oceans (WMO / IHO 2000) — Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern (around Antarctica), Arctic. The Southern Ocean was officially recognised as the fifth ocean by the IHO in 2000 (the US Board on Geographic Names followed in 2021).

cards.front:
The deepest point in the world's oceans, the 'Challenger Deep', is located in the:

(A) Puerto Rico Trench
(B) Mariana Trench
(C) Java Trench
(D) Peru-Chile Trench
cards.back:
(B) Mariana Trench

World Geography — The Mariana Trench in the western Pacific contains the Challenger Deep — the deepest known point (~10,984 m, measured by the Deep Sea Challenger in 2012). If Mt Everest were placed in the trench, its peak would still be under 2,000 m of water. Puerto Rico Trench is the deepest in the Atlantic (~8,376 m); Java/Sunda Trench the deepest in the Indian Ocean (~7,258 m); Peru-Chile / Atacama Trench is along the eastern Pacific.

cards.front:
The Strait of Malacca — one of the world's busiest shipping lanes — separates:

(A) Oman and Iran
(B) Malaysia and Indonesia's Sumatra
(C) Saudi Arabia and Africa
(D) Cuba and Florida
cards.back:
(B) Malaysia and Indonesia's Sumatra

World Geography — Strait of Malacca — ~800 km long, 65 km wide at its narrowest — connects the Indian Ocean (Andaman Sea) to the Pacific (South China Sea). Separates Peninsular Malaysia and Singapore from Sumatra, Indonesia. ~25 % of global seaborne trade and ~40 % of Asia's oil passes through it. Other strategic straits — Hormuz (Oman-Iran, 20 % of global oil), Bab-el-Mandeb (Red Sea-Gulf of Aden), Bosphorus (Black Sea-Mediterranean).

Match the ocean current with the ocean where it flows. A. Gulf Stream. B. Kuroshio. C. Humboldt. D. Agulhas. List-II: 1. North Atlantic, 2. North Pacific, 3. South Pacific, 4. Indian Ocean (off SE Africa).

(A) A-1, B-2, C-3, D-4
(B) A-2, B-1, C-3, D-4
(C) A-1, B-3, C-2, D-4
(D) A-4, B-2, C-3, D-1

Agulhas — warm, Indian Ocean (off Mozambique/South Africa). Other key currents — Labrador (cold, NW Atlantic), Canary (cold, E Atlantic), Benguela (cold, W Africa), California (cold).

cards.front:
The 'Dead Sea', famous for its extreme salinity, is bordered by:

(A) Egypt and Saudi Arabia
(B) Israel, Palestine and Jordan
(C) Turkey and Syria
(D) Iran and Iraq
cards.back:
(B) Israel, Palestine and Jordan

World Geography — Dead Sea — a landlocked hypersaline lake (not strictly a 'sea') bordered by Israel/Palestine on the west and Jordan on the east. Salinity ~34 % (~10× ocean). Its surface is ~430 m below sea level — the lowest land point on Earth. Shrinking rapidly (~1 m/year) due to water diversion of the Jordan river, its main feeder.

cards.front:
The International Date Line runs mostly along which meridian?

(A) 0°
(B) 180°
(C) 90°E
(D) 90°W
cards.back:
(B) 180°

World Geography — The International Date Line runs mostly along 180° longitude in the Pacific, zig-zagging around nations (Kiribati, Samoa) so that island groups stay in one calendar day. Crossing the IDL westwards, add a day; eastwards, subtract a day. 0° is the Prime Meridian (through Greenwich). 90°W crosses New Orleans; 90°E passes through Bangladesh / Tibet.

cards.front:
The 'Sargasso Sea' — unique because it is a sea without coastlines on any side — lies within the:

(A) Indian Ocean
(B) North Atlantic
(C) South Pacific
(D) Arctic Ocean
cards.back:
(B) North Atlantic

World Geography — Sargasso Sea — bounded not by land but by four ocean currents of the North Atlantic gyre (Gulf Stream, North Atlantic, Canary, North Atlantic Equatorial Current). Calm, warm, relatively motionless waters full of 'sargassum' seaweed. Spawning ground for European and American eels. Famous for the 'Bermuda Triangle' legend (the Sargasso Sea surrounds Bermuda).

(A) Singapore
(B) South Africa
(C) Saudi Arabia
(D) Sri Lanka
cards.back:

The New Development Bank (NDB) is headquartered in Shanghai.

cards.front:
Which of the following is NOT a member of OPEC (Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries)?

(A) Saudi Arabia
(B) India
(C) Iran
(D) Venezuela
cards.back:

World Geography — OPEC — 13 founding / continuing members (as of 2024) — Saudi Arabia, Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Venezuela (founding 5, 1960) + Algeria, Libya, Nigeria, UAE, Gabon, Equatorial Guinea, Congo, and others. India is a net oil importer, not a producer-exporter of any scale — and not an OPEC member. OPEC+ (since 2016) is a broader grouping that includes Russia, Kazakhstan, Mexico and others.

(A) The lotus
(B) The peacock

cards.front:
NATO (North Atlantic Treaty Organisation) was founded in which year in response to the Cold War?

(A) 1945
(B) 1949
(C) 1955
(D) 1961
cards.back:
(B) 1949

World Geography — NATO was established on 4 April 1949 by the North Atlantic Treaty (Washington Treaty). Originally 12 members; now 32 (Finland joined 2023, Sweden 2024). HQed in Brussels. Core principle — Article 5, collective defence (an attack on one is an attack on all), invoked only once (after 9/11, 2001). Warsaw Pact (the Soviet-led counter) was founded in 1955 and dissolved in 1991.

India is a founding member of which regional economic grouping formed in 1985?

(A) ASEAN
(B) SAARC
(C) APEC
(D) NAFTA
cards.back:
(B) SAARC

cards.front:
The LONGEST MOUNTAIN RANGE on Earth (above water) is the:

(A) Himalayas (~2,400 km)
(B) Rocky Mountains (~4,800 km)
(C) ANDES of South America (~7,000 km) — longest continental range running along 7 countries from Venezuela to Argentina
(D) Alps (~1,200 km)
cards.back:
(C) ANDES of South America (~7,000 km) — longest continental range running along 7 countries from Venezuela to Argentina

World Geography — LONGEST CONTINENTAL MOUNTAIN RANGE — the ANDES (~7,000 km / 4,300 mi) along WEST coast of SOUTH AMERICA; passes through 7 countries (from north to south): VENEZUELA, COLOMBIA, ECUADOR, PERU, BOLIVIA, CHILE, ARGENTINA. Formed by SUBDUCTION of the NAZCA plate beneath the SOUTH AMERICAN plate. HIGHEST peak: ACONCAGUA (Argentina, 6,961 m) — also highest peak OUTSIDE Asia; LOCATION of high-altitude civilisations (Inca, capital Cusco at 3,400 m); LAKE TITICACA (Bolivia-Peru border at 3,812 m — highest navigable lake). Passes: include ATACAMA DESERT (driest on Earth) to the west. NOTE: Technically the LONGEST MOUNTAIN RANGE on Earth is the MID-OCEANIC RIDGE (~65,000 km, mostly UNDERWATER); but the question specifies 'above water' / continental. HIMALAYAS (~2,400 km) — highest, not longest. ROCKIES of North America (~4,800 km, USA-Canada) — second-longest continental. Other major ranges: ALPS (Europe, 1,200 km), URALS (Russia, 2,500 km — divides Europe & Asia), ATLAS (Africa), SIERRA MADRE (Mexico), DRAKENSBERG (S. Africa), GREAT DIVIDING RANGE (Australia).

Passes: include ATACAMA DESERT (driest on Earth) to the west. NOTE: Technically the LONGEST MOUNTAIN RANGE on Earth is the MID-OCEANIC RIDGE (~65,000 km, mostly UNDERWATER); but the question specifies 'above water' / continental. HIMALAYAS (~2,400 km) — highest, not longest. ROCKIES of North America (~4,800 km, USA-Canada) — second-longest continental. Other major ranges: ALPS (Europe, 1,200 km), URALS (Russia, 2,500 km — divides Europe & Asia), ATLAS (Africa), SIERRA MADRE (Mexico), DRAKENSBERG (S. Africa), GREAT DIVIDING RANGE (Australia).

cards.front:
The DEEPEST point in the world's oceans is CHALLENGER DEEP, located in the:

(A) Puerto Rico Trench (Atlantic)
(B) MARIANA TRENCH in the Pacific Ocean — ~10,984 m (36,037 ft) deep; east of the Mariana Islands near Guam
(C) Tonga Trench (Pacific)
(D) Java Trench (Indian)
cards.back:
(B) MARIANA TRENCH in the Pacific Ocean — ~10,984 m (36,037 ft) deep; east of the Mariana Islands near Guam

World Geography — MARIANA TRENCH — crescent-shaped depression in the WESTERN PACIFIC OCEAN; east of the MARIANA ISLANDS (near Guam); ~2,550 km long, ~69 km wide. DEEPEST POINT: CHALLENGER DEEP (southern end), measured ~10,984 m (36,037 ft) below sea level — deeper than Mount Everest (8,849 m) is tall. If you put Everest at its bottom, it would still be submerged by >2 km of water. NAMED after the British Royal Navy ship HMS CHALLENGER (1872-76 expedition, first sounded the depth at 8,184 m — far short of actual). FORMED by subduction of the PACIFIC PLATE beneath the PHILIPPINE plate. FIRST MANNED DESCENT: JACQUES PICCARD (Swiss) and DON WALSH (US Navy) in 1960 aboard the bathyscaphe TRIESTE — reached 10,911 m. 2012: JAMES CAMERON (filmmaker) solo descent in DEEPSEA CHALLENGER submersible. 2019: VICTOR VESCOVO in LIMITING FACTOR — recorded 10,927 m. Temperature near bottom: ~1-4°C. Pressure: 1086 bars (~1072 atm) — over 1000 times surface atmospheric pressure. Life exists even here — microbes, amphipods, snailfish. OTHER DEEP TRENCHES: Tonga Trench (10,882 m), Philippine Trench (10,540 m), Kuril-Kamchatka, Kermadec, Puerto Rico (Atlantic, 8,376 m — deepest of Atlantic), Java/Sunda (Indian Ocean, 7,290 m — deepest of Indian).

cards.front:
The LARGEST DESERT in the world (by area) is the:

(A) Sahara Desert (~9.2 million sq km, North Africa)
(B) Arabian Desert (~2.3 million sq km)
(C) ANTARCTIC DESERT (~14.2 million sq km) — cold desert; a ‘desert’ is defined by low precipitation (<250 mm/year), not by heat
(D) Gobi Desert (~1.3 million sq km, Mongolia-China)
cards.back:
(C) ANTARCTIC DESERT (~14.2 million sq km) — cold desert; a ‘desert’ is defined by low precipitation (<250 mm/year), not by heat

World Geography — BY SCIENTIFIC DEFINITION — a ‘desert’ is an area receiving LESS THAN 250 mm (10 in) of annual precipitation, NOT necessarily hot. By that metric: LARGEST DESERT on Earth = ANTARCTIC POLAR DESERT, ~14.2 MILLION sq km (5.5 million sq mi); covers the entire continent of Antarctica; receives only 50-200 mm equivalent precipitation as snow per year. 2nd-largest: ARCTIC DESERT (~13.7 million sq km). 3rd: SAHARA (~9.2 million sq km, NORTH AFRICA — largest HOT desert). RANKING of large HOT deserts: SAHARA > ARABIAN (2.3M, Arabian peninsula) > GOBI (1.3M, Mongolia-China) > KALAHARI (0.93M, Southern Africa) > PATAGONIAN (0.67M, Argentina-Chile) > GREAT VICTORIA (0.65M, Australia) > GREAT BASIN (0.49M, USA) > SYRIAN > CHIHUAHUAN > THAR (Great Indian, 0.2M — India-Pakistan). INDIA’S THAR covers W Rajasthan, parts of Gujarat, and across border into Sindh, Pakistan — 7th-largest SUBTROPICAL desert. DRIEST place on Earth (lowest recorded precipitation): ATACAMA DESERT (northern Chile) — some regions haven’t received rain in 400+ years; cold-current effect from Humboldt current. HOTTEST (record): FURNACE CREEK, DEATH VALLEY (California) — 56.7°C (10 July 1913, disputed); LUT DESERT (Iran) — surface temp 70.7°C by satellite.
cards.option1: Sahara Desert (~9.2 million sq km, North Africa)
cards.option3: Gobi Desert (~1.3 million sq km, Mongolia-China)
